News.title: Royal Mail message to anyone who still writes address on envelope in pen
News.content:
Royal Mail message to anyone who still writes address on envelope in pen

People are urged to follow certain guidelines when posting a letter with a handwritten address

View 3 Images The Royal Mail has guidelines for people to follow if they write on envelopes and parcels by hand (stock image) (Image: Getty)

Royal Mail has a message to anyone who writes addresses on parcels or envelopes and posts them through a letterbox. The Royal Mail is said to handle up to 6.6 billion letters each year, so following general guidelines and advice can help avoid delays and delivery issues.

‌



Writing a clear and readable address on an envelope is crucial for Royal Mail, as it helps its automated sorting machines to quickly read and process the mail. Having clear, well-formatted, and left-aligned text minimises sorting errors, reduces delivery delays, and ensures your letter arrives at the right place rather than getting lost or sent back.

‌



In advice shared to customers on the Royal Mail website, it says: "Use clear and easy to read handwriting (or font if you are printing the address). Use a pen or ink that is clear against the colour of the envelope or parcel."

‌



Royal Mail does not ban a specific type of pen. However, it requires customers to use a pen or ink colour that creates a strong, clear contrast against the colour of the envelope or parcel.

Use an ink colour that stands out sharply so sorting machines and postal workers can read the address easily. Royal Mail specifically suggests using black ink for optimal readability, especially on lighter surfaces or labels. It says: "It's important that the address shows up against the colour of your envelope. (Tip - stick on a white label with black ink.)"

View 3 Images How to address your mail – clear addressing tips (stock image) (Image: Getty )

‌



It recommends avoiding light or faded ink colours (such as light grey, pale yellow, or faint pink) that blend into the envelope's background. Also, avoid using writing tools that smear or blur easily when handled during automated sorting.

The Royal Mail adds: "Write the address clearly on the front, following our guidelines, and always include a postcode if possible. You can search for up to 50 postcodes or addresses, free of charge, with our Postcode Finder."

How should Royal Mail customers address their letters and parcels?

The name and address go on the bottom left corner of the front of the envelope or parcel.

Use clear and easy to read handwriting (or font if you are printing the address).

Use a pen or ink that is clear against the colour of the envelope or parcel.

Left align the text (no centred or 'stepped' lines).

No commas or full stops.

Leave a generous margin around the address.

Place the correct postage on the top right.

‌



View 3 Images These guidelines show the best way to address your mail for fast delivery in the UK and abroad (stock image)

How can Royal Mail customers write an address correctly?

For the top lines, the Royal Mail explains: "Write or print the name of the person (or people) you are sending to on the first line, above the address. It's best to include their surname as well as their first name. You can add a line for an organisation name."

For the middle lines, the Royal Mail says: "Use a line for the property number and street name. If the property has a full name, this can take up one line and drop the street name onto the next line. On the following line, you can put the name of the local area or village name.

Article continues below

"Next, write the name of the town in capital letters. You don't need to include a county name, as your letters and parcels will still reach the right place. However, you can include it if you prefer."

The final line should be the UK postcode, again in capital letters. After the area code, add the country name to the final line, again in capital letters for international destinations.

News.title: 'I know my mate’s a cheat and now I’m feeling guilty'
News.content:
Dear Coleen,

I’m a man in my early 30s and have a good mate who’s doing his best to blow his life up at the moment. He drinks too much, gets into scrapes and the other night he confessed he’d slept with a co-worker, even though he’s in a long-term relationship with the loveliest girl, who’s also an old friend of mine.

I don’t think he’s got a drink problem per se, but he’s acting like he’s 18 and back at uni, even though he’s 32. I think part of it is his new job and he’s trying to keep up with or impress his new, younger colleagues.

I know talking to him is pointless because I’ve tried, but I feel I owe it to his girlfriend to say something. I care about her and feel she ought to be put in the picture. I only know about him sleeping with this one woman, but there might be others he’s not told me about.

View 2 Images The reader says: "I’m pretty disgusted by his behaviour and don’t want his girlfriend to get hurt." (Image: Getty Images)

‌



I’m pretty disgusted by his behaviour and don’t want his girlfriend to get hurt. All my female friends think I should say something to her, but I don’t know. What do you think?

Coleen says,

You should try talking to him again and this time explain he’s put you in a difficult position because his girlfriend is your friend, too, and you don’t want to see her get hurt. Be honest in terms of how you feel about his behaviour.

As far as telling her goes, it’s often a case of “shoot the messenger”, so be aware of that. She could be devastated and cry in your arms, then make up with her boyfriend and you’re kicked to the kerb.

It’s also worth reminding him that his girlfriend might find out because these things usually come to light at some point.

‌



Not everyone is discreet and gossip spreads. And you should also tell him that if it happens again, you don’t want to know about it. Maybe his younger colleagues are impressed, but you’re not.

I lost good friends because of this situation. They worked with my husband, who was having an affair, and suddenly they stopped coming over for Sunday dinner, which confirmed my suspicions that something was going on.

When I spoke to them after it came out, they explained they couldn’t tell me but, equally, they couldn’t sit at my table pretending everything was OK. I respected them for that. So, another thing you could do is not sit at their table.

News.title: Manhunt launched after 'shooting' in Wales village as chopper scrambled
News.content:
Manhunt launched after 'shooting' in Wales village as chopper scrambled

Police are hunting for suspect following reports of a shooting at a property in south Wales, which left the victim with minor injuries

View Image A manhunt has been launched after reports of a shooting in a south Wales village. (Image: Google Maps)

A manhunt is underway following reports of a shooting in a remote village in south Wales.

‌



Police rushed to the scene in the Laleston area of Bridgend shortly before 8pm on Monday evening with a police helicopter spotted circling over the town. A man is said to have suffered minor injuries during the incident.

‌



A police spokesperson confirmed officers were responding to reports of a shooting. A 29-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of affray and being in possession of an air weapon with intent to endanger life. She remains in police custody.

‌



Police are still hunting for a second suspect, Wales Online reports.

A police spokesperson said: "South Wales Police was called at 7.55pm on Tuesday, August 4, to reports of a shooting at an address in Laleston, Bridgend.

Article continues below

"A 29-year-old woman from Bridgend has been arrested on suspicion of affray and being in possession of an air weapon with intent to endanger life and remains in police custody.

"A man suffered minor injuries because of the incident, investigations into the incident are ongoing.”

News.title: Body found in search for boy, 13, missing at sea off coast of Hornsea
News.content:
Body found in search for boy, 13, missing at sea off coast of Hornsea

A body has been found in the search for a 13-year-old boy who went missing off the coast of Hornsea in East Yorkshire

View 2 Images The boy got into difficulty while swimming off the coast of Hornsea, East Yorkshire (Image: Kevin Allitt/PA Wire)

A body has been found in the search for a 13-year-old boy who went missing off the coast of East Yorkshire.

‌



Emergency services were called to Hornsea at about 6pm on Tuesday following concerns for the safety of a boy who was swimming in the sea off the South Promenade area.

‌



"Upon attending, it was discovered that a 13-year-old boy had reportedly got into difficulty whilst swimming in the water," Chief Superintendent Phil Booker, of Humberside Police, said.

‌



Police launched an "extensive search and rescue operation" was launched to locate the boy, involving HM Coastguard, Hornsea Inshore Rescue and the RNLI.

View 2 Images The incident happened less than 20 miles from where 15-year-old Grace Keeling was swept out to sea in January (Image: Getty Images)

The force has since confirmed that the child's body has been found.

‌



Ch Supt Booker said: "This is an incredibly heartbreaking outcome, and our thoughts are with the boy's family and friends at this devastating time."

Footage and photographs taken at the scene showed a lifeboat on the sea and an HM Coastguard helicopter circling above.

The incident happened less than 20 miles from where 15-year-old Grace Keeling was swept out to sea in January.

‌



Grace died at Withernsea beach alongside her mother, Sarah Keeling, 45, and local man Mark Ratcliffe, 67, who entered the water to help her but immediately got into difficulty themselves, an inquest heard in May.

The search for Grace’s body lasted 13 days before it was found trapped among giant boulders used as sea defences to the south of where the incident occurred.

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

Article continues below

That includes compulsory water safety lessons in schools, a nationwide public awareness campaign, better life-saving equipment at high-risk waterways, the introduction of Sam's Law, and a dedicated Minister for Water Safety. Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Alert as rule change means 864,000 in UK face new HMRC deadline on Friday
News.content:
Alert as rule change means 864,000 in UK face new HMRC deadline on Friday

A new system is now in place and with it comes a new August 7, 2026, deadline

View 3 Images HMRC is bringing in new rules gradually (Image: Pexels)

New HMRC rules mean around 864,000 taxpayers in the UK face an August deadline for the first time this week.

‌



Making Tax Digital is being phased in by HMRC and a key change means that those who do their own tax returns now have to do quarterly submissions. Those with a turnover over £50,000 in the 2024/25 tax year should be using MTD as of April 6, 2026. This group is affected by this week's new deadline of Friday, August 7, 2026.

‌



The rule changes are being phased in year by year. That means those who had a turnover of more than £30,000 in the 2025/26 tax year will need to use MTD from April 6, 2027. Those who were over £20,000 in the 2026/27 tax year will need to use it from April 6, 2028.

‌



View 3 Images Self assessment is changing (Image: PaulMaguire via Getty Images)

Kevin Mountford, personal finance expert and co-founder of Raisin UK, said: “With just a couple of days remaining until the August 7 Making Tax Digital deadline, the 864,000 sole traders and landlords affected should act now. They need to use HMRC-recognised accounting or bookkeeping software to total the income and expenses held in their digital records, and send that summary directly to HMRC.

"Anyone relying on an accountant should check that the update has been submitted on their behalf. Some taxpayers may be putting the task off because they are unsure what information is needed or whether their records are complete, but the simplest first step is to log into their accounting software, check that their income and expenses are up to date and contact their accountant or software provider immediately if anything is unclear.

‌



“Although HMRC will not issue penalties for missing a quarterly update during the first year, delaying it could create a bigger administrative and financial headache later. Taxpayers must still submit the outstanding updates before they can complete their annual tax return, so allowing them to build up risks and turning a manageable quarterly task into a last-minute scramble.

"Taking a few minutes now to check what has been recorded and what still needs to be submitted can provide greater clarity and prevent uncertainty from building. That clarity is particularly valuable when confidence around money is already low. Raisin UK’s Closing the Confidence Savings Gap research found that half (50%) of UK adults feel their finances are under pressure and just over half (53%) have less money to spend freely than they did 12 months ago.

View 3 Images There is no choice and it's a legal requirement (Image: Alamy/PA)

Article continues below

"For sole traders and landlords managing fluctuating incomes, falling behind on tax reporting can add another layer of uncertainty at a time when many already feel they have little financial breathing room. The predicted tax bill generated through the new system should therefore be treated as a prompt to plan, not simply a figure to review.

"Setting aside money regularly in a separate easy-access savings account can help taxpayers avoid spending funds that will eventually be owed to HMRC, while allowing that money to earn interest until the bill is due.

"Used properly, quarterly reporting could help replace one large January shock with smaller, more manageable financial decisions throughout the year.”

News.title: German airport shuts runway down as 'drone carrying detonator' spotted
News.content:
German airport shuts runway down as 'drone carrying detonator' spotted

Investigators have been called in after a drone thought to be carrying a detonator was spotted at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany

View Image The runway at Leipzig/Halle Aiport was closed (file) (Image: Education Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

An airport in Germany was forced to close its runway after a drone carrying what appears to be a detonator was found close to a Ukrainian aircraft.

‌



The drone, which has been deemed a possible explosive device by investigators, was found at Leipzig/Halle Airport late last night.

‌



The device was found close to a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane causing the airport’s southern runway to be closed while experts examined the object using explosives-disposal methods.

‌



There are also reports of an unidentified flying object with possible links to last night’s incident which are currently being investigated by authorities.

A DHL cargo plane was forced to abort its landing at the airport after the runway was closed. It then collided with an unidentified object about 400 metres above the ground, roughly six kilometres from the airport, reports claim. Damage to the plane was discovered after it landed safely at Hanover.

‌



There have been a string of unauthorised drone flights in recent weeks at sites across Germany including military installations, seaports, logistics hubs and energy infrastructure - with airports placed on high alert.

A bomb disposal squad was dispatched to Leipzig/Halle Airport at around midnight shortly after the drone was discovered.

Attached to the drone was a mass, which has been identified as explosive material, containing a detonator. The explosive was defective, however, so the bomb did not go off, Bild reports.

Article continues below

Following earlier reports that German Federal Police planned a remotely controlled detonation of the object, local media now saw that the drone and package will be placed in a special container so it can be examined for possible evidence.

NATO investigators also intend to participate in the investigation.

Four Ukrainian aircraft were said to be in the immediate vicinity of the drone bomb. Investigations are still underway at the airport, with no disruption to passenger flights, German media reports.

News.title: Police chief considers joining legal action over PC Harper killers' early release
News.content:
The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and is not eligible for early release.

Speaking on the Today programme, Thames Valley Police chief Jason Hogg urged the government to reconsider its position.

Only prisoners convicted of murder, rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from the scheme in England and Wales - while those convicted of manslaughter remain eligible.

"I fully understand the challenges around the crisis in the prison system," he said.

"But the decision made and where that line has been drawn, I do not believe that people responsible for taking the life of another citizen in our country should be released early."

He said on Wednesday: "I was informed yesterday that the Police Federation are considering legal action, I am in discussions with the Police Federation with regards to this matter".

Asked whether this meant he would join them, he said: "I think we need to get some legal advice in relation to this. This is something I certainly would consider."

After campaigning by PC Harper's wife Lissie following his death, Parliament passed "Harper's Law", which gives mandatory life sentences to the killers of emergency services workers. It doubles the maximum penalty from 12 months to two years for those who assault police or other emergency workers.

But the new rules - introduced in 2022 - did not apply in the sentencing of the police officer's killers, and so do not prevent them from being released early.

Hogg said: "The law isn't retrospective and we all understand that, but the fact that they are released early simply seems perverse."

Aileen O'Connor, branch chair of Thames Valley Police Federation also told the BBC her organisation was considering legal action.

"We are in talks this morning, I'll get an update this afternoon whether that is an avenue that we can explore and if it is an avenue we can explore then I'll get behind that 110%," she told BBC Breakfast.

As for what shape a potential legal challenge might take, she said: "Ultimately that's for the specialists, the barristers and those in that legal sector to make that decision whether there is a challenge there.

"If there is a challenge then we will look to take that challenge."

Sentencing Minister Jake Richards told the BBC it would be wrong to pick out individual cases and block two of PC Harper's killers from early release.

Although the government had reviewed what sentences would be excluded from the early release scheme, he confirmed "manslaughter is not one of those offences".

Richards said: "It would be wrong to pick out individual cases within different offending cohorts. That wouldn't be right. It wouldn't be lawful either. So it is correct that those two individuals will be subject to the new regime from October".

On Tuesday Justice Secretary Alex Norris warned a prison capacity crisis would be likely if fewer prisoners were allowed early release.

Norris apologised to families who would be affected by the early release scheme and stressed that the government wanted to go further "but we cannot".

"We have to make this decision, we've been able to make some changes to it, but we have to have the rest of the sentencing act changes otherwise we run out of prison places in November and that can't happen," he said.

The justice secretary said 5,000 extra releases will take place in 10 batches from October.

Approximately 1,000 prisoners will now not be released early following the revision to the scheme, he clarified.

The government also announced an extra Â£10m will go to front-line victim support services, including a new national helpline.

News.title: Ex-MP urges Tories to block council candidate jailed for antisemitic abuse against her
News.content:
A former Labour MP has said the Conservatives should not allow a former neo-Nazi who was jailed for antisemitic abuse against her to stand as a local election candidate.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine was convicted of racially harassing Luciana Berger, who is Jewish, in 2016, while already serving a separate jail sentence for sharing antisemitic posts.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has defended the decision to select him as a candidate in Somerset, saying that while his crimes were "appalling" he had been rehabilitated and was now "part of the fight against antisemetism".

But Baroness Berger said he should be barred from standing for public office - and Jewish groups have rejected a Tory invite to meet him.

Baroness Berger said Bonehill-Paine's harassment "affected my life in lots of different ways because of the volume of the material that he was disseminating and putting out, the extremity of it in terms of just frankly how shocking and awful it was".

The Labour peer added: "I think that we need to have a bar when it comes to standing for public office.

"I strongly believe that this individual today falls very, very short of that."

Bonehill-Paine spent three years in prison after he was jailed in 2015 for posting antisemitic material ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally.

A year later in 2016, he was convicted of racially harassing then-Labour MP Berger, a former shadow cabinet minister who is now a member of the House of Lords.

Baroness Berger attended court at the OId Bailey in London to give evidence in the trial of Bonehill-Paine.

In a Substack article, Baroness Berger said Bonehill-Paine had shown "no contrition" throughout the trial and claimed that at one point "he performed a full Nazi salute to his supporters in the public gallery".

"It told me everything I needed to know about how this individual saw the world, and about the utter contempt he held for the people he targeted," Baroness Berger wrote.

In sentencing remarks, the judge said it was "difficult to envisage a worse case than this of racially aggravated harassment of this kind", adding Bonehill-Paine had "sat in the dock smirking throughout the trial" and had "plainly enjoyed" Ms Berger's discomfort.

Baroness Berger resigned from Labour in protest at the handling of antisemitism allegations in 2019, before rejoining in 2023 after receiving an apology from former party leader Sir Keir Starmer.

News.title: Dewormer and scabies drugs being sold as cancer treatments, BBC investigation finds
News.content:
Animal dewormer and a drug used to treat scabies are being sold and promoted as unproven cancer treatments, a BBC investigation has found.

Following a tip off, an undercover journalist was able to buy fenbendazole and ivermectin from a stairlift salesman in south Wales, and also found them for sale on Amazon.

Macmillan Cancer Support said it was concerned by the findings and that a growing number of people were asking about the medicines, despite "no clinical evidence" that they work.

Amazon removed the products after we contacted them, and said it had "proactive measures in place" to stop prohibited products being listed by third-party sellers.

Senior doctors are worried vulnerable patients could be put at risk by taking the medicines, as they say it could harm or delay conventional treatment.

Six months ago, Rebecca Holder contacted the BBC after a visit from stairlift salesman Jason Sarver.

She said Sarver and her father Bob, who had a brain tumour, lung cancer and needed help with his mobility, had been discussing stairlifts when the salesman changed the topic to talk about the drugs.

News.title: Couple woke to find shirtless intruder in Travelodge room
News.content:
A couple woke to find a shirtless man in their hotel bedroom after he was mistakenly given a key card to their door, BBC Scotland News has learned.

Kim Hutchison, 60, and Harry Grieve, 57, from Buckie, Moray, were staying in a Travelodge in Dundee when the early morning incident happened last month.

Hutchison said she was "petrified" before the man - wearing just shorts - left after about a minute of arguing over who was actually in the wrong room.

Travelodge apologised to the couple and said room access security policies were not correctly followed. It is the latest in a series of similar incidents at Travelodge hotels reported to the BBC.

Earlier this year, a man was jailed for sexually assaulting a woman in her hotel bed after Travelodge staff gave him a key card and her room number.

Kyran Smith had gone to the reception of the Maidenhead branch of the hotel chain in the early hours in December 2022 and said he was the woman's boyfriend.

Travelodge later said it was investigating more reports of strangers accessing rooms - after two women told the BBC that people they did not know came into their rooms while they were alone.

News.title: Vegetables to get smaller and more expensive due to hot weather, farmers warn
News.content:
This year's harvest could be the worst on record as farmers warn the exceptionally dry spring and summer could lead to "shrinkflation" in UK supermarkets.

England and Wales saw their driest July since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, and a drought has been declared across large parts of the country.

The Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank said the UK's cereals and oilseed harvest could be 2.5 million tonnes less than âearlier forecasts.

Tim O'Malley, the chairman of Nationwide produce, said it was "as bad as its ever been" and that shoppers will likely see higher prices or smaller vegetables in supermarkets.

The harvest of barley, oats and rapeseed, which are used in beer, breakfast cereals and vegetable oil, is estimated to drop to just 19.5 million tonnes, the worst since records began in 1984.

That is compared with a previous low of 19.8 million tonnes in 2020, and would cost farmers Â£390m in lost revenue, the ECIU estimated.

The crops are also used for feeding livestock, making them crucial across most of the food chain.

O'Malley said consumers could feel the impact in the vegetable aisle too, where grocers are likely to swap in smaller produce at the same price, which is known as shrinkflation.

"I think we're going to see shrinkflation," he told Radio 5 Live's Wake Up to Money.

News.title: New guidance on single-sex spaces comes into force
News.content:
Single-sex spaces open to the public, such as toilets and changing rooms, should be organised based on biological sex, according to official guidance that has come into force.

The code, published by Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), says trans people should use either gender-neutral facilities or the ones that match their biological sex, in places such as gym changing rooms or rape crisis centres.

The guidance was published in June but is now in place in England, Wales and Scotland - despite opposition among some MPs.

It comes 16 months after the UK Supreme Court ruled "sex" in equality law means "biological sex" rather than the gender someone identifies as.

Trans-rights campaigners have called the guidance unworkable, but groups that campaign for sex-based rights welcome the clarity it brings.

The guidance from the EHRC, the equality watchdog for England, Scotland and Wales, provides practical advice for services, public bodies and associations on how they should interpret the 2010 Equality Act.

It applies to organisations as diverse as cafes, leisure centres, public toilets, domestic violence shelters, bowls clubs and many more.

The code says where it is proportionate for facilities, such as public toilets and changing rooms, or services like a rape crisis centre, to be single sex then only those of the same biological sex should use them.

This means, for instance, a trans woman, a person born a biological male who identifies as a woman, should not use women-only facilities. And a trans man should not use men only facilities.

But the code also says it could amount to discrimination against a transgender person if they were forced to use services related to their biological sex. It says gender-neutral spaces are an alternative.

The Equality Act provides protections for people on the grounds of both biological sex and gender reassignment.

Transgender people argue they should be able to use services that align with the way they identify and live their life, rather than their biological sex.

In response, campaigners including some women's and gay rights groups say this undermines sex-based protections, particularly for women.

It is the tension between these two sets of rights that led to both the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 and the publication of this updated guidance.

It suggests legal action on how the code is put into practice is likely. Both from trans-rights groups who think the guidance itself is wrong and from sex-based rights groups who will want to challenge any organisations who they believe are not following the code.

News.title: Temperatures to drop briefly ahead of potential new UK heatwave
News.content:
Temperatures are set to drop across the UK over the next few days, ending the latest heatwave that has affected some areas of southern and eastern England.

Humidity levels will fall too, which should cool down homes and make nights more comfortable for sleeping.

The change in conditions follows another historic day in a summer that has seen many long standing heat records toppled or tied. On Tuesday, the UK registered its 34th day of temperatures reaching 30C (86F) or higher in a calendar year, equalling the record set in 1995.

Forecasts suggest that this record is likely to be beaten as early as next week, with some showing the potential for a sixth heatwave to develop.

News.title: Key questions as Infantino faces Fifa executives
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino will meet with senior leaders of football's world governing body on Wednesday as criticism of his now scrapped plan to sell off Fifa's commercial and event operations intensifies.

After secretary general Mattias Grafstrom sent a highly critical internal memo to Fifa staff, Infantino summoned members of the Fifa management board to Morocco.

Tuesday also saw chief of global football development Arsene Wenger insist he was "not involved" in Infantino's Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, adding that aborting it was "absolutely necessary and beyond question".

Prince Ali, president of the Jordanian Football Association, then accused Fifa of creating a situation which "amounts to blackmail" over unpaid prize money and support for Infantino's re-election.

These claims have not been verified by the BBC, and Fifa made no comment when approached. But Prince Ali's statement is indicative of the strength of feeling among the member associations that oppose Infantino.

At the weekend, Uefa said it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership. Several member associations - including Wales, with England set to follow suit - have withdrawn support for his re-election.

Now Infantino will meet with Fifa's hierarchy to try to secure his position.

News.title: Body found in search for boy, 13, missing at sea
News.content:
A body has been found in the search for a teenager who went missing off the East Yorkshire coast, police have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to the South Promenade, in Hornsea, at about 18:00 BST on Tuesday after reports that a 13-year-old boy had got into difficulty while swimming.

Police said an "extensive search operation" had involved teams from HM Coastguard, Yorkshire Ambulance Service, and Humberside Fire and Rescue. Crews from Hornsea Inshore Rescue and the RNLI also attended.

Ch Supt Phil Booker said: "This is an incredibly heartbreaking outcome, and our thoughts are with the boy's family and friends at this devastating time."

News.title: Burnham 'looking into' conducting Epstein inquiry, says victims minister
News.content:
Andy Burnham is "looking into" the possibility of holding a public inquiry into the UK activities of the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, according to victims minister Alex Davies-Jones.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Davies-Jones said that the prime minister had agreed to meet Epstein's victims.

She said the government is also reviewing whether the alleged actions of former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed could also be part of an inquiry.

Davies-Jones resigned from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government in May, later accusing his government of failing to listen to Epstein's survivors. She was reappointed as victims minister when Burnham took office.

Speaking on the programme, she said she had discussed holding a public inquiry into the alleged behaviour of Epstein and Al Fayed with the prime minister and cabinet secretary Dame Antonia Romeo during her re-appointment.

Asked whether an inquiry was now possible, Davies-Jones said: "We are looking at this, we are reviewing what is possible. Again, same with Harrods survivors."

She added: "I have been assured that the prime minister is taking this very seriously.

"He will meet with those victims and he is looking at what is possible, now he has access to all of the information as prime minister to see what action we can take."

After resigning in May, Davies-Jones told the Commons in June that people whose lives were devastated by Epstein's abuse have too often been reduced to a footnote.

Asked what assurances or guarantees she had asked from Burnham in relation to the survivors when he re-appointed her to government, the minister said: "I did have those discussions with the prime minister before he became the prime minister."

"He agreed to meet with the Epstein victims," she continued, adding that Burnham "has assured me that he will meet them now he's prime minister and will work with us to look at systemic change across the system for all victims."

BBC Newsnight understands that as Burnham was finalising plans to become prime minister, he was sent a document by leading Labour campaigners on Violence Against Women and Girls.

It contained a key suggestion: to hold a full public inquiry into the UK activities of Epstein, the alleged behaviour of the late Harrods boss Mohamed Al Fayed and into allegations in a BBC Panorama and Times investigation that West Ham co-owner David Sullivan preyed on women.

David Sullivan has described the claims as false. He said he was "absolutely not the person the media has decided to paint me as".

The document called for an "impunity" inquiry to ask how powerful men were able to carry out the alleged behaviour.

On Epstein, the document calls for a focus on UK borders, asking how he was able to fly in and out of UK military bases on his private jet, often with allegedly trafficked women. Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown highlighted this issue in February.

Davies-Jones is understood to be familiar with the Labour document.

Anoushka De Georgiou, an Epstein survivor, told BBC Newsnight: "I welcome reports that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering public inquiries into the Epstein and Maxwell, Harrods/Mohamed Al-Fayed, and David Sullivan cases."

"Survivors have heard promises before, so what matters now is action, not headlines."

News.title: Antisemitic incident reports rise by a fifth in first half of 2026
News.content:
The number of antisemitic incidents recorded across the UK since the start of the year is up by a fifth compared to last year, figures show.

The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026.

It represents a 21% increase on the number of similar incidents reported in the first half of last year.

It also marks the second highest total of antisemitic hate incidents ever recorded by CST in the first half of any year since the organisation began collecting data in 1984.

Policing Minister Sarah Jones said the numbers were "appalling" and showed people "living in fear just for being who they are".

The incidents logged in the first few months of 2026 include a series of arson attacks against Jewish organisations and synagogues in London.

Four volunteer ambulances were set alight in Golders Green in March. The following month two visibly Jewish men were stabbed nearby, in an attack which was treated as an act of terrorism.

The CST said it recorded noticeable surges in antisemitic incidents following these events, with the highest daily total following the double stabbing on 29 April.

Hatred continues to be directed at British Jews at a higher level than before 7 October 2023, when Hamas attacked Israel and the war in Gaza began.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East is one of the factors behind the rise in antisemitism. Some 41% of the incidents recorded by the CST used anti-Jewish language or motive at the same time as making reference to either the conflict, Israel, Palestine, or Hamas.

CST chief executive Mark Gardner said: "These attacks are directed against British Jews but they are also attacks on Britain and our society."

He said they "should concern everyone who cares about Britain and the threats against it, whether state-directed from Iran, or internally driven by Islamist, far-right, far-left, or other ideological extremes."

Separate data released last week revealed that antisemitism is at heightened levels globally.

A report by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism found that the UK recorded the biggest rise in antisemitic incidents last year of any country with a major Jewish population outside Israel.

It also found that 2025 was the deadliest year for Jews in the diaspora in more than three decades.

The government's independent adviser on antisemitism, Lord John Mann, said these new CST figures, "demonstrate that anti-Jewish racism in the UK remains at all all-time high and continues to pose a significant threat to our democracy".

He added that he is especially concerned "to see the nature of antisemitism in the UK becoming increasingly violent".

The CST also analyses the types of incidents which occur across different sectors. It found that in the first half of 2026, antisemitism in schools reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year. It jumped by 59%, from 112 reported incidents in the first half of 2025, to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026.

A government-commissioned independent review into antisemitism in schools and colleges is currently being carried out by Sir David Bell. It is expected to report in the autumn.

News.title: Former RAF medic can clear debts and mortgage after choosing £300k over Lamborghini
News.content:
A former RAF medic can pay off his mortgage and clear his debts after winning Â£300,000 in a competition he entered for Â£4.28.

Ryan Briggs, 46, from Haverfordwest in Pembrokeshire, spent 23 years in the Royal Air Force, completing tours of Iraq and Afghanistan, before joining the NHS as a paramedic during the Covid-19 pandemic.

He was given the choice of a 2026 Lamborghini Temerario - worth an estimated Â£270,000 - or Â£300,000 in cash, after winning a competition organised by Elite Competitions, and chose the cash.

"I can now reduce my hours [at work] in the future if I wanted to. I'm fit and healthy now, but that can change. It takes a lot of pressure off," he said.

Ryan met his wife Kelly, a logistics mover, when they were both in the RAF, aged 19.

She left shortly after, and was planning to move back to northern Scotland - but instead the pair conducted a "shotgun wedding".

"It worked for us, because we are still happily married 27 years later," said Ryan, a father-of-two.

He said he had grown up with a "fascination" with planes after his father had taken him to air shows at RAF St Athan, Vale of Glamorgan, inspiring him to join the RAF.

News.title: Man charged over death of nine-year-old girl on industrial estate
News.content:
A man has been charged in connection with the death of a nine-year-old girl in Arbroath.

Officers were called to the Elliot Industrial Estate shortly after midnight on Sunday following reports that the child, from West Yorkshire, had been found injured.

She was taken to Ninewells Hospital in Dundee alongside four other people, but later died as a result of her injuries.

Police said a 35-year-old white British man, who was known to the girl, had been arrested. He has now been charged and is scheduled to appear at Forfar Sheriff Court on Wednesday.

Det Insp Mike Ness, of Police Scotland's major investigation team, said no-one else was being sought in connection with the incident.

He said the girl's family members, who were camping in the area, were being supported by specialist officers.

Det Insp Ness added: "Our thoughts remain with those affected by these events.

"A police presence will remain in the area while our enquiries continue."

News.title: Princess Eugenie gives birth to baby girl in Portugal
News.content:
Princess Eugenie has given birth to a baby girl at a hospital in Lisbon, Portugal.

The baby was born on Monday at 18:20 BST, weighing 6lbs 9oz.

This is Princess Eugenie's third child with her husband, Jack Brooksbank, following the births of her sons August Philip Hawke Brooksbank, who was born in 2021, and Ernest George Ronnie Brooksbank, who was born in 2023.

A statement from Buckingham Palace read: "Their Majesties The King and Queen and other members of The Royal Family were delighted to be informed of the news."

In a post on Instagram, the princess, 36, wrote: "Jack and I are so excited to announce Baby Girl Brooksbank!!

"We are beyond in love with our girlie."

They are yet to announce a name.

The new arrival - who will not be an HRH - will be 15th in line to the throne, moving ahead of their great-uncle the Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Edward.

The couple live between Portugal and Ivy Cottage, in the grounds of Kensington Palace.

They announced Princess Eugenie's pregnancy in May. She posted a photograph of her young sons holding a baby scan with the caption: "Baby Brooksbank due 2026!"

The Palace said on social media at the time: "His Majesty The King has been informed and is delighted with the news."

News.title: Anthropic AI created fake profiles and impersonated people in attempted hack
News.content:
Two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in an attempted cyber-attack during testing by the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).

In the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people.

AISI said on Tuesday Mythos - and OpenAI's Sol - AI models had engaged in a level of "autonomy and deception" it had not seen before, though it clarified most of the malicious actions were carried out by Mythos.

Anthropic and OpenAI noted in response to AISI's report that its test had reduced or removed normal safeguards.

AISI evaluators first noticed "unusual data transfers leaving our research systems" during a test, then found that "some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations".

In the most serious case, a Mythos agent followed the routine of a human cyber-attacker by trying to trick people into giving it access to GitHub, a large platform where technology developers store software code.

The agent was trying to insert "malicious code" into GitHub's system.

It identified and researched the people who maintained GitHub and created a series of fake accounts based on those real people.

It sent messages and files through a file-sharing service as part of an effort to pressure and trick the people into approving its malicious code.

When challenged, "it edited its earlier activity to appear harmless and considered adopting a fresh identity to continue," AISI said.

Throughout the attempts, it was human review that stopped the agent from succeeding in delivering the malicious code to GitHub.

While AISI said the Mythos agent had not been instructed specifically to avoid or carry out such behaviour, it was "the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world".

The rival AI companies, which are poised to be listed on the public stock market, have been in the headlines in recent weeks after announcing their tools were responsible for several cyber-hacking incidents.

News.title: More than 170 migrants rescued after boat catches fire in Channel
News.content:
More than 170 migrants have been rescued after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire on Tuesday morning, as the UK government said "all will be returned" to France.

The boat was attempting to cross to the UK when its engine caught fire, according to the French maritime prefecture of the Channel and North Sea.

It had originally reported 157 migrants were rescued, but has since revised that figure up to 173. All have been taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer in France, with 11 people suffering from minor injuries.

French prosecutors have opened an investigation, and an Egyptian national has been taken into policy custody in connection with the incident.

Border Security Minister Anna Turley said the incident "shows the dangers of these illegal crossings and the ruthless gangs behind them".

"That's why we are bearing down on them," she said.

French authorities said the boat left France on Monday night.

Overnight "five people on board the vessel required rescue... the remaining people on board refused the assistance offered by the French patrol boats", the French maritime prefecture said.

"Determined to reach the United Kingdom, migrants crossing the Channel in small boats refused assistance offered by French emergency service, accepting it only in situations of extreme emergency," it said in a statement.

Because of the "structural fragility" of boats used to cross the Channel, it said they decided not to intervene further at that stage.

But this morning the engine caught fire and the "vessel's integrity deteriorated very rapidly".

Rescue boats went to the scene from France and the UK, including the RNLI Eastbourne lifeboat and the UK Border Force vessels BSC Contender and BSC Courageous.

The French maritime prefecture said the operation involved 40 firefighters, 13 police officers, seven interpreters, and a number of medical personnel.

It had previously reported that 157 migrants were rescued, but on Tuesday afternoon revised that figure up to 173.

On top of the initial five rescued, two French boats rescued 105 migrants and the British boats rescued 63. All of them were taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer for treatment.

The total number on the boat broke the previous record of 165 people, who reached the UK late last month in a 42ft (13m) boat, making it the largest single vessel to attempt to cross the Channel carrying migrants.

News.title: John Lewis 2026 beauty advent calendar pre-orders are live – here’s what’s included
News.content:
John Lewis has taken a notably broader approach with its 2026 beauty advent calendar, curating a lineup that balances trendy names, established beauty icons and accessible premium brands. Rather than leaning heavily into ultra-luxury skincare alone, the retailer has assembled a collection that feels designed to appeal to a wide range of beauty lovers, with hydration, glow and everyday essentials forming the backbone of the edit. Familiar favourites from Charlotte Tilbury, Clarins, Clinique and Dermalogica sit comfortably alongside cult names such as Medik8, Malin+Goetz and Foreo, creating a calendar that's as practical as it is indulgent.

What makes the calendar particularly appealing is its versatility. Instead of focusing on products that feel aspirational but niche, many of the inclusions are genuine staples that slot easily into an existing routine, from Medik8's hydr8 B5 serum and Dermalogica's daily microfoliant to L'Occitane's best-selling almond shower oil and the Clarins lip comfort oil.

There's still room for a touch of luxury, too (it is Christmas after all) with La Mer's lip balm and a Jo Loves candle adding a premium edge, while the Foreo UFO 3 mini offers one of the calendar's standout hero products for anyone curious about beauty tech. Trendy brands haven’t been skipped either with Skin Rocks and Sculpted by Aimee on the list.

Where my excitement slightly wanes is with the Rituals, Nuxe and This Works products as you can find these brands in almost every calendar. And do we really need another glittery nail polish in our lives (Mavala pure diamond nail polish is one of the products)? I’d swap out the perfume mini, Versace’s crystal emerald, to something a bit more special.

Retailing at £250, the John Lewis beauty advent calendar encompasses 41 products in 25 drawers, of which more than 50 per cent are full size. It’s £15 more expensive than last year, but this time you get five more products including two more that are full-sized.

When is the John Lewis beauty advent calendar available to buy?

You’ll need to sign up to MyJL Beauty app, where you’ll be able to pre-order the calendar. Pre-orders will be shipped from the 3 September, and will go on general sale from 7 September.

As students head back to school, doctors and teachers are warning parents to take a closer look at what's inside their children's backpacks, saying overloaded bags can increase the risk of injury and make the school day harder.

Today's backpacks often carry far more than textbooks. Many students haul laptops or tablets, chargers, notebooks, water bottles, lunch boxes, sports gear and other personal items, creating loads that experts say can put unnecessary strain on growing bodies.

The American Academy of Pediatrics says parents should watch for signs that a backpack is too heavy, including children leaning forward while walking, struggling to carry the bag or shoulder straps digging into their skin.

open image in gallery The modern school backpack has evolved, but it hasn’t necessarily gotten lighter ( AP )

Dr. Sadika Kendi, who chairs the academy's injury prevention efforts, said parents shouldn't wait until a child complains about pain before lightening the load.

"It's worse if, for example, they trip and fall and they have a huge, heavy backpack on their back," Kendi said. "Then that's just more weight that could increase the severity of an injury."

Kendi also said there is not enough evidence to support the commonly cited recommendation that backpacks weigh no more than 10% to 15% of a child's body weight. Instead, she said families should focus on carrying only what is necessary and keeping backpacks as light as possible.

open image in gallery According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, signs a backpack may be too heavy include a child leaning forward to support its weight or having difficulty walkingDr. Sadika Kendi, a physician who chairs the academy’s injury-prevention efforts, says back injuries are uncommon but possible, particularly if a child falls while carrying a heavy backpack ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

Teachers are also encouraging parents to rethink what students really need each day.

Phoenix history teacher Samantha Ness said many students already have classroom textbooks but are still expected to bring laptops and chargers every day, while some fill their backpacks with non-school items.

"They're using their backpacks more as purses and like storage than they are actually using them for school," Ness said, noting older students often carry makeup, nail polish and other personal belongings alongside school supplies.

open image in gallery Dr. Sadika Kendi, a physician who chairs the academy’s injury-prevention efforts, says back injuries are uncommon but possible, particularly if a child falls while carrying a heavy backpack ( AP )

In Fairfax County, Virginia, some parents are also questioning whether children need to carry both printed textbooks and school-issued laptops, particularly when block scheduling means students may not need every subject every day.

Experts recommend choosing a backpack with two wide, padded shoulder straps, a padded back and multiple compartments to spread the weight evenly. Waist or chest straps can also help reduce strain.

The American Academy of Pediatrics also advises children to lift heavy backpacks by bending at the knees instead of the waist and to clean out their bags regularly to remove unnecessary items.

One safety tip doctors say parents often overlook is taking backpacks off before getting into a car.

"Don't wear it in a car or any form of transportation while that car is moving," Kendi said. "It's just incredibly dangerous."

She said wearing a backpack while seated can prevent a seat belt from fitting properly, increasing the risk of injury in a crash or sudden stop.

A man has paid tribute to his “amazing” father who was killed in a largefire that broke out in a Cotswolds town.

Gardener and landscaper Francis Owens, 74, died in a blaze on Monday, as the fields behind Berrington Road in Chipping Campden caught fire.

Emergency services received reports of the fire at 5.38pm and deployed 13 fire engines to tackle the fire, but Francis died at the scene.

Patrick Owens paid tribute to his father on social media, saying he was “very much loved” by their family and described him as “the Renaissance man of Chipping Campden”.

Speaking to The Independent, Mr Owens said: “He was my mum Mandy’s best friend, and he devoted his whole life to her. He doted on her.

“He was an amazing father. He taught me so much, and he was such a good husband to my mum. They'd been married 50 years.”

open image in gallery Chipping Campden is a popular tourist town in the Cotswolds ( Getty )

Mr Owens has set up a tribute to Francis, whose landscaping company was called ‘A Luddite’ because he worked without machines, by setting up a shrine with his walking cane and a shovel.

About his father, who he said would “help anybody”, Mr Owens added: “Back in 1976, the Evesham Journal did a piece on him as the UK's smallest lorry driver (standing at 4ft 10in).

“He had to have blocks nailed to the pedals so he could drive them. He didn't have creature comforts like we do now.

“I'm also a lorry driver because it got into my veins. I wanted to make him proud.”

Nathaniel Hooton, the deputy chief fire officer at Gloucestershire Fire and Rescue Service, said crews “worked extremely hard” to bring the fire under control.

“As a service we extend our sincere condolences to the family of the deceased and to the wider community. Our thoughts are with them at this difficult time,” he added.

“This was a multi-agency response. We worked extremely hard with colleagues from neighbouring fire services to bring the fire under control.

“We would like to thank our colleagues from Hereford and Worcester Fire and Rescue Service and Warwickshire Fire and Rescue Service for their support and assistance.”

The cause of the fire is not yet known.

A spokesperson from Gloucestershire Constabulary added: “Following a fire in Chipping Campden, a man in his 70s from the local area was sadly confirmed dead at the scene.

“His family and the coroner have been informed and our thoughts remain with all those who knew him at this time.

“Police do not suspect any third-party involvement in the death."

Airline passengers know to expect possible flight delays when weather forecasts call for thunderstorms, heavy snow or strong wind. The omens are less obvious on a hot summer day with clear skies.

Yet extreme heat also disrupts flights and travel plans. On the hottest days, thinner air can make it harder for aircraft to get off the ground safely. Airlines may have to lighten the load by removing passengers or cargo, or carrying less fuel.

The snag is well known at airports in desert climates around the world, from the U.S. Southwest to the Middle East. But even less extreme heat can create similar challenges at airports with higher elevations or shorter runways. Researchers say human-caused climate change could make such disruptions more common.

With heat waves searing parts of the United States and Europe this summer, Las Vegas illustrated how extreme heat can interfere with air travel. American Airlines offered compensation to customers who voluntarily gave up their seats on a July 24 flight from Harry Reid International Airport after temperatures reached 114 degrees Fahrenheit (47 degrees Celsius).

The airline described reducing a plane's weight as a standard industry practice in hot-weather destinations when conditions require it to ensure a safe takeoff. The explanation comes down to physics.

Hot air is thinner than cool air, making it harder for a plane's wings to generate lift and for jet engines to generate the thrust needed for takeoff, explained Ross Aimer, a retired United Airlines captain and CEO of Aero Consulting Experts.

“There is a science behind all this,” Aimer said. “You can’t deny the science of flight and what it takes for an airplane to operate.”

Airplanes struggle in hot, thin air

Aimer likens the effect of high temperatures on airplane performance to athletes competing at high altitude. During this year’s World Cup, foreign teams competing in Mexico City — located more than 7,300 feet (2,225 meters) above sea level — had to contend with thinner air that can leave players fatigued more quickly.

“Just like human beings, jet engines require lots of cool, dense air to perform well,” Aimer said.

Before every departure, pilots and airlines determine whether an aircraft can safely take off by calculating several key factors, including the airplane’s weight, the airport’s elevation and the outside temperature, said Alan Price, a retired Delta Air Lines captain.

Aircraft at higher elevations are already operating in thinner air, so temperatures don’t have to climb as high to affect takeoff performance. Denver, for example, sits more than 5,000 feet (1,524 meters) above sea level.

Runway length also matters. Airliners need room to build enough speed for takeoff when temperatures soar, and shorter runways leave less distance to do that, Price said. That’s one reason airports such as New York’s LaGuardia and Washington’s Reagan National can be more likely to face takeoff restrictions or weight limits during very hot weather.

If the pilot's preflight math shows an aircraft cannot safely depart as planned, airlines may choose to reduce cargo, carry less fuel and make a refueling stop later, wait for cooler temperatures or ask passengers to volunteer for a later flight.

But there comes a point when removing weight isn’t enough to make a safe takeoff possible.

“At some point, the numbers just don’t make sense,” Aimer said. “You could roll down a runway as long as you want, and you still can’t take off.”

Delays due to hot weather could become more common

The Federal Aviation Administration does not set a single maximum temperature for takeoff. Instead, the FAA says, operating limits vary based on an aircraft's make and model, its weight and the airport’s altitude.

A 2017 study by researchers from Columbia University, NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and the Logistics Management Institute projected that some airports could see weight restrictions on 10% to 30% of flights departing during the hottest part of the day by midcentury if greenhouse gas emissions continued to rise. The study examined 19 airports around the world and found that airports with short runways, high elevations and hotter climates would be affected most.

A more recent study concluded that current climate prediction models indicated planes taking off from four European airports would have to shed the weight equivalent of 10 passengers per flight by 2065.

While triple-digit temperatures come with desert living, the kind of hot days that might affect flights are becoming more frequent in both Phoenix and Las Vegas.

Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport has averaged 43 days each year since 2020 when the temperature reached at least 110 F (43 C), according to an analysis of weather station data by The Associated Press. The number of such days increased gradually over several decades before surging in the 2020s to more than triple the average during the middle of the last century.

At Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, temperatures reached that threshold an average of about 18 days a year between 2020 and 2025 — more than double the annual average during the 1940s through 1960s, the AP analysis found.

The 2020s have also been exceedingly hot at Palm Springs International Airport. The airport in Southern California has recorded an annual average this decade of 55 days with temperatures reaching 110 F — an 83% increase compared to the 2000s, when the weather station there began recording data.

Safety determines when airlines reduce weight

Airlines have dealt with these issues for years. During a stretch of scorching heat in June 2016, American canceled several round-trip regional flights between Palm Springs, California, and Phoenix. The following year, the airline canceled dozens of regional flights in Arizona as temperatures in Phoenix climbed toward 120 F (49 C).

In July 2018, some airlines bumped passengers at Denver International Airport to later flights as temperatures reached 98 F (37 C), KDVR-TV in Denver reported.

Delta Air Lines also asked for volunteers to step off a plane in Las Vegas during an excessive heat warning in July 2023 because of weight restrictions tied to the extreme temperatures. That flight was ultimately canceled after passengers spent hours aboard the aircraft in the heat.

Airports can be especially vulnerable to the urban heat island effect, which is the phenomenon of built-up areas becoming hotter than their surroundings, said Jennifer Brady, a data scientist with Climate Central.

With little shade or green space, vast expanses of heat-absorbing pavement and constant activity from airplanes, ground vehicles and air conditioning systems that generate waste heat, “all of the elements are there for it being one of the hottest spaces in a city,” Brady said.

___

Wildeman reported from Hartford, Connecticut.

News.title: OpenAI and Anthropic’s AI systems launch several ‘potentially harmful’ hacks on their own
News.content:
AI systems made by Anthropic and OpenAI have launched “potentially harmful” hacks on real people, the UK’s AI watchdog has revealed.

The systems were caught making fake online identities to launch cyber attacks on secure systems, according to the AI Security Institute.

It is just the latest discovery of such “rogue” behaviour by AI tools. It follows a major disclosure by OpenAI that one of its experimental systems had broken into another artificial intelligence company – after which both the ChatGPT maker and Anthropic, which runs the Claude Chatbot, revealed they had found a host of similar cyber attacks.

Now, the institute has said that agents powered by Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol engaged in unauthorised actions during security evaluations the government organisation conducted to assess the models' capabilities.

"Some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations," AISI said in a blog post.

The report underscores the lax state of ⁠safeguards around the process of testing agents, which AI companies are simultaneously ​marketing ⁠as the future of business.

AISI, which receives access to advanced AI models under voluntary agreements from major labs, put the agents through a fictional cybersecurity scenario to test their capabilities.

It ran the challenge 122 ⁠times, and identified 19 unsanctioned actions across a total of 10 test runs. Anthropic's agent was behind 17 of ​the actions, ⁠and OpenAI's agent the remaining two.

The ideal summer spot? Away from scams. Get All-in-One Protection for Your Digital Life LEARN MORE 

The most egregious ‌action involved an agent writing malicious code and creating fake online identities in an attempt to get a human to approve the code, AISI said, adding that no real-world harm was found as a result of any of ‌the breaches.

While AISI did not say which agent was behind the ‌fake identities, Antropic confirmed its agent was responsible.

"We're grateful to the UK AISI for their leadership on this incident, which underscores the need for a broader conversation about how to safely evaluate increasingly capable AI agents," Anthropic said in a statement.

It also said it was working with AISI to ⁠obtain more details on the incident and conduct its own investigation.

Andrew Yoon, a researcher at CivAI, a California non-profit that examines AI capabilities and dangers, said: "The fact that Mythos engaged in such deceptive actions, with apparent awareness that it was targeting a real person, suggests that Anthropic does not have as good a handle on their models as they think."

OpenAI shared details in a company blog post, noting that both of its agent's unapproved actions involved accessing the internet in ways that were forbidden by the prompt.

"We are committed to working across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting ‌high-risk evaluations safely, including convening stakeholders such as national AI institutes, independent evaluators, other AI labs, and other groups ​in the coming weeks," OpenAI said.

OpenAI also disclosed in its blog post a separate incident whereby ‌a misconfiguration by Irregular, a third-party testing provider, allowed ⁠its agents to mistakenly connect to the internet. It mirrored a similar disclosure about misconfiguration that Anthropic made ⁠last week.

Reuters reported last week that OpenAI had widened its hacking probe after finding evidence of other agent breakouts.

Unlike the July security breach of ‌AI firm Hugging Face by ​an OpenAI agent, the agents in the AISI evaluation did ‌not escape an isolated testing environment to reach the ​internet. Rather, the agency had permitted internet access in line with its standard testing procedures, AISI said.

Manchester United are poised to offload two goalkeepers, with Radek Vitek set to join Middlesbrough in a deal potentially worth up to £14 million, while Altay Bayindir prepares for a loan move to Celta Vigo.

Vitek, a 22-year-old Czech shot-stopper, is nearing a permanent switch to last season’s Championship play-off finalists Middlesbrough following an impressive loan spell at Bristol City.

The young keeper initially arrived at Old Trafford from Sigma Olomouc in 2020, having also spent time on loan at Accrington and Blau-Weiss Linz before his successful stint at Ashton Gate.

The Press Association understands that United have secured matching rights and a buy-back option as part of the agreement with Boro, which includes bonuses that could push the fee to £14m, alongside a sell-on clause of up to 35 per cent.

Since joining United from Fenerbahce in 2023, Bayindir has primarily served as a back-up option. His temporary departure includes performance-related bonuses, with the Spanish club also covering his wages.

Celta Vigo will have the opportunity to make the move permanent, reportedly for a fee of £3.5m, which would also include a sell-on clause for United.

These moves follow Andre Onana’s return to Trabzonspor on loan, signalling a significant reshuffle in United's goalkeeping ranks.

Michael Carrick is actively restructuring his squad this summer, with number one Senne Lammens now joined by summer signing Karl Darlow.

More signings are expected before the transfer window slams shut, with United set for a much busier campaign after only playing 40 matches across all competitions last season.
