Sports.title: Arsenal agree £75m fee with Newcastle for Bruno Guimarães as clubs reach compromise
Sports.content:
Bruno Guimarães is set to leave Newcastle’s pre-season training camp in southern Spain and fly to London before a £75m move to Arsenal. The out-going Newcastle captain is scheduled to undergo a medical in north London in the next couple of days after the two clubs finally compromised on the fee.

While Arsenal had initially wanted to pay no more than £60m for the Brazil midfielder, who turns 29 in November and has two years remaining on his contract, Newcastle demanded a minimum of £80m.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Having sold Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively earlier this summer, Newcastle had no need to sell Guimarães and would have preferred to keep a key player who was integral to their 2025 League Cup triumph.

Since the Brazilian’s arrival from Lyon in January 2022, Newcastle have struggled to win games without Guimarães on the pitch. In his 153 League appearances he scored 30 goals, contributed 26 assists and, as Eddie Howe’s former team twice qualified for the Champions League, became an enduring crowd favourite. The loss of Guimarães is likely to hit Newcastle fans appreciably harder than even Alexander Isak’s defection to Liverpool last year.

Guimarães though was determined to join Arsenal even before Howe stepped down as manager last week. He flew to La Manga to meet the club’s in-coming manager, Matthias Jaissle on Monday but is understood to have told Jaissle he wanted out and could not be persuaded otherwise. The parting is believed to have been cordial and in marked contrast to Isak’s acrimonious exit last summer.

Lyon will receive a windfall in the region of £7m due to a sell on clause that stipulates they are entitled to 20% of any profit Newcastle make on the sale of Guimarães.

Sports.title: Fifa accused of using ‘blackmail’ to force support for Infantino’s re-election bid
Sports.content:
The Jordan Football Association president, Prince Ali bin al-Hussein, has accused Gianni Infantino’s administration of “blackmail”, claiming that Fifa threatened to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back the president’s bid for re-election.

In a major intervention Prince Ali, who ran for the Fifa presidency against Infantino in 2016 and finished third, listed a number of problems dogging the global governing body and said Jordan’s players have not yet been paid for appearing in the Arab Cup last year. Prince Ali is head of the West Asian Football Federation, which includes influential states such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates that have thus far backed Infantino to stay on.

It came on a day when Infantino’s authority was dealt a further blow as two more key allies distanced themselves from his failed World Cup private investment plan. His No 2, the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, was revealed to have called the botched Fifa Forward Enterprise a “sad and reproachable series of events” in an email to the organisation’s staff. Meanwhile the former Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger, who is now Fifa’s chief of global development, said the project’s withdrawal was “absolutely necessary and beyond question”.

Infantino is steadily losing backing from countries who previously had sent letters to endorse his continuation for a fourth term in charge. It is understood that Greece is the latest federation to have pulled its support, following the lead taken by countries such as England, Wales, Finland and Serbia. More European federations are expected to follow in the coming days, while a number of nations in Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – are also giving serious consideration to withdrawing their backing.

Prince Ali’s statement, published on X, painted the picture of a small country facing a litany of roadblocks when it came to receiving help from the global governing body. Jordan competed in their first World Cup this year but he explained some of their fans had not received visas, despite purchasing tickets, and expressed anger at being taxed by the US for being based in the country.

“We have been waiting for reward money for our players since December for the Arab Cup in Qatar, which is a Fifa event,” his statement read. “The money our team should receive for having reached the final has not been delivered yet, while at the same time Fifa brags about how many billions they have in reserve.

View image in fullscreen The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (centre), and secretary general, Mattias Grafström (right), with Arsène Wenger during the 2026 World Cup. Photograph: ANP/Shutterstock

“It is clear the problem really is with leadership. For months, Fifa has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters – until it was verbally communicated to me during the World Cup that if I endorsed Infantino it would go a long way to helping our FA out.

“We pride ourselves in Jordan in upholding ethical values. We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now. But the whole situation amounts to blackmail and we refuse to give in to that.”

Other countries are understood to have been put under concerted pressure to formally back Infantino before the Fifa election in March, although details of how it was applied remain unclear in those cases.

Grafström’s email had urged Fifa staff to keep morale high after what was perceived to be a successful World Cup. His message stopped short of criticising Infantino by name and promised to shield colleagues from the strife enveloping their organisation.

“A sad and reproachable series of events – which were thankfully concluded with the FFE project permanently abandoned – for as much as we feel dismayed by them, should not overshadow this reality,” read a section of the email.

11:54 Is Gianni Infantino’s time up as Fifa president? - The Latest

He referred to “a turmoil, which is difficult to comprehend and accept” and said: “Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue, and that is why we should always keep our professionalism, sense of perspective and composure.”

Wenger, who assumed his current position in November 2019, confirmed he had been among the many senior Fifa staff sidelined by Infantino’s plan. “I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports,” he said.

“The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency, and integrity.”

Fifa was contacted for comment regarding Prince Ali’s accusations.

According to reports, Infantino has called Fifa staff to a crisis meeting in the Moroccan capital, Rabat, on Wednesday as he tries to cling to his position.

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Folarin Balogun to Spurs? Pedro Neto to Manchester City?
Sports.content:
It’s been a quiet summer thus far for Folarin Balogun, so why not stir up some controversy by signing for the arch rivals of your boyhood club? The Monaco striker, who started his career at Arsenal, is being linked with a move to Tottenham Hotspur, who need a goalscorer to ensure they do not finish 17th again. The American’s agents have offered him up to Roberto De Zerbi’s side to see if they are willing to bite. One forward certainly of interest to the Italian manager is Chelsea’s Nicolas Jackson but no bid has been made.

This seems like a sensible point to put some Tottenham and Manchester City gossip in. If Savinho heads down south, as has been discussed for a long old while, Enzo Maresca would like Pedro Neto to replace him as a wing demon, having worked with the Portugal international at Chelsea. In further Spurs winger news, Manor Solomon was close to leaving for West Ham but Hull have entered the race as part of their accelerated transfer activity as they seek to ascertain if the Israeli is a Housemartins fan.

Tijjani Reijnders has never fully settled at Manchester City because finding a role for him is difficult. Nottingham Forest seem to have a cunning plan for the midfielder but, again, where he fits in at the City Ground is one to ponder, especially with a £55m being bandied about. Meanwhile, Manchester United believe Morgan Gibbs-White is an ideal candidate to replace Bruno Fernandes, if the Portuguese decides to depart Old Trafford, but that will take a while.

A more likely bit of business at the Etihad Stadium is the signing of goalkeeper Gerónimo Rulli from Marseille. The Argentinian is seen as an ideal replacement for James Trafford who is packing his bags for Leeds.

It is quiet no more around the Crystal Palace chequebook as Steve Parish is eager to spend some cash on Zavier Gozo of Real Salt Lake. The teenage winger is highly-thought of in MLS and could see south-east London as the ideal next step in his development.

Jadon Sancho supposedly has loads of offers on the table but he just needs to choose the right one. Clubs in Europe and Saudi Arabia are keen on landing the former England international who is available for nothing after leaving Manchester United in the summer.

After completing the signing of Freddie Potts from West Ham, Club Brugge have their eyes on another Londoner. Crystal Palace’s Romain Esse, from Lambeth, has made it on to the Belgian side’s radar after his loan spell with Coventry. Speaking of wingers in the English capital, Abdul Abdulmalik of Boreham Wood is wanted by Swedish side Djurgårdens. A bid totalling £1m has been rejected but another could be coming to really test the National League side’s resolve.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

And Romelu Lukaku’s time in Europe could be coming to an end. After being prolific yet underrated for much of his career, Atlanta United want him to try his hand in MLS. The Napoli striker is, inexplicably, still only 33 and, despite suffering from fitness problems in recent times, was still a handful at the World Cup.

Sports.title: Which footballer made the biggest leap in competitive levels between games? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“Malachi Fagan-Walcott’s final game of last season was for York City against Rochdale in the National League. His first competitive game of 2026-27 season was for Hearts against Sturm Graz in a Champions League qualifier. Has a player ever made a bigger leap in competitive levels between consecutive club games?” asks Tom Reed.

Does a jump from the Welsh League to the FA Cup count as a bigger leap? Probably not, but this was an FA Cup semi-final, rather than a Champions League qualifier, and it’s a cracking yarn regardless. “I’ll nominate Gary Plumley,” writes Russell Connor. “Gary made almost 200 appearances for Newport County in four separate spells over the course of a decade but by 1987 he had effectively retired and was running a wine bar while making occasional appearances for Ebbw Vale in the Welsh League.

“In the build-up to the FA Cup semi-final in 1987, Watford found themselves short a goalkeeper after both Tony Coton and Steve Sherwood broke a thumb and finger respectively. As luck would have it, Gary’s dad Eddie was chief executive of Watford at the time which led to Gary being signed by the club to play in the game.

“Watford lost 4-1, and by all accounts Plumley didn’t cover himself in glory. His reward was a cheque for expenses, which he used to buy a fridge. The family referred it to as the Watford Fridge. Here’s an interview with Plumley about the game.”

You can also read read this from the Guardian archive.

View image in fullscreen Glen Hoddle is mobbed by Spurs fans after their FA Cup semi-final victory against Watford in 1987. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

“Erling and Alf-Inge Haaland bought the only surviving copy of the first printed edition of Snorri Sturluson’s medieval history of Norwegian kings and donated it to their hometown of Time in Norway,” writes Kári Tulinius. “Have other footballers bought and donated rare books or other antiques?”

“In 2017, the then Spurs midfielder Mousa Dembélé bought a 700-year-old building in Antwerp which he began converting into a hotel,” writes Tom Reed. “During the renovations a treasure trove of 18th-century porcelain, glass, pottery and tableware was discovered. Dembélé donated a portion of the treasure, reportedly valued at over £1m, to the local museum and the rest went on display in the lobby of the newly renovated hotel which he (perhaps optimistically) named De Gulde Schoen (The Golden Shoe).”

Poachers turned gamekeepers

“On Sunday, Sean Murdoch was the referee for St Mirren v Dunfermline in the Scottish League Cup. Murdoch was previously a goalkeeper and played for Dunfermline. Are there any other examples of a former player refereeing a match for a club they had played for?” asks Ian Golightly.

We had this question in 2010, when the answers included:

Steve Baines, the only referee in the English professional leagues to have had significant experience as a player.

Dick Jol, who refereed the 2001 Champions League final between Bayern Munich and Valencia.

Ben Haverkort, who as a player received 73 yellow cards and six reds, many for verbally abusing referees.

View image in fullscreen Gillingham players remonstrate with the referee Steve Baines during a match against Norwich. Photograph: Christopher Lee/Action Images/Reuters

There is a more recent example in the women’s game: Cheryl Foster MBE, who won 63 caps for Wales and spent most of her club career at Liverpool. She then retrained as a referee; within three years of playing her final game, she was on the Fifa international list. Foster became one of the world’s best referees and took charge of the 2023 Women’s Champions League final between Barcelona and Wolfsburg.

View image in fullscreen The referee Cheryl Foster (centre) on duty for a Women’s Super League match between Manchester City v Arsenal. Photograph: Mike Egerton/PA

“There’s a picture of me picking the ball out of the little Jeep that drove the ball on to the pitch and I had the biggest smile,” said Foster when she retired last year. “To describe those feelings of doing major tournaments and a big final is incredible.”

The oldest goalscorers in town (II)

In last week’s Knowledge we looked at some of the oldest goalscorers in football history. But we missed one that was scoring in plain sight. You missed the second oldest goalscorer, 58-year-old Mykola Lykhovydov from Real Pharma in Ukraine,” writes Mykola Kozlenko. “There was even an article about him in the Guardian last year. He will not beat the new record though, as his club was relegated from professional football this summer after finishing last for two seasons in a row. At least unless they get promoted back and he is still around 60 ... ”

And though it wasn’t at first-team level, Tom Weir points out that, in 1992, the former Scotland manager Ally MacLeod scored a penalty for Queen of the South reserves at the age of 61.

Knowledge archive

“In the preliminary round of the English League Cup, Rochdale beat Tranmere 2-1 in a penalty shoot out. Is this the fewest goals scored in such a shoot out?” asks Paul Gage.

double quotation mark We had a similar question in 2008, when Mike Gibbons asked about the worst penalty shoot outs. Here’s what we said back then: As Bill Martin, Florian Kinast and Paul Fields all point out, the shoot-out in the 1986 European Cup final takes some beating. Barcelona and Steaua Bucharest had played out 120 of the most tedious minutes of football ever witnessed in a major final, and with the score at 0-0 the game went to penalties, at which point both teams missed their first two. The Romanians then found their shooting boots and knocked home their next two, but Barça, then managed by Terry Venables, twice more failed to beat Helmuth Duckadam in the Steaua goal. Duckadam, who became known as ‘the hero of Seville’, had saved all four spot-kicks from José Alexanko, Ángel Pedraza, Pichi Alonso and Marcos Alonso, enabling Steaua to run out 2-0 winners. Sadly Duckadam, who at 27 was reaching his peak years as a goalkeeper, was forced to retire shortly after his finest hour. “Just a few weeks after his epic moment,” writes Florian, “Duckadam’s career came to an end due to a rare vascular disease in his right arm.” Florian also points to Thailand’s 1-0 win on penalties over Bangladesh in the 1973 Merdeka Tournament, in which Singapore also beat Cambodia 1-0 in a shoot out. The world record for the worst-ever penalty shoot-out, however, is predictably held by a pair of English sides. In January 1998 the Under-10 sides Mickleover Lightning Blue Sox and Chellaston Boys met in the Derby Community Cup. The game finished 1-1 and the Blue Sox won 2-1 on penalties, though not until a remarkable 66 spot-kicks had been taken. Thanks to Paul Haynes for that one. All these and many other penalty-related facts, including the best-ever shootouts, can be found at the ever-marvellous rsssf.com

View image in fullscreen The gloves Helmuth Duckadam wore to save all four penalties for Steaua Bucharest against Barcelona in 1986. Photograph: Lucian Alecu/Alamy

Can you help?

“Mikel Arteta (one title) is the only manager with title-winning experience (in England) heading into the new season. Is this the only time since 1889-90 that there is only a single title among the managers at the start of the season?” wonders Jeremy Finch.

“Kerim Alajbegovic joined Leverkusen on 1 July after his buyback clause from Salzburg was activated for €8m. He’s currently in the process of moving to Juventus for €37m, meaning Leverkusen will profit to the tune of around €1m per day Alajbegovic was at the club. Has any player ever provided a greater ratio of profit per day than this?” asks Richard Wilson.

“As a fan of the Liga MX club Tigres UANL, it’s great to see them enter the record books (or trivia nights, at least) by having the shortest professional player in the world: 5ft 1ins Diego “Chicha” Sanchez,” begins Steve Smith. “Not only that, but he scored an excellent goal against San Luis on Saturday. Made me wonder: just how short are the shortest goalscorers for the top division leagues in Europe?

“Which footballer has played for the most clubs?” asks Paul Gage.

“I’ve driven through the North East on many occasions, and have regularly gone past Gateshead FC’s home (Gateshead International Stadium) and Newcastle United’s St James’ Park on the same journey,” writes Jack Birch. “Google Maps suggests the distance between these is 3.5 miles (or 2.3 miles if you are walking). Are there a combination of towns that beat this?”

“The Wrexham defender Max Cleworth had the letters of ‘Wrexham’ within his name,” notes Mark Lumby. “Have any other players had their club within their own name?”

Sports.title: Héctor Bellerín: ‘When you leave a club like Arsenal, it’s scary. It hurts’
Sports.content:
One day when he was 18 or 19, still near the start of his journey, Héctor Bellerín got a call from Mikel Arteta inviting him round. He remembers asking lunch or dinner but this was neither. “When I arrived that afternoon, he was sitting with a financial adviser and they started to ask: ‘How much do you spend on this?’ ‘How much do you spend on that?’. I was young, I’d just started to make money and spend money: on clothes, cars, the things we all do when you’re not really aware. I was pitching low. I felt embarrassed, ashamed, but I left with a lesson in humility and affection.

“Mikel was the first player who showed me that I was important to him, that I mattered. He demonstrates real care, if not through a hug. I said: ‘Thank you.’ He said: ‘If you do the same for a teammate one day I’m happy.’ The legacy he left is one I try to pass on so young players feel looked after and that’s an experience that defines Mikel very well.”

More than a decade later, it is one of many experiences, a lot of them in London, that help to define Bellerín too. Thirteen years between them, Arteta and Bellerín were teammates then; real mates, too. They have been player and coach, a shift in roles that was not always simple. On Wednesday they will be opponents. It is a pre-season friendly at the Aviva Stadium, not the Emirates Stadium, but for Bellerín it is special. The Real Betis full-back, 31 now, has never faced his former club. Only once could he have, on loan at Sporting, and then he got a knee injury – the timing so inconveniently exact that he cannot help wondering if it was in his head. He does so with his former club, led by his friend, as Premier League champions.

“I have an incredible feeling of love for the club,” he says, settling into a sofa 30 miles west of Dublin, still in his training kit. Fascinating company, he talks Serge Gnabry, Santi Cazorla and Nacho Monreal. He recalls the kindness of Tomas Rosicky telling him how to get the better of him in training, an experience he is repeating with José Antonio Morante, the 19-year-old winger who faces him daily, and the darker side of the sport, too. And he talks life and people and politics, having a voice and refusing to be silent: not because he sought one, not even because he is sure it changes things much, but because that’s the way he is, the personality built.

He talks about an industry which, he admits, often makes his “blood boil”, football becoming the “maximum exponent of greed”. About the pressure and the abuse. But he talks about how he loves the game too, how for all those other facets to him he is a footballer and always has been, how he is “addicted” to it, committed to it, and deserves his place here. On this occasion, though, he talks mostly about Arsenal, and there is warmth in every word.

“There are still players I grew up with: Bukayo [Saka], Ben White, the manager, coaches, staff. It still feels like family for me. My appreciation and affection for them is immense. I became a footballer there. I’m sure that my life, my way of being, of thinking, my conscience, all the things that represent me, were latent in me but they needed a place where they could be expressed. London gave me that space where I could explore my world, mature. There are places that could constrain you, but London was somewhere I could expand, explore life.”

View image in fullscreen Héctor Bellerín says ‘80% of my football came through Mikel [Arteta’s] mind’ during his time at Arsenal. Photograph: Paul Ellis/Reuters

It started lodging with the Twitching family in Enfield, on the Ridgeway: Donna and John and their kids, Tia and Ben. Bellerín was 16 from Barcelona. He was joined by Jon Toral, a teammate since they were eight, who played in India last season, and who embraced a new world with him then. “Roast dinner was a tradition. I didn’t understand that on Sunday you only ate once and then leftovers. That ‘journey’ was funny: last time I was in London I went to a pub to find a Sunday roast … but by then it’s vegan. Kentish Town. Elements of my personality totally come from England.

“The first thing Liam Brady, the academy director, gave me and Jon was an Oyster card. Jon would put on Sky, watch all the games, then the darts, then the snooker. We were earning €400 a month but there was a feeling of independence. I would ask Donna: ‘Where can I go?’ Camden, Covent Garden … to Brixton to play pool. We didn’t feel either overprotected or abandoned. We had to catch two buses and the tube for training. Over 12 years, I lived in all different places. I spent the pandemic living in a 17th-century farm in St Albans where the only way in was down a sand track.

“I would have loved to have been to the title-winning parade, but we still had games here. I was there in that moment of transition in Mikel’s first year as manager. But we won the FA Cup which was a key moment. One of the lovely things when they won the league was lots of people sent messages and I felt part of it. There are so many people I talk to, we’re all Gunners, and it was like a liberation, a release after so long.

“I was talking to Nacho [Monreal] and Santi [Cazorla]: it would be great if the three of us could go for a game. We were the group with Mikel. We knew that with Mikel one day Arsenal would win the league. In training he would ask: ‘What did you do at Barcelona? I would do this …’ [Later] I was with him a year and a half [as coach] and I could say that 80% of my football came through Mikel’s mind. His is a totally different vision. There’s an understanding, an observation, he sees patterns, and has a very specific language. I’d go so far as to say that he has put extra years on my career. I play totally differently to how I did at 19. That’s about experience but also a lot about what I learnt from Mikel: how to help my teammate, create advantages in my space. Bloody hell, I owe Mikel so much.”

“Our relationship going from teammates to coach and player was strange,” Bellerín says, pausing a moment. “I’m not sure we knew how to manage the transition. But face to face there was always that past there which meant we could talk honestly. I had decided that I had to go, but it wasn’t a conversation; it was lots of them going back a year. I feel huge admiration for him. And Betis arrived in the moment that I needed it.”

View image in fullscreen Héctor Bellerín says: ‘In Seville I have found a city that embraced me’. Photograph: Marc O’Sullivan/The Guardian

Why did you need it? There’s a pause. “There’s not a specific reason. Something happened but it’s not a thing; it’s more that there’s a kind of disconnect in which I felt that I could no longer help the club and the club could no longer help me. We managed that in the most amicable way. Maybe I needed to be close to my roots, home. It had been a long time. When you leave a club like Arsenal, it’s scary, eh. Scary. It hurts, mate: look, however much you know that your moment is over, it was your home. You were there for 10 years, you leave friends behind, a life … you don’t know what you are going to find on the other side. I was lucky.”

There is something about Betis, the club his grandmother and father supported, and about the city. Bellerín found a place. From the daily cycle into training to the writing classes, the fashion designing, the veganism and environmental activism, the commitment to sustainability and willingness to speak about toxic masculinity and the avarice of the game. The refuge from that: “What most struck me was the dressing room. There is something ‘horizontal’ in the relationship with other employees. At my other clubs that didn’t exist. That’s the essence of us, what sustains us. And it fits with my values. In Seville I have found a city that embraced me, allowed my existence beyond football.”

And the football has worked out nicely too, for him, Betis and Arsenal. “It’s been good for both of us. Look where Arsenal are. We’re in the Champions League, we won the cup. I’m in a very good moment. It was right. The Champions League final hurt but it’s important that doesn’t overshadow Arsenal’s progress. They are where they deserve to be; it’s a very sweet moment. To be able to face them now, the best team in Europe, is the business.”

Sports.title: Trabzonspor aim to sign Mohamed Salah this week after opening transfer talks
Sports.content:
The Turkish Super Lig side Trabzonspor say they have begun transfer ⁠negotiations with Mohamed Salah, with the club chair adding they hoped to sign the Egypt forward later this week.

“Negotiations have been launched ⁠to transfer professional footballer ⁠Mohamed Salah, ​who is in a free status, to our club,” the club said in a statement.

Speaking to the broadcaster ⁠A Spor, the Trabzonspor chair Ertugrul Dogan said that while the transfer was not completed, Salah is expected to arrive ⁠in Istanbul for a medical on Wednesday and then go to Trabzon to sign with the ​Black Sea side.

He did not confirm ‌when the contract would be ‌signed, but said it would likely be on Thursday.

Salah left Liverpool this summer after nine ‌years, having scored 257 goals in 442 appearances, where he won the Premier League twice and the Champions League once.

In the 2024-25 season Salah scored 29 Premier League goals and provided 18 assists, equalling the league record for most goal involvements in a season and setting the record for a 38-game campaign.

He was named Premier League Player ‌of the Season and won the Golden Boot and the Playmaker Award, becoming the first player to take all three in one campaign.

His output ​waned last season, with seven goals and seven assists in 27 league matches and he was left on the bench in Champions League games, leading to a public spat with Liverpool’s then-manager Arne Slot.

The 34-year-old began his career in Europe at Swiss side Basel in 2012 and ⁠later joined Chelsea. He also had brief stints at Fiorentina and Roma between 2015 and 2017 ​before joining Liverpool.

Trabzonspor – generally ​considered to be the fourth-biggest team in Turkey after Istanbul ​sides Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, and ‌Besiktas – finished third ​in the Super Lig ​last season and will enter the Europa League playoffs.

Salah had been close to joining Istanbul club Besiktas, whose football director Onder Ozen said negotiations had stalled over financial and image-rights demands, according to local media.

Sports.title: The Fifa family: which confederations could support Infantino or turn against him?
Sports.content:
The pressure is growing on the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, with many countries withdrawing their support following the bungled World Cup sell-off. However, how key is Infantino’s relationship with each confederation and is it likely that an election contest will actually happen? We look at the key considerations, confederation by confederation.

1) How does each confederation view Infantino’s re-election?

Uefa (Europe) has firmly led the moves under way to achieve Infantino’s removal. The threat last week to boycott all Fifa competitions if the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme was not scrapped contributed hugely to its failure. In a scathing statement on Saturday, Uefa said the current Fifa leadership had “not only lost Uefa’s confidence, but also that of many other members of the football family”, and pledged to push for change. Some Uefa member associations, including the English and Welsh FAs, have withdrawn their letters of support for Infantino’s re‑election and efforts are continuing to ensure others follow suit in a bid to weaken his position irretrievably. Nick Ames

Reports of AFC (Asia) support for Uefa are premature; the confederation is divided. The AFC has spoken out, strongly in relative terms compared to its usual pronouncements, against the proposed World Cup deal and has called for reform of Fifa. The AFC has been a staunch supporter in the past but if it looks as if Infantino is in trouble the AFC leadership, which was genuinely angry at how the proposal was made (probably more so than the actual details of the deal), could switch sides, which would probably confirm Infantino’s downfall if Uefa and Concacaf oppose but it is not a foregone conclusion – some in Asia are not convinced that Uefa has the numbers. The big problem is that, while the AFC leadership may want Infantino out, most individual Asian federations do not want him to be replaced. The AFC president, Sheikh Salman, has ambitions of his own and has been historically successful at preserving AFC unity but this will be tricky especially as west Asian nations such as Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia support Infantino and are influential in Asia. It could be that the only way to ensure Asian unity is to have an Asian candidate. Jordan’s Prince Ali bin Hussein’s claim of “blackmail” could prove a significant moment, however. John Duerden

Concacaf (North and Central America, and the Caribbean) is among the confederations that have come out strongly against Infantino and his FFE proposal, first directly rejecting it and then releasing a statement after it was withdrawn that took direct aim at Infantino. A release speaking on behalf of Concacaf’s 41 member associations called the plan “a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first”, and a “unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership” and said that “a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency is imperative”.

That is about as direct a call for no confidence in Infantino as you are likely to get outside of an election itself. It should be noted, of course, that the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is also a Fifa vice-president and would be a leading candidate to run for president should there be a united desire among confederations to oust Infantino. Montagliani has kept silent on the subject when asked in the past but this statement, which speaks for him, shows at the very least he is not immune to the idea of going against Infantino. Alexander Abnos

View image in fullscreen Victor Montagliani, pictured consoling Lionel Messi after the World Cup final, is a potential successor to Gianni Infantino. Photograph: Will Oliver/EPA

Patrice Motsepe, president of the Confederation of African Football, has said the 54 member associations are in unanimous support of Infantino’s re-election in Morocco next year. Osasu Obayiuwana

Since the rumpus over Infantino’s proposed FFE broke and died, the South American confederation, Conmebol, has been notably silent. Its president, Alejandro Domínguez, has been posting birthday wishes to individuals, clubs and institutions from Uruguay where he is visiting ahead of the 2030 centenary of the first World Cup. Unlike Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC, which publicly opposed Fifa’s aborted FFE proposal, Conmebol took several days before issuing a fence-sitting statement stressing football first, and requesting further information and clarification. That was the only official response at all, and there has been absolute silence since.

“Conmebol’s current position is best described as cautious support rather than open confrontation,” says Marina Mendez, a director of AD Sporting Industry Professionals and a friend of Conmebol who consults on football in the region. “The distinction is politically significant. It suggests Conmebol wants to preserve its institutional relationship with Fifa and maintain room for negotiation, rather than join a public campaign against Infantino. This should not necessarily be interpreted as unconditional personal loyalty. Conmebol’s approach is pragmatic: it is protecting South American football’s access, influence and negotiating position within Fifa while assessing how the international balance of power develops.”

Brazil and Argentina are the main countries, and Domínguez looks after the relationship with both, with most of the other countries expected to follow suit. “They are not federations likely to confront Infantino directly because they will always prefer to be on the right side of the non-Europeans,” says an industry insider who does not wish to be named. Marcela Mora y Araujo

It remains to be seen what the 11 Oceania Football Confederation member associations will do. New Zealand, the leading member of the confederation, was quick to come out against the World Cup proposal – though the reaction of the OFC itself was noncommittal – and there is still support for Infantino among the other federations. John Duerden

Uefa The parties go back a long way. Infantino was Uefa’s secretary general from 2009 until 2016 and it backed him strongly when he first ran for the Fifa presidency. But there has long been push and pull between the global governing body and that of football’s most powerful continent. Relations have deteriorated in recent years, Uefa fending off Infantino-led initiatives such as a biennial staging of the World Cup and a proposed investment in 2018 by SoftBank. Things appeared to reach a head in May 2025 when delegates from several European federations walked out of Fifa’s annual congress in protest at Infantino’s late arrival. They accused him of pursuing “private political interests”. That turned out to be the tip of the iceberg. The past year’s near-interminable list of Fifa-related controversies have further ensured that the differences between the two are irreconcilable. NA

AFC It has been a close relationship, Salman and AFC have backed Infantino since he beat Salman in the 2016 election. It is not just about money either, though this is of course important. He is seen as approachable, available and open. Fifa has historically been seen as a European (and to a lesser extent South American) institution in Asia, and while Infantino is from Uefa, he is seen as a leader who gives equal weight to all. One president said to me that in the past, conversations with Fifa were like receiving decrees from above but now there is a genuine dialogue. World Cup expansion has gone down well, 64 teams would be welcomed too, and there are more tournaments held in Asia these days. Infantino has already been reminding Asia about this. JD

View image in fullscreen Sheikh Salman and the AFC have backed Gianni Infantino since he beat Salman in the 2016 election. Photograph: Vincent Thian/AP

Concacaf Infantino’s most direct relationship has been as the president under whom the World Cup was awarded to the US, Mexico and Canada, after a bid from the US lost out to Qatar for the 2022 hosting rights. Aside from that, there was not much of a direct, historic relationship between Infantino and Concacaf – at least, not until the letter released by the confederation over the weekend. AA

CAF Infantino’s association with African football began in 2016, when he backed Ahmad Ahmad of Madagascar to topple the late Issa Hayatou as CAF president in March 2017. Being an eyewitness to that election, at the African Union HQ in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, I recall the anger with which Hayatou confronted Infantino and Fatma Samoura, then Fifa secretary general, over their involvement in an election.

Infantino, under Ahmad’s ill-fated four-year tenure between 2017 and 2021 – which ended in his untimely removal from office over ethics violations – got Fifa to take over the daily administration of the CAF from August to December 2019, with Samoura going to Egypt to take charge of the organisation. Many in African football saw this as a neo-colonial act and a direct violation of the CAF’s autonomy and independence. Infantino was involved in the ascension of Motsepe to the presidency in March 2021. OO

Conmebol Along comes Infantino, the Uefa salvation who promises an anti-corruption ticket. After Julio Grondona’s death, an AFA (Argentina Football Association) election found more votes than members and Fifa intervened, naming a committee of industry insiders to oversee a cleansing of the house. Infantino was present in the AFA headquarters at its inaugural press conference. Imagine Infantino launching an English FA governance intervention.

In 2018, in Buenos Aires for a Libertadores final to be played by two clubs from the same city for the first time in Argentina’s history (policing was a mess and fan violence before the second leg led to its suspension and eventual move to Madrid) Infantino was invited by the then president of Argentina, Mauricio Macri, to be guest of honour at the G20 held in the city later that week.

Infantino, as we know him today is created then, photographed gifting football shirts to the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman and Donald Trump, POTUS at the time. “Yes, that G20 was key for Infantino, because he’d inherited a corruption scandal. He needed to instil the belief that football would cease to be a mafia, that he would achieve this. And he managed,” Macri, now president of the Fifa Foundation, told the Guardian: “From an ethical point of view he is impeccable. There is nothing odd in Fifa today, Fifa manages fortunes, more than ever, because Infantino is successful; he organises competitions that are more and more profitable, and it’s all above board. I should say the same applies to Conmebol.”

The Conmebol president, Nicolás Leoz, fell in the same Fifagate swoop, although he had left office in 2013. A series of interim and short-lived presidencies ensued until January 2016 when current president Domínguez took his post. Unanimously voted in by the 10 member associations, he pushed for every professional club to have a female team and introduced “hydration” breaks before this World Cup, albeit less structured ones. Infantino has also maintained a functional and stable relationship with the AFA president, Claudio “Chiqu” Tapia. “This relationship is politically relevant because Macri has been an opponent of “Chiqui” Tapia,” Mendez says. “This demonstrates Infantino’s ability to maintain links with both sides of Argentine football’s internal power structure.” Tapia was approached for comment. MMA

View image in fullscreen Claudio Tapia of Argentina’s FA has a stable relationship with the Fifa president. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters

OFC Like Asia, Infantino has worked hard to build relationships both of the personal and financial kind. It is common to hear officials describe him as a friend. The expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams finally gave Oceania an automatic World Cup spot – something that Fifa had promised in the past but never delivered. And the idea of having more spots in a 64-team competition was also attractive. Under Infantino, New Zealand co-hosted the Women’s World Cup with Australia. Fifa also supported the establishment of the Oceania Professional League that kicked off in January to provide much-needed pro club football for the region. JD

3) How financially dependent is the confederation on Infantino and Fifa?

Uefa Not at all. While the World Cup is Fifa’s most essential driver of revenue, Uefa can lay claim, among other things, to the highly lucrative Champions League and the vast sums that it attracts on an annual basis. Expanding its tournaments and staging them more often is one of the only ways available for Fifa to keep pace. Private investment would not harm its cause, either. Uefa’s annual revenues have recently totalled around double those of Fifa; as things stand football’s powerhouse can cope perfectly well on its own. NA

AFC Like always in Asia, it varies. There are rich federations on either side of the continent but in between there are some that are almost completely dependent on Fifa money. Bhutan, for example, gets $1.5m a year, which makes up the majority of its budget. Even Australia, which has reached the knockout stages of the past two World Cups, has lost around $17m over the past two years, which may explain its rather vague statement calling for more time when the plan was first heard. JD

View image in fullscreen Paul Okon Engstler, Jackson Irvine and Harry Souttar after Australia’s World Cup exit; even their federation, one of AFC’s richest, loses money. Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters

Concacaf This is a very top‑heavy confederation, perhaps more so than any other in the world. The US and Mexico have been regional powers for most of the past 30‑40 years, and recently Canada has shown signs it can compete on the field and is addressing business issues off of it. Just below them is a middle class consisting of Panama, Jamaica, Costa Rica and Honduras. The remaining 33 Concacaf nations are fairly small by comparison, and thus naturally more reliant on funding from Fifa via the forward programme and other initiatives. The fact that smaller Caribbean nations feel empowered to join with the big dogs says a lot about how at risk they feel they may be without Infantino at Fifa’s helm. AA

CAF The confederation funds activities from its own commercial revenue, so it is not dependent on Fifa and Infantino in that sense. But the majority of CAF’s 54 member associations are financially challenged and are dependent on the annual grants that the world governing body gives them to meet their operating costs. OO

Conmebol It represents only 10 nation members. Variations among them notwithstanding, the federations are self-sufficient economically and their local leagues are attractive and profitable. Their national teams are the No 1 sporting attraction, pulling in vast numbers of fans who are emotionally attached to their heroes, who in turn love to play for their country. The main sources of revenue for clubs are TV rights, marketing and the sale of players. For this, the top market is the Premier League (which operates entirely outside the FA and therefore Fifa) and the other European leagues, which are also largely independent of their FAs. Montevideo has produced more World Cup players than any other city in history, so even a financially struggling association such as Uruguay’s continues to rely more on the income from the development of youth talent than Fifa aid. There were six Argentinian managers with extensive international trajectories at this World Cup. Exporting home‑grown talent, of which there is plenty, is a bigger source of revenue than Fifa project distribution funds. Two of the most colourful stories of the World Cup, the Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha and the New Zealand defender Tim Payne, transferred to Chilean and Paraguayan clubs respectively following their popularity during the tournament. Popularity due in no small part to the efforts of streamers and influencers from Argentina and Brazil. MMA

OFC Oceania is made up of small federations that tend to be reliant on what Fifa gives them. So the recent World Cup proposal would, had it gone through, have made a huge difference financially. JD

4) Would a breakaway cause an existential threat?

Uefa Europe has the strongest club and international teams in the world. Parting ways from Infantino and Fifa would be unlikely to cause serious damage, although it could cause issues with clubs who have been looking to expand their global reach through the revamped Club World Cup. It is plausible that bigger teams from other continents would seek to join forces with Uefa and compete in new tournaments given the kudos and financial opportunities available when competing with the majority of the sport’s giants. NA

View image in fullscreen European clubs such as Chelsea have been looking to expand their global reach through Fifa’s revamped Club World Cup. Photograph: Justin Lane/EPA

AFC It is a generalisation but, in Asia, Fifa as an institution does not make the headlines that it does in western Europe. Usually, interest in a country comes when they are affected specifically by a decision, as when bidding for a tournament. In my experience, there just isn’t the same interest in the day‑to‑day running of the organisation. Breaking with Infantino would not be a massive threat to Asia but there is some concern about a return to a more Europe‑dominated Fifa, if that were to materialise. While pretty much everyone has supported Infantino from 2016 until the past few days, Asian federations that have done so are seen in some quarters as being corrupt and/or greedy but the Europeans, who did exactly the same, are now trying to paint themselves as the moral guardians of the sport. JD

Concacaf If a breakaway would cause an existential threat, then Concacaf is living it right now. One could certainly read it as a principled stand, but it’s hard to separate the confederation’s statement with Montagliani’s current position as Infantino’s most likely successor, should the latter need to stand down. AA

CAF The relationship between Infantino and Africa’s 54 national associations is largely seen as a “master-servant” one, in which he basically tells the FA/federation heads, through Fifa officials, to do his bidding. Those who do not toe the political line of Zurich, as decided by Infantino, may well end up having their books audited over how they have spent their Fifa grants. Many FA/federation presidents faced Fifa ethics proceedings and subsequent bans as a result. OO

Conmebol “There’s no morality involved, just politics,” the industry insider says. Mendez concurs: “It’s not a simple case of morality, it’s a power struggle and a rupture in perspectives about football in general and the business of football in particular. Today, Eurocentrism is dominating, and things like sponsored hydration breaks and Super Bowl-style half-time shows impose a North American regard hitherto unseen.” MMA

OFC Oceania welcomed the fact that Infantino had a “global” mentality and went out of his way to engage with smaller nations far from the centre of global football power. If the confederation does break away, it would want something similar in the opposition candidate and not a return to the old days when the confederation was an afterthought in the corridors of power. JD

5) How important is the current and historical relationship?

A strong relationship between Uefa and Fifa would make for a far more harmonious global football scene but, as described above, there is huge work to do before that can be repaired. NA

It’s very important – barring some new organisation stepping in to run world football in a better way, Fifa is Concacaf’s best link to the traditional power centres of world football. The US, Mexico and Canada derive a lot of their value as federations from how they’ve been able to perform at men’s and women’s World Cups – that’s not something they’ll want to give up lightly, which is perhaps why they did not threaten a boycott the way Uefa did. AA

CAF Africa’s political power within Fifa began to rise in 1974, when João Havelange successfully courted the continent as a block and made it an important pillar of his electoral victory over Sir Stanley Rous in Germany, becoming the first and only non-European, to date, to be Fifa president. Sepp Blatter, Havelange’s successor in 1998, also leveraged Africa’s support in a similar fashion to defeat the Uefa president Lennart Johansson. Delivering on his promise to the continent that it would host a World Cup during his presidency, which South Africa did in 2010, bolstered his popularity and support base on the continent. But the last 10 years of the Infantino presidency have made many resent the undue influence of the world governing body in Africa’s affairs. OO

View image in fullscreen Sepp Blatter, pictured with the then South Africa president Jacob Zuma at the 2010 World Cup, cultivated support in African football. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Conmebol Fifa as we know it was essentially invented, developed and moulded by the Brazil and Argentina federation presidents Havelange and Grondona respectively. They specifically wanted to break Europe’s stronghold. Initially, they started funding grassroots via “partnerships” with big brands, which benefited from reaching wider markets. A vivid example is the giant sign with a Coca-Cola bottle on every corner of the pitch, seen in places such as Russia and China where advertising was otherwise prohibited, every single time a corner kick was awarded. After Havelange’s time at the helm was up, Blatter took the lead. Blatter kept Grondona close by, his right-hand man, while the business venture grew and grew, and places for other confederations increased. When Fifagate blew up, most leaders close to the top faced trials and disgrace; Grondona was saved by death.

Infantino’s reign was a continuation of keeping Conmebol as a key ally. The historic power derived from on-the-pitch success in the region, and the crown jewel that is Lionel Messi, have contributed to keeping the small confederation big. “The relationship is neither purely personal nor purely institutional. It is built on mutual strategic value,” says Mendez. “The coming election will be Uefa versus footballistic populism,” the industry source said. “Conmebol owns Fifa.” MMA

Sports.title: Manchester United set to appoint former Hearts manager Eva Olid as new head coach
Sports.content:
Manchester United are set to appoint the former Hearts manager Eva Olid as their new head coach to replace Marc Skinner, following his exit on Monday, multiple sources have told the Guardian.

Talks with the 40-year-old are understood to be very advanced and she is expected to be introduced to the United squad on Wednesday.

United are confident that the Spanish coach is the right person to lead them into a new chapter, as first reported by the Telegraph, as the Women’s Super League club focuses on developing young, homegrown players.

Olid led Hearts to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title last term on a dramatic final day of the season, but it had already been confirmed in April that she was to leave the Edinburgh club this summer by mutual agreement. She was in charge of Hearts for five years and also guided them to the 2024 Scottish Cup final, where they were beaten by Rangers.

She has previously coached in the United States with Houston Dynamo, working with their women’s team and their under-19s men’s squad, before she had a spell with the Catalan Football Association.

United are understood to be impressed by her playing style and her ability to develop and improve players, and they carried out extensive background checks on Olid prior to publicly announcing Skinner’s departure on Monday, with succession planning having already been well under way.

Skinner left partly because of frustration at United’s transfer strategy. The club are understood to feel the current level of spending across the WSL is unsustainable and they want a different approach, focusing on their own younger talents and improving their academy to deliver longer-term success.

View image in fullscreen Marc Skinner left Manchester United party because of frustration over the club’s transfer strategy. Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/Reuters

United finished fourth in the WSL last term. They start the new season away to big-spending London City Lionesses on 4 September.

The news comes on the day that the United captain, Maya Le Tissier, said her team will “stick together” and be ready for the new WSL season, despite Skinner departing.

Le Tissier and the rest of the playing squad were informed by Skinner that he would be leaving, in a meeting on Monday morning shortly before the news was announced, and on Tuesday Le Tissier and her England teammate Ella Toone paid tribute to Skinner for his contribution to the club over five years in charge, which included winning the 2024 Women’s FA Cup.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Le Tissier said the “energy he brought to the club was amazing”, while Toone told reporters: “He wanted to tell the team before it came out. It was nice that he was able to tell us [and] he was able to say goodbye, because he’s done a lot for the club. We can’t thank him enough for everything he’s done, the hard work and the passion that he’s put into leading this team.”

Le Tissier said that neither she nor Toone have been consulted on who the next head coach should be but added: “I think the club have been pretty clear with what they’ve said, bringing through the youth, that’s what something Manchester United has been kind of made for, and they’ve always done that historically. I think they’ve been pretty clear with that. When we speak to the new manager, the ambitions will be clear.

“Me and Tooney are at Man United because we want to win and we’ll be doing everything we can to make that happen. We’ve got a great team, a great squad, great girls. I’m ready to do that.

“No matter who comes and goes, we’ve always had that togetherness and that fight for each other and we stick together in tough moments. There’s been a few over the years and we’ve always come through as a team, and, yeah, this one might be difficult right now, we’re in the start of pre-season and we want to make sure that we’re 100% ready for the start of the season.

“We spoke to the girls today, we’ll stick together, we always do. We’ve got to go out on the pitch, enjoy playing football and being with each other and we’ll get through it.”

Sports.title: Football legend LUIS FIGO: Infantino's behaviour is the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested I've ever seen. Nothing gets in the way of pleasing his friends and he must go NOW
Sports.content:
Football legend LUIS FIGO: Infantino's behaviour is the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested I've ever seen. Nothing gets in the way of pleasing his friends and he must go NOW

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

I could write 10,000 words on the problems at FIFA. But the solution needs only three: Infantino must go.

I have loved football all my life. I was a professional player for 20 years. And believe me, I have met some rogues in my time in the game.

But what I have seen exposed in the last 10 days is the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed.

The man who would do that - the man who would try to force through such major changes just to enrich himself and his friends - is a relic of the game’s past and should have no part in its future.

If it was such a good idea, why not tell your members when you had them all in a room before the World Cup Final?

If it was such a robust plan, why not tell your members the risks as well as what you describe as the benefits?

Portugal legend Luis Figo (right) pictured with under pressure FIFA president Gianni Infantino

Infantino is holding crisis talks with staff after calling an urgent meeting in Morocco tomorrow

If the scheme was a no-brainer, why not be honest about the fact that it was going to give you a $30m-a-year job at the end of it?

But none of this was done. Because it’s not a good idea. It’s not robust when you fail to be transparent about the crippling returns that private equity always seek.

It’s not bold when you fail to explain that once you have sold your share it is gone forever and you have disinherited your successors from ownership of the World Cup.

And it’s not honest when you fail to mention that, after you have delivered the head of the World Cup on a platter to your mates in DC, they are going to give you a job worth five times your current salary.

None of this comes as a surprise when you consider the litany of abuses he has inflicted on football’s reputation; from suspending and reversing disciplinary decisions to breaking the laws of the game over a half-time show, nothing gets in the way of pleasing his friends.

Nor is it a surprise when you read the comments of (Jordan FA president) Prince Ali, highlighting the mob-like behaviour of Infantino’s FIFA; obstructing his FA’s work and funding in order to secure a nomination letter so that the reign of terrible self-interest can continue.

Football does need a discussion about money. But not the money that could go out of the game to investors or on bloated administrator salaries.

I mean the money that should be spent on building pitches and training coaches to make sure that every child in the world has the chance to fall in love with the most beautiful sport on the planet.

I mean the $5bn in FIFA’s reserves for a start. How many shares could that buy in this grubby, underhand plot? All of them! So there is no need for outside investment after all.

The FIFA president 'deviously' and 'cravenly' plotted to sell the World Cup to private investors

This plan – like the Super League before it – was blown apart by the media exposing every devious twist and turn before its advocates had their messaging straight. And thank goodness it was.

Infantino has debased the office of FIFA President that he promised to elevate. He has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest at the expense of the game he is supposed to serve.

He has lost the support of his senior staff, his closest advisers, the vast majority of people who devote their lives to this sport and even, it would seem, the FIFA Peace Prize winner.

It is too late to save his dignity but it is not too late to save football. He should go. Now.

Luis Figo played almost 800 games in a glittering club career spanning Sporting Lisbon, Barcelona, Real Madrid and Inter Milan. He also won 127 caps for Portugal and has been a UEFA football advisor since 2017.

Sports.title: Mohamed Salah closes on Turkey move: Former Liverpool star pictured in Trabzonspor kit and sends message to fans - as supporters gather at the airport ahead of his arrival
Sports.content:
Mohamed Salah closes on Turkey move: Former Liverpool star pictured in Trabzonspor kit and sends message to fans - as supporters gather at the airport ahead of his arrival

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Mohamed Salah was greeted by crowds of Trabzonspor fans after arriving in Istanbul ahead of completing a move to the Turkish club.

Fans had gathered in anticipation for Salah's arrival after the former Liverpool star travelled to the city on a private jet.

Salah was pictured on the jet wearing a Trabzonspor shirt, featuring his name and the number 61 - which is regularly used as a symbol of the city and the club.

A video was released by the club with Salah addressing fans ahead of his imminent arrival.

'Trabzon are you ready, I can hear you,' Salah said. 'See you very soon.'

The pictures and video were released as the 34-year-old began travelling from the Greek island of Mykonos, where he has been on holiday following his World Cup involvement with Egypt.

Bordo-Mavili formasıyla ilk kez kameraların karşısında… İlk mesajı Büyük Trabzonspor Taraftarına:



“Bize Her Yer Trabzon!” ❤️💙#SalahIsComing pic.twitter.com/Sr1KcRDwpk — Trabzonspor (@Trabzonspor) August 5, 2026

Mohamed Salah was greeted by Trabzonspor fans at the Ataturk Airport as he closes on a move to the Turkish side

Salah was seen conducting the crowds that had gathered ahead of his high-profile transfer

🔴🔵 Trabzonsporlu taraftarlar, Atatürk Havalimanı Genel Havacılık Terminali'nde Muhammed Salah'ı bekliyor. 📽️ pic.twitter.com/HhiszHpHXg — AA SPOR (@aa_spor) August 5, 2026

His club future is now close to being decided, having become a free agent after agreeing to tear up the final year of his Liverpool contract.

Trabzonspor had invited their supporters to pay to join a live stream following Salah's flight to Turkey, as fans gathered outside the Ataturk Airport ahead of his arrival.

A private jet took off from Mykonos Airport around 10.30am as Salah began his journey.

Turkish giants Besiktas were understood to be the Egyptian's first choice but talks with them stalled last week.

Trabzonspor revealed their talks with Salah on Tuesday night, with the club informing their 1.9million followers on X of his travel arrangements, as well as telling fans a welcome programme would be in place.

The club wrote: 'Public Announcement: Negotiations have begun regarding the transfer of professional footballer Mohamed Salah to our Club.'

The club then posted: 'Professional footballer Mohamed Salah, with whom we have begun transfer negotiations, will be at Istanbul Atatürk Airport General Aviation Terminal at 12:00 on Wednesday, August 5.

'The player is scheduled to arrive in Trabzon on the same day in the evening hours.

Salah had earlier been pictured on a private jet as he travelled from Mykonos to Istanbul

The former Liverpool star is set to sign a two-year contract with the Turkish club

Fans had arrived at the airport after Trabzonspor announced Salah's travel schedule for the day

Salah is set to continue his journey to Trabzon later today to complete the transfer

Trabzonspor fans celebrated the high-profile arrival of Salah ahead of the new season

'The time and other details regarding the welcome program in Trabzon will be shared with the public through our club's official communication channels during the day.'

Trabzonspor also shared a 17-second AI video of a camera shot panning from pyramids over mountains to a view of their 41,000-seater stadium Papara Park.

Salah's future has been the subject of huge interest since the surprising decision was announced back in March that he would leave Liverpool one year into his two-year contract extension.

Many anticipated that Saudi Arabia would be the most likely destination after Al-Ittihad made a £150million bid in summer 2023.

But Trabzonspor are now set to sign the winger, who fell out with Arne Slot at Anfield last term.

The Turkish side finished third last season behind Fenerbahce and champions Galatasaray.

Salah, who is the third-highest goalscorer in Reds history with 255, did not engage in talks with teams before the end of the season out of respect to the Merseyside club.

His long-serving agent, Ramy Abbas, repeatedly insisted nothing had been decided and reaffirmed that stance during the World Cup.

But since returning from the competition in the US, talks have accelerated with interested parties.

A Trabzonspor fan was seen kissing a tifo of Saah after his arrival at Istanbul airport

Salah is renowned for his remarkable professionalism and will back himself to remain at a high level deep into his thirties.

Salah was the star man as Slot’s side won the Premier League in Slot's first season, the Egyptian's second English title, but his level dipped last term with just ten goals compared to a staggering 34 when he spear-headed the 2024-25 title win.

Liverpool are yet to replace the player who was voted Professional Footballers' Association (PFA) Players' Player of the Year three times at the club.

With the start of the season fast approaching, Bradley Barcola of PSG remains the most likely high-profile attacking signing.

But the 23-year-old, valued at £145million by his club, plays predominantly on the left and Jamie Carragher recently warned against buying him as a replacement for Salah.

Salah would be the most high-profile signing in Trabzonspor's history and if his expected move is confirmed, will join Man United loanee Andre Onana.

Ex-Man City defender Stefan Savic also plays for the Turkish side, who have won their domestic title seven times.

Sports.title: Aston Villa braced for fresh Arsenal bid for Ezri Konsa as Gunners agreed £75m fee for Bruno Guimaraes... and Mo Salah jets in to Turkey: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
Aston Villa braced for fresh Arsenal bid for Ezri Konsa as Gunners agreed £75m fee for Bruno Guimaraes... and Mo Salah jets in to Turkey: WINDOW WATCH

It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Coventry aim to break transfer record AGAIN

Coventry are attempting to break their transfer record for the second time this week after offering nearly £26million for Ghana star Caleb Yirenkyi.

The midfielder, who plays for Danish club Nordsjaelland, represented his country at this summer’s World Cup as they drew 0-0 with England and exited at the first knockout stage.

Back in the top flight for the first time in 25 years, the Sky Blues have already signed goalkeeper Carl Rushworth for £22.5m as well as defender Aurele Amenda and winger Loum Tchaouna. They have also turned on-loan midfielder Frank Onyeka’s move from Brentford into a permanent switch.

TOM COLLOMOSSE

Caleb Yirenkyi featured for Ghana against England in the 0-0 draw at the World Cup

Arsenal set to come back for Konsa

Aston Villa are braced for a fresh bid from Arsenal for England defender Ezri Konsa amid attempts to tie him to a new contract.

Daily Mail Sport reported last month that Konsa was the Gunners’ top target for central defence though their initial proposal was well below Villa’s £60million valuation of the 28-year-old.

Konsa has remained on Arsenal’s radar since. He has two years remaining on his current deal at Villa Park and the club would like him to sign a new one.

Having already seen key men Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans depart this summer, and with Lucas Digne poised to join Paris Saint-Germain, Villa boss Unai Emery would have an even bigger rebuilding job were Konsa to depart.

Having recouped more than £140million for Rogers, who joined Chelsea, and Tielemans, who signed for Manchester United, Villa are not under financial pressure to sell Konsa and are unlikely to do so without a high-level replacement lined up.

But along with Bruno Guimaraes and Vinicius Junior, Konsa is a key target for Arsenal – especially with William Saliba facing a lengthy injury absence – and they are unlikely to give up hope.

TOM COLLOMOSSE

Ezri Konsa would join England team-mate Declan Rice if Arsenal can pull off a deal

Come in No 61! Salah on his way to Turkey

The fee is inclusive of bonuses for the highly-rated 22-year-old and there is also a 35pc sell-on clause plus matching rights and a buy back option for the Czech.

Tottenham defender Ashley Phillips, 21, is also in talks over a move to Boro.

Kim Hellberg has brought in seven signings so far this summer, including Will Lankshear from Spurs in a deal worth up to £20m.
