World.title: Did Fauci properly take the Fifth? The Senate could put that claim to the test
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Dr. Anthony Fauci, the point man for America’s pandemic response who was once the doyen of Hollywood (see here and here), turned in a less-than-stellar performance before the Senate Homeland Security Committee. After giving a short, entirely self-serving opening statement during which he accused Committee Chair Sen. Rand Paul of having an "unhinged obsession" with him, Fauci invoked the 5th Amendment Self-Incrimination Clause, which allows a witness to refuse to answer questions if doing so might incriminate him, 111 times to avoid answering questions. But was his invocation proper, and, regardless, what can the Senate do about it?

Several factors suggest Fauci’s invocation was improper. Two are critical.

The first is Fauci’s pardon. Prior to leaving office, Joe Biden issued a blanket pardon to Fauci for any federal crimes he might have committed "from January 1, 2014, through [January 19, 2025] arising from or in any manner related to his service as Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, as a member of the White House Coronavirus Task Force or the White House COVID-19 Response Team, or as Chief Medical Advisor to the President."

CAN FAUCI HIDE BEHIND THE FIFTH? GAME-CHANGING BIDEN PARDON MAY NOT PROVIDE COMPLETE COVER, EXPERTS SAY

The second is time: Fauci retired in 2022, making it unlikely that any state crime he might have committed would fall within the applicable statute of limitations, assuming any state could credibly claim that he committed a crime or that venue was proper in that state. In Hoffman v. United States (1951), the Supreme Court said the privilege against self-incrimination protects against real dangers, not remote or speculative possibilities.

Two other things are clear. First, a witness can refuse to answer questions that might implicate him in a crime, not to avoid embarrassment. The Fifth Amendment is available only to avoid criminal exposure, not public ridicule. Prior to the hearing, Sen. Paul released over 1,000 pages from Fauci’s diary in which he chronicled fawning media stories about him as well as conversations with politicians, media personalities, and celebrities who heaped praise on him. They also suggest that he directed staff members to nominate him for various awards that netted him around $900,000. There are also entries suggesting he did not believe several of the public statements he made at the time about the virus’s origin or the efficacy of the measures he implemented to prevent the spread of the disease. Second, a witness cannot invoke the Fifth Amendment because he thinks he will be charged with perjury even if he provides truthful testimony.

On the other hand, there are factors in Fauci's favor. First, President Trump and several Republican Congressmen are arguing that Biden’s last-minute pardons, which would include Fauci’s, are null and void because, they claim, Biden’s staff used his auto-pen to sign those pardons without Biden’s knowledge or approval. If Fauci’s pardon is invalidated, he could be prosecuted by the Justice Department for federal crimes he might have committed during the period covered by the Biden pardon. Second, several state attorneys general have now said they are initiating investigations to see whether Fauci committed any state crimes related to his government service. Perhaps they envision a perjury charge for deposition testimony Fauci provided in Covid-related litigation. That effort might end up going nowhere, but Fauci is certainly entitled to take them at their word that he still faces legal jeopardy. These statements alone make it far more likely that a judge would ultimately determine that Fauci’s invocation of the Fifth was proper.

Now that Fauci has invoked the Fifth and refused to answer the Senators’ questions, what can Congress do about it? Well, it has several options.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: WHY FAUCI'S 111 FIFTH AMENDMENT PLEAS COULD END UP BEFORE THE COURTS

The one they are currently contemplating is voting to hold him in contempt of Congress. This would require a majority vote by the Committee and by the full Senate. Since Republicans are in the majority, it is possible, if not likely, they have the votes to do that. If so, the matter would be referred to the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia (currently, Jeanine Pirro) to decide whether to seek charges against Fauci. If that happens, a judge will decide whether Fauci properly invoked the Fifth, using the standard established by the D.C. Circuit in Ellis v. United States (1969).

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Another alternative would be to grant Fauci use and derivative use immunity, in which case Fauci would have to testify, but if he was subsequently charged by either a state or the federal government, the prosecutor would have to prove that none of the evidence introduced against him was derived directly or indirectly from his compelled testimony. It was the prosecution’s failure to establish this that resulted in Oliver North’s conviction being overturned.

Congress could vote to give Fauci transactional immunity, meaning he could not be prosecuted for any of the conduct that is the subject of his testimony, full stop. Of course, if he were to lie after receiving immunity and being compelled to testify, he could still be prosecuted for perjury.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In short, this saga still has a few more episodes to go.

John G. Malcolm is a former federal prosecutor and is Vice President of the Meese Institute for the Rule of Law at Advancing American Freedom.

World.title: AMB GORDON SONDLAND: America's aid to Israel isn't charity — it's a bargain for US security
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Every few years, Americans ask the same question: Why do we send billions of dollars to Israel?

Given a national debt approaching $40 trillion and an annual defense budget of roughly $1 trillion, it is a fair question. Every dollar spent overseas deserves scrutiny. But the debate almost always focuses on one side of the ledger—what America gives Israel—while largely ignoring the other: what America receives in return.

That is the wrong way to evaluate any investment.

THE US-ISRAEL STRATEGIC ALLIANCE – PARTNERSHIP, NOT CHARITY

Before making my case, let me disclose my own perspective. I am a cultural Jew, but not a practicing one. I don’t keep kosher. I rarely attend synagogue. I raised a family that is half Jewish and half Christian. I have no financial interests in Israel. My support for Israel has never been based on religion or ethnicity. It rests on a far simpler question: Does this alliance make America stronger?

After serving as a U.S. ambassador and spending a lifetime in business, I believe the answer is unequivocally yes.

The United States has many indispensable allies. Britain provides extraordinary intelligence cooperation through the Five Eyes partnership. Japan anchors our strategy in the Indo-Pacific. South Korea deters aggression on the Korean Peninsula. Australia is an increasingly important military partner as China expands its reach. Poland has become one of NATO’s strongest front-line allies. Every one of those relationships advances American interests.

Yet Israel occupies a category almost by itself.

NETANYAHU OPENS UP ABOUT WORKING RELATIONSHIP WITH TRUMP, SAYS ISRAEL IS 'JUNIOR PARTNER'

Few allies combine world-class intelligence, battlefield-tested military innovation, cutting-edge cyber capabilities, missile-defense development, entrepreneurial technology, and democratic resilience while sitting at the crossroads of the world’s most volatile region. If Israel did not exist, the United States would spend decades—and likely hundreds of billions of dollars—trying to recreate the strategic advantages it provides.

That relationship did not emerge overnight. President Harry Truman recognized Israel within minutes of its declaration of independence in 1948, but the modern strategic partnership evolved over decades. During the Cold War, Israel became a dependable democratic partner in a region where Soviet influence was growing. After the Cold War, intelligence cooperation expanded dramatically as terrorism replaced superpower confrontation as America’s primary security concern. More recently, Israel has become an indispensable partner in confronting Iran, developing advanced missile defenses, countering cyber threats, and fostering the regional cooperation reflected in the Abraham Accords. The alliance has endured under Republican and Democratic presidents alike because it has consistently served American interests, not because any administration gave Israel a free pass.

Critics understandably point to the roughly $3.8 billion America provides annually in security assistance to Israel. Standing alone, that figure sounds enormous. Put into context, however, it represents well under half of 1% of America’s annual defense budget. Judged solely by cost, it is easy to criticize. Judged by return, it is remarkably inexpensive.

Consider what America receives.

CHAOS ERUPTS AS HOUSE PASSES $1.15T DEFENSE BILL WITH ISRAEL PROVISION: 'STOP STOKING JEW HATRED'

Israeli intelligence has helped expose terrorist plots, monitor Iran’s military and nuclear programs, disrupt weapons trafficking, and deepen America’s understanding of one of the world’s most dangerous regions. Joint research has produced advances in missile-defense systems such as Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and Arrow, while cooperation in cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, unmanned aircraft, electronic warfare, and battlefield medicine has strengthened both militaries. Israel often confronts emerging threats years before they reach American forces, giving the United States the opportunity to adapt technologies and tactics without paying the far greater price of learning those lessons on future battlefields.

Nor is this simply a transfer of taxpayer dollars overseas. Much of the assistance ultimately returns to the United States through purchases and coproduction of American aircraft, precision-guided weapons, and other defense systems, supporting American workers and helping sustain the defense industrial base upon which our own armed forces depend. Israel is not merely a recipient of American assistance; it is an active contributor to America’s security, technological leadership, and military readiness.

There is another reason the relationship stands apart.

Israel remains the Middle East’s only durable liberal democracy. Governments change through elections, not coups. Courts challenge the executive branch. Journalists aggressively scrutinize political leaders. Arab citizens vote, serve in parliament, sit on the Supreme Court, attend universities, own businesses, and participate throughout Israeli society. Israel, like every democracy, has imperfections, but it remains fundamentally different from the authoritarian systems that dominate much of the surrounding region.

TRUMP WELCOMES NETANYAHU TO WHITE HOUSE AS RAGING IRAN WAR THREATENS TO SOUR US-ISRAEL RELATIONSHIP

That does not mean Israel deserves a blank check.

Friends should tell one another uncomfortable truths. America should criticize Israel when it believes Israel is wrong, apply diplomatic pressure when necessary, and insist that its closest ally uphold the highest standards. We have disagreed with Britain, France, Germany, Japan, and Turkey at various moments in history without questioning the value of those alliances. There is a profound difference between correcting an ally and abandoning one. Mature alliances survive disagreements because they are rooted in enduring strategic interests, not the controversy of the day.,

If Israel were ever to cease to exist, the consequences would extend far beyond its borders. Iran would almost certainly emerge as the dominant military and ideological power from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. Hezbollah and Hamas would claim a historic victory, emboldening extremist movements around the world. Moderate Arab governments would lose a critical intelligence and security partner. Russia and China would rush to expand their influence throughout the region. The United States would almost certainly find itself deploying more ships, more aircraft, more intelligence assets, and perhaps more troops to contain a Middle East that had become dramatically more dangerous.

The irony is difficult to miss. Those who believe abandoning Israel would save America money almost certainly have the arithmetic backward. Replacing what Israel contributes—in intelligence, innovation, deterrence, military cooperation, and regional stability—would cost far more than sustaining the alliance we have today.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Foreign policy is not an exercise in sentiment. Nations do not choose allies because they are perfect; they choose them because the relationship advances their own security and prosperity. America should continue to challenge Israel when it believes Israel is wrong. But it should never confuse disagreement with abandonment.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Good allies are valuable. Great allies are rare. Measured not by headlines or politics but by long-term return on investment, few alliances have contributed more to American security than the partnership between the United States and Israel. That is why, despite its costs, it remains one of America’s best foreign policy investments.

World.title: Progressive William Lawrence wins Democratic primary in one of the country’s biggest House races
World.content:
Democrat William Lawrence, a co-founder of the progressive Sunrise Movement, has won his party’s primary in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, NBC News projects — a big victory for the insurgent left that also sets up a dramatic general election contrast with Republicans in a crucial battleground seat.

Voters in five states participated in primaries Tuesday, including several with major battleground districts up for grabs in November. And few are more hotly contested than this Michigan district, where Lawrence bested two prominent Democratic rivals with national security backgrounds after having differentiated himself as the more liberal candidate and as an aggressive critic of data centers.

Meanwhile, the battle between his two Democratic opponents, former Ambassador Bridget Brink and retired Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam, became increasingly bitter as the race drew to a close, and the two candidates ultimately appear to have split the more moderate wing of the party.

Lawrence will take on GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in one of the most tightly divided swing seats in the country. President Donald Trump carried the district by just 1 percentage point in 2024, and super PACs and other outside groups have reserved more ad spending there than in all but one other House race in the country.

Lawrence won support from an array of prominent progressives and outside groups, and a mysterious super PAC spent more than $1 million in the race’s final weeks to boost him and tear Maasdam down. The spending raised concerns among some Democrats that Republicans might be boosting Lawrence because they think he’ll be easier to beat in the general election.

Michigan voters are also cementing other key battleground House races Tuesday, albeit with less fanfare.

In Michigan’s 4th District, Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga will face off against Democratic state Sen. Sean McCann in the Kalamazoo-area district. Huizenga had Trump’s backing, while McCann was endorsed by top Democrats in the state like Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson.

Republicans are still waiting to find out who will be their nominee against Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet. And in the 10th District in suburban Detroit, which is being left open by GOP Rep. John James and his run for governor, Trump-endorsed military veteran Mike Bouchard will run against Democrat Christina Hines, a former special victims prosecutor.

In Virginia, the matchups are set in four districts expected to fit into the battleground puzzle in different ways this fall.

In the Norfolk area, Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans and Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria head to a rematch of the 2022 2nd District election, which Kiggans won. In the Richmond-area 1st District, Republican Rep. Rob Wittman will face Henrico County Commonwealth’s Attorney Shannon Taylor in a district that could be competitive this fall — one that Trump won by 5 points in 2024.

Farther out on the battlefield, Democratic Rep. Eugene Vindman will face off against Republican Doug Ollivant, a retired Army lieutenant colonel, in the Fredericksburg-area 7th District, a race in which Vindman will start with a significant resource advantage. And Republican Rep. John McGuire will run against Democratic former Rep. Tom Perriello in a district Trump won by 12 points in 2024.

Missouri is home to one of Republicans’ best opportunities to gain a seat this fall after the GOP-controlled state Legislature redrew the congressional map to put Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver into a seat Trump won by 18 points in 2024.

Republican Rick Brattin, a state senator backed by Gov. Mike Kehoe and the Club for Growth, is projected to win the nomination there, with Trump having weighed in for him in the race’s final days.

In Washington state, Republicans are targeting Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in a district Trump won by 3 points in 2024. She will face state Senate Republican leader John Braun, who has Trump’s endorsement, this fall.

Meanwhile, two Democratic incumbents faced serious primary challenges Tuesday. One, Rep. Wesley Bell of Missouri, is projected to win his primary, a rematch against former Rep. Cori Bush, whom he defeated in 2024. The other, Rep. Shri Thanedar of Michigan, is narrowly leading state Rep. Donavan McKinney in a race that has not yet been called.

Voters in a handful of safe seats are also picking nominees who are all but certain to win this fall.

In Michigan’s Oakland County, state Senate Democratic leader Jeremy Moss cruised to victory in Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ district, with Stevens running for the Senate.

In Missouri, Salem Radio Network host Chris Stigall won the Republican primary in the seat from which GOP Rep. Sam Graves is retiring.

And in Washington’s 4th District, Trump-backed Yakima County Commission member Amanda McKinney will move on to face retired Air Force Maj. John Duresky, a Democrat, in a red seat Trump won by about 20 points in 2024.

GOP Rep. Dan Newhouse, one of the last remaining House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump in 2021, is retiring.

World.title: Trump-backed John James wins Michigan’s GOP primary for governor
World.content:
Rep. John James has won Michigan’s Republican nomination for governor, NBC News projects.

James, who represents the Detroit suburbs, prevailed in the primary despite being vastly outspent by his opponent, wealthy businessman Perry Johnson.

President Donald Trump, despite harboring early concerns that a bid for higher office would put the two-term congressman’s competitive House district at risk, endorsed James and last week traveled to the state to campaign for him.

James, 45, will face Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary, this fall in one of the most fiercely contested battleground states. Term limits prevent Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, from seeking re-election.

An Army veteran who lost two Senate races before winning his House seat in 2022, James presented himself throughout the race as a capable public servant with applicable business experience, given his work with his family’s logistics company.

“This is an amazing state with all the great ingredients, but for the past seven-and-a-half years, under Gretchen Whitmer, we’ve been led to higher taxes, more crime on the roads — and frankly, the roads we have aren’t fixed yet,” James said during a televised debate last month, throwing back to Whitmer’s 2018 campaign vow to “fix the damn roads.”

“We’re going to work together to make sure that our children can read, to make sure that we put criminals in jail, and we hold those accountable who continue to let them back out,” James added. “And we’re going to be making sure that we come together to accomplish the mission of increasing hope and purpose with tested, positive leadership that has actually been tested from the battlefield to business to delivering for you right now.”

Johnson, 78, pounded the state with more than $31 million worth of ads, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking firm. He drew on his work in quality control and improving business efficiencies while campaigning on a plan to eliminate the state’s income tax. Johnson also drew on his personal wealth, self-funding his run while declining political donations.

“In the state of Michigan, people are really tired of the politicians,” Johnson told NBC News in an interview last month. “I am an outsider. Nobody denies this fact. I’m the outsider of outsiders.”

James’ campaign spent a fraction on advertising — $2.8 million, according to AdImpact.

One potential factor in the results was the absence of former state Attorney General Mike Cox, who dropped out of the primary on July 17 and threw his support to James. Several polls had shown Cox grabbing a substantial share of the Republican vote and raised the possibility of an unpredictable three-way split that could have benefited Johnson.

Meanwhile, the general election challenge eased a bit for Democrats in May when former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan ended his independent bid for governor. Duggan, a longtime Democrat, had expressed disappointment with both major political parties but caught attention — and grief — from Democrats who noted his reluctance to aggressively criticize Trump.

Michigan voters have not elected a Democrat to succeed a Democrat as governor in more than 65 years.

Benson deputy campaign manager Alyssa Bradley wrote in an email that the secretary of state “begins the general election with something no other candidate can claim: a record of delivering.”

An accompanying campaign memo took a parting shot at both Republican candidates for governor.

“John James and Perry Johnson spent this year lobbing personal attacks at each other and competing for Donald Trump’s attention, not talking to Michigan families about the cost of housing, healthcare, or keeping the lights on,” the memo read. “Both Republican candidates focused on election denying and Donald Trump, while Jocelyn has stayed focused on the issues affecting Michigan families every day.”

World.title: Rep. Wesley Bell defeats former Rep. Cori Bush in a Missouri Democratic primary rematch
World.content:
ST. LOUIS — Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in a Democratic primary rematch, NBC News projects, in the latest chapter of a long-term fight over a deep-blue St. Louis-based district.

Bell overwhelmed Bush on the airwaves, fending off her push to make the race a referendum on his support for U.S. aid to Israel.

In total, Bell’s campaign and outside allies outspent Bush by a staggering 27-to-1 ratio, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking service. United Democracy Project — the super PAC linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel advocacy group known as AIPAC — spent $2 million to support Bell, largely through negative ads attacking Bush. One such ad slammed Bush for being critical of former Vice President Kamala Harris.

It was a reference to Bush’s criticizing the Biden-Harris administration for supporting Israel amid what she deemed a genocide in Gaza. She endorsed Harris in the 2024 election.

As Bell cast his vote Tuesday, he criticized Bush for focusing on Israel and talking “over and over ... about an issue that is not impacting folks right here in St. Louis.”

“And while we take those issues seriously, you know, the M in Missouri doesn’t stand for Middle East,” Bell told NBC News. “It stands for Missouri.”

At a campaign stop later Tuesday, Bush hit back at Bell’s claims and said Missourians “are not happy” that he filled his “campaign coffers” with money from outside groups.

“Why are they meddling in our primaries?” she asked. “Why does he allow that?”

AIPAC loomed large in the race after it helped Bell oust Bush two years ago. United Democracy Project poured $9.3 million into ads in that primary, according to AdImpact, accounting for nearly half of the spending in the race.

Sidney Clark, a Democratic candidate for state representative currently serving in local government, said he supported Bell in 2024 but was voting for Bush this cycle because Bell, in his view, has “been paid for.”

“There are people out there who are using their money and financial influence to buy candidates, and I think that’s the wrong direction for our country,” Clark said after having voted at a St. Louis polling place.

Airest Wilson, another Democratic voter, told NBC News that candidates who take corporate money cross a red line for him — even if they are otherwise aligned with his political views.

“They don’t get that money for free,” he said. “You got to represent their interests. You can’t represent the constituents freely.”

“Cori, it took a lot of courage, but she rejected dark money. So that’s why I support Cori,” Wilson added.

This year, Bush ran two TV ads in the primary, each touching on multiple issues. But both linked Bell to AIPAC and cast him as more interested in sending money to Israel than Missourians, including those suffering from the aftermath of last year’s tornado.

Bell presented himself as a fighter against President Donald Trump, saying of Bush in one of his ads: “She fights Kamala Harris, Joe Biden and other Democrats.”

Bush said Tuesday that if she were to lose, it would not be a setback for the progressive movement.

“If there is a loss, then that just means that there is more work for us to do,” she said.

Asked whether she could see herself voting for Bell if he wins the primary, Bush told NBC News: “See myself voting for a Republican? Oh, I don’t think that’s on the ballot for me.”

World.title: GOP’s Ty Masterson and Democrat Cindy Holscher to meet in Kansas governor’s race
World.content:
Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson will face Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher in Kansas’ election for governor this fall, NBC News projects, setting up a contest that represents the GOP’s best gubernatorial pickup opportunity this year.

Both candidates won their respective primaries on Tuesday. Masterson rode an endorsement from President Donald Trump to emerge from a crowded GOP field, while Holscher focused on a progressive, anti-establishment message to defeat a fellow state Sen. Ethan Corson, who was backed by term-limited Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly.

Holscher pitched herself in ads as someone who “gets that working people are tired of being sold out by both parties.” She also made her support for a proposed moratorium on new data center construction a big part of her message.

Corson massively outspent Holscher in the primary, and leaned heavily on his support from Kelly, who won two terms in a state Trump won by double digits in the past three presidential contests.

One of his recent TV ads featured Kelly praising him as someone who can “stand up to Trump and ICE” and has the “strength and judgement and backbone” for the state’s top job. Another ad, run by a pro-Corson PAC called Heartland Priorities, showed Kelly lauding Corson for having a “record of standing up for Kansas values” and for “stepping up and fighting back” against Trump.

Kelly, who has maintained strong job approval ratings, told the Kansas City Star in a recent interview that Corson was the only Democrat in the race capable of winning the support of the state’s “extraordinarily moderate” Republican and independent voters in November. She said that, “if he’s not elected, I’m very concerned about the direction Kansas will go in,” while also suggesting that Holscher was an “extremist.”

Meanwhile, on the GOP side, Masterson and his allies were outspent on the airwaves by his opponents, but his support from the president put him over the top.

In a tele-rally last week, Trump lauded Masterson as a “fighter,” a “winner” and as someone who has “done a fantastic job — throughout life, actually.”

“We love each other, we love that state,” Trump said.

In Kansas, registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats nearly 2 to 1. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter has rated the general election contest as “lean Republican.”

World.title: Rep. Chuck Edwards drops re-election bid after censure recommendation over harassment claims
World.content:
Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C. has said he is dropping his bid for re-election, days after the House Ethics Committee recommended censure over sexual harassment allegations.

“After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign. I will complete my current term,” Edwards announced early Wednesday in a post on X. “Serving Western North Carolina has been the honor of my life. Thank you for your trust, prayers, and support.”

Edwards, 65, had faced mounting pressure over his conduct with two female staffers. He has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.

On Monday, the ethics panel said it was recommending that the full House censure Edwards after it found that he “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.” A censure is a formal disapproval by the House.

“The Committee found that Representative Edwards violated the House Code of Official Conduct by failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers,” the Ethics Committee said in its 25-page report following a monthslong investigation into allegations against him.

The bipartisan panel said Edwards denied that any of his actions were intended to be sexual or romantic in nature. He cooperated with the investigation, according to the report.

The committee said it found no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with or propositioned any of his staffers. It also concluded that the allegations “do not implicate quid pro quo sexual harassment” or violate “the ‘letter’ of federal sexual harassment law.”

But the panel added that “his pattern of behavior would lead a reasonable observer to interpret it as such, including providing the young women with lavish and recurrent gifts, making comments regarding their appearance and dress, inviting them to intimate dinners and vacations, sending notes regarding his effusive affection, and inviting them to other activities as a way to spend time together.”

Edwards has not been in Congress long.

A former state lawmaker, he ousted Rep. Madison Cawthorn in the GOP primary in 2022 but kept a low profile on Capitol Hill, unlike his predecessor, before the ethics probe.

Edwards previously called the allegations “baseless” and said in a statement to NBC News in May that he welcomed an investigation. His counsel wrote a 15-page rebuttal to the committee’s findings, calling them “unfounded.”

World.title: Missouri voters block GOP-led effort to raise bar to pass constitutional amendments
World.content:
Missouri voters blocked a Republican-led effort to raise the bar for passing citizen-led constitutional amendments, NBC News projects.

Under current state law, such ballot measures require a simple statewide majority for passage, a process that has been used in recent years to grant abortion rights, expand Medicaid and legalize marijuana.

But Amendment 4 would have required citizen-led ballot initiatives to win a majority in each of Missouri’s congressional districts, boundaries that are drawn by state lawmakers. Other ballot measures, like those referred from the Legislature, would not have been subject to this higher bar.

It would have created “the strictest passage threshold in the country for citizen-initiated ballot measures only,” according to Hannah Ledford, the deputy director of the Fairness Project, a group that supports citizen initiative processes. She added it could have left Missouri’s direct democracy process “functionally dead.”

Missouri is one of 26 states that allows voters to legislate directly by petitioning to place a constitutional amendment on the ballot.

The amendment was first proposed by Republican state Rep. Ed Lewis, after Missouri voters used the method to advance a spate of progressive priorities in a state where the GOP has full control of government. Many recent amendments would have failed under the stricter standard proposed by Amendment 4.

“This amendment is really an amendment to protect our Constitution,” Lewis said on a radio program earlier this month. “We have the absolute lowest and weakest process and that’s why we’ve had six initiative petitions passed in the last eight years that have really done real harm to our state and to our Constitution.”

The state’s Republican-controlled Legislature has repealed or limited some changes made through ballot initiatives, including repealing paid sick leave.

Opponents of the proposal heavily outspent its supporters, pouring more than $6 million into broadcast ads, according to data from the tracking firm AdImpact. The measure’s backers did not air any broadcast ads, AdImpact’s data shows.

The more-moneyed campaign against Amendment 5, a proposal to end income taxes and expand sales taxes, also included arguments against Amendment 4 in their ads.

The effort to change the constitutional amendment process also came after Republican lawmakers redrew the state’s congressional map last year to carve up the lone Democratic-held district. Earlier Tuesday, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said that a referendum that sought to undo the new map would not appear on the state’s ballot, arguing the effort was unconstitutional.

Missouri isn’t the only state where Republicans have sought to make it more difficult for citizen-led constitutional amendments to pass. In November, North Dakota and South Dakota voters will decide whether to bump the threshold up from a statewide majority to 60%. And in Utah, there will be a similar measure on the fall ballot specifically related to tax increases.

World.title: Cooler temps aid in battle against Spokane fires that have forced hundreds from their homes
World.content:
SPOKANE, Wash. — Fire crews continued to make progress battling three wildfires overnight, strengthening containment lines and mopping up a spot fire, an incident commander said Tuesday.

But the fires are 0% contained, officials said. The three fires, in Spokane and Stevens counties, were fueled this weekend by gusty winds that exacerbated the fire risk.

There was no growth in two of those fires, while crews doused a spot fire near the Autumn Lane Fire and built containment lines around that blaze, which was around 5,603 acres Tuesday, said Joe Tieso, operations section chief for an incident management team.

Crews were patrolling part of the fire zone, and “it’s looking really good,” Tieso said at a morning briefing.

The three fires in the Spokane area — the Old Trails Fire, the Fairview Fire and the Autumn Lane Fire — together have burned more than 8,000 acres and destroyed hundreds of structures, according to fire officials.

Dozens of homes are seen burned to the ground after a wildfire hit the northern part of Spokane, Wash., on Monday. Lindsey Wasson / AP

“Although firefighters continue making progress, all three fires remain active with areas of significant heat and interior burning,” an update on an official information website about the fires said on Tuesday.

President Donald Trump on Tuesday approved an emergency aid request for Washington to help with the fires, the Federal Emergency Management Agency said. Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson said he is in the process of a Major Disaster Declaration request, which would provide assistance to individuals.

“We are laser-focused on getting assistance to those Washingtonians who have lost so much,” Ferguson said in a statement Tuesday.

People watch the Old Trails Fire in Spokane, on Saturday. Young Kwak / AP

One of the three fires, the Old Trails Fire, was allegedly started by arson. Aaron Farinacci, 37, was charged Monday with first-degree arson, and a judge continued his bond at $1 million during a virtual appearance Tuesday afternoon from the Spokane County Jail.

Farinacci sat with his hands folded in front of him, only saying that he understood his rights and reading his name and date of birth.

Farinacci is scheduled to be arraigned Thursday.

More than 700 structures, including homes, have been destroyed, officials estimate.

World.title: Perez Hilton hospitalized after reports he livestreamed self-harm
World.content:
Police said they attended the Miami-area home of celebrity blogger and podcaster Perez Hilton, after they received reports that he engaged in self-harm in livestreamed video Tuesday night.

A spokesperson for the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said in an email that deputies responded to reports of someone “who was livestreaming acts of self-harm on social media.”

The statement was sent in response to an inquiry about Hilton, but it did not name him.

In a follow-up statement, the sheriff’s office said the person was “safely recovered” and taken by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue to a local hospital, where he was receiving medical attention.

It said deputies spoke to family members at the scene, who confirmed the person had been alone inside the residence.

The video, which was streamed on TikTok before the platform pulled it, appeared to show Hilton covered in blood, with visible cuts and holding what appeared to be a knife. In the video, viewers pleaded with him and asked for his phone number so they could alert authorities.

Video from Hilton’s neighborhood taken by NBC South Florida showed multiple sheriff’s patrol vehicles stopped and a street shuttered by yellow tape.

The co-CEOs of the talent management firm that represents Hilton, Golden Artists Entertainment, said in a statement Tuesday night that they “are aware of the concerning content circulating online involving our client, Perez Hilton.”

“At this time, we have not been able to make direct contact with him, despite our ongoing efforts to reach him,” co-CEOs Dante Rusciolelli and Rebekah Kochan said. “Our primary concern is Perez’s health and well being, as well as the well being of his family.”

Hilton, 48, made a name in the early 2000s publicizing and sometimes belittling celebrities who made public gaffes or otherwise found themselves in trouble with the law.

Hilton, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, has three children born via surrogacy. In a June 17 video on Instagram, he announced that his family was moving back to Miami after having lived in Las Vegas for 3½ years.

“God told me to move to Miami,” he said in the video, in which he also discussed a recent hospital stay.

In a follow-up video, Hilton and the children expressed excitement about the move.

“Manifesting abundance, manifesting just family, peace, good times,” Hilton said. “Manifesting health, good health — that’s what’s most important.”

In addition to his website, Hilton has expanded his online presence with “The Perez Hilton Podcast with Chris Booker,” on which the two parse the latest celebrity news and gossip.

In 2010, he said he would stop bullying people on his website as part of his effort to discourage bullying among teenagers. “I really want to be part of the solution and not part of the problem,” he told Ellen Degeneres on her show “Ellen.”

World.title: White House declassifies info on secret FBI probe into Trump's firing of Comey
World.content:
The White House on Wednesday declassified information claiming the FBI opened an investigation into whether President Trump was acting as an asset for Russia when he fired FBI Director James Comey, a theory an administration official said was not backed up by evidence.

The official said the investigation, known as Oxford Comma, was a subcomponent of Crossfire Hurricane, the FBI probe into potential collusion between the 2016 Trump campaign and the Russian government — an investigation that has long drawn Mr. Trump's ire. The predicate of Oxford Comma was the newly elected president's decision to fire Comey in 2017.

The case was marked sensitive, which is generally done to keep a case off the books from other agents, the official said. The agents who opened the case said they believe it was going to be the least intrusive method to address a serious national security risk.

Oxford Comma was eventually rolled into Special Counsel Robert Mueller's larger probe into Mr. Trump, the official said, and was later found not to have any merit when the rest of the Mueller investigation was closed down.

"I was unaware that the predicate for the obstruction included a claim that Donald Trump was somehow acting on behalf of Vladimir Putin," the official said. "The short of it is, almost everything in the FBI's possession at that point had debunked or ruled out that Trump or his campaign was colluding with Russia at that time."

Mr. Trump fired Comey in May 2017, just months into his first term as president. The White House initially cited Comey's handling of the investigation into Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's emails as the reason for his dismissal, though Mueller's report claimed Mr. Trump was frustrated with Comey for refusing to publicly state that the president was not personally under investigation for potential ties to Russia.

Comey's firing ended up as the catalyst that set a larger investigation into Mr. Trump in motion. After Comey's dismissal, then-Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein appointed Mueller as a special counsel to investigate claims of Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election, and any potential ties to the Trump campaign.

Mueller ultimately did not find evidence that members of the Trump campaign "conspired or coordinated" with Russia, though it did describe some contacts between the campaign and Russian government-linked individuals.

Mr. Trump has frequently accused the FBI and other intelligence agencies of conducting unethical investigations into his campaigns and presidency, and has vowed to launch probes of his own. He has long criticized Comey, calling him a "dirty cop," while Comey has lashed out at Mr. Trump, calling him "morally unfit" to be president.

Earlier this year, Comey was charged with threatening Mr. Trump's life by posting photos of seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47." Comey has alleged he is being vindictively and selectively prosecuted, which the Justice Department has denied. Last year, he was separately charged with making false statements to Congress, though the indictment was dismissed.

World.title: Pills from Lindsay Clancy's house examined on Day 6 of murder trial
World.content:
The Lindsay Clancy murder trial resumed for a sixth day Tuesday with more testimony from prosecution witnesses and a look at the prescription pills that were found in her house.

Clancy, 35, has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — at their home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on Jan. 24, 2023.

Testimony about Lindsay Clancy's prescription pills

Massachusetts State Police Lt. Joseph Rabbit said he found four prescription pill bottles in a kitchen cabinet when executing a search warrant at the Duxbury home after the murders. He said Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband Patrick Clancy and a lawyer came to the district attorney's office on Feb. 6 with more prescription pill bottles in a CVS bag.

Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham pulled out pill bottles, one by one, and asked about how many pills were prescribed compared to how many were left in the bottle. The prosecution has argued that while Clancy was prescribed several drugs for her mental health struggles, she was not taking many pills from each bottle.

Lindsay Clancy's prescription medications CBS Boston

The defense maintains she was overmedicated, and says a cocktail of several prescription drugs sparked a postpartum psychosis that led to Clancy killing her children.

"These were all pills that were issued on prescriptions in about a three-week period of time," defense attorney Kevin Reddington said in his questioning.

Crime lab workers testify

Several prosecution witnesses employed at the Massachusetts State Police Crime Lab took the stand on Tuesday. There was testimony about blood collected from the home in Duxbury — jurors were shown the blood-stained knife previously seen in Clancy's bedroom.

Two Crime Lab technicians also testified that prescription drugs were detected in blood and urine tests done on Lindsay Clancy. The tests are unable to pinpoint exactly how many different drugs Clancy had in her system, they explained.

The Crime Lab witnesses testified that they found nothing in the three children's systems.

South Shore Hospital surgeon testifies

The prosecution's first witness of the day was Dr. Cristina Karpio, a general surgeon at South Shore Hospital who treated Clancy immediately after the murders. She said Clancy's complex spinal injuries from her fall out of the second-story bedroom window required a transfer to Brigham & Women's Hospital in Boston.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Dr. Karpio about the severity of Clancy's injuries. The defense has tried to counter the prosecution's argument that Clancy's suicide attempt was faked.

"Did you know that your patient had coded shortly after being brought to Brigham & Women's Hospital?" Reddington asked.

"No," Dr. Karpio said.

"Did you know that she had to have massive transfusions right after being brought to the hospital in Boston?" Reddington asked.

"No," Dr. Karpio said.

Lindsay Clancy agrees to "stipulation of facts"

Before the jury entered the courtroom on Tuesday, Lindsay Clancy agreed to a "stipulation of facts."

She was sworn in by a court officer and answered questions from the judge, confirming that she and the prosecution agree on certain facts in the case.

"This stipulation basically relieves the government of having to bring in dozens, if not more, witnesses to prove chain of custody of blood, fluids, the bands, DNA, all of that," defense attorney Reddington said. "Rather than have days of testimony, the stipulation will avoid that."

Specifically, both sides agreed that toxicology testing on the three children was done correctly in the Crime Lab.

The day of scientific testimony drew frustration from Reddington at times.

"Your Honor, there's no objection to any of this physical evidence," he said.

Reddington has repeatedly told the court that Clancy admits what she did, and he wants the trial to be focused not on who did it, but why.

It's anticipated that doctors who treated Lindsay Clancy for psychiatric issues will take the stand as early as Wednesday.

Legal analyst on Lindsay Clancy trial

WBZ legal analyst Jennifer Roman explains that days of dry testimony are inevitable in a case like this. Eight witnesses took the stand Tuesday, most of them crime scene lab scientists testifying about testing blood in very scientific terms.

Much of the blood testimony related to Lindsay Clancy's suicide attempt. She's paralyzed from a spinal fracture that night and both sides debate whether she jumped from her bedroom window.

"Whether or not she flung herself out the window is part of the prosecution's theory that this was sort of a faked suicide attempt. She didn't mean to commit suicide. There were superficial wounds on her wrists and her throat, so she did that for show, to make it look like she was trying to commit suicide," Roman said of the prosecution's theory.

What's happened in the Lindsay Clancy trial this week?

The jury in Plymouth Superior Court heard entries from Clancy's diary Monday and testimony about her state of mind before and after the murders. She admits to killing her children but claims it was due to severe postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors say her suicide attempt was fake and premeditated and the murders were planned.

The jury has heard from 32 witnesses after five days of testimony.

If convicted, Clancy faces life in prison without a chance of parole. If she's found not criminally responsible for the deaths of her children, she will be sent to a state mental health facility in Massachusetts.
