World.title: Electricité : à gauche, Bernard Cazeneuve joue sa propre partition
World.content:
En 2011, il n’avait rejoint l’équipe de François Hollande pendant sa campagne victorieuse qu’à la condition que le candidat retire de son programme l’arrêt annoncé de la production de combustible MOX en France — suivant une recommandation d’Areva, son producteur.

Dans la Sarthe fin juin, invité par son ancien collègue de gouvernement Stéphane Le Foll, actuel maire du Mans, à s’exprimer sur son programme en matière de nucléaire, l’ancien Premier ministre n’hésitait pas à critiquer La France insoumise et les Ecologistes qui se “trompent” en ne voulant pas faire comme lui. Surtout qu’il peut se prévaloir de sa constance sur la question, quand d’autres membres de son camp ont viré de bord.

Lorsqu’il quittait le pouvoir en 2017, en même temps que François Hollande, la France était engagée dans une trajectoire de réduction de sa production d’électricité nucléaire (une décision qu’il ne cautionne pas), avec une planification à mettre en œuvre pour fermer des réacteurs. Mais depuis, l’heure est à la relance : le prolongement de la quasi-totalité des réacteurs est examiné par le gouvernement, et de nouveaux doivent voir le jour dans une dizaine d’années.

Des conseillers pronucléaires

Pour élaborer son programme, Bernard Cazeneuve peut compter sur les éclairages de Marc Fontecave, chimiste et professeur au Collège de France, ou de Louis Gallois, ancien dirigeant de plusieurs entreprises publiques, ont confirmé les intéressés à POLITICO — le second n’a pas souhaité entrer dans le détail “d’échanges privés”.

Marc Fontecave, qui préside également le conseil scientifique d’EDF, se penche depuis plusieurs mois sur la stratégie énergétique du pays dans ses cours ouverts à tous au Collège de France. Le scientifique est un opposant aux “catastrophistes” du climat, le surnom qu’il donne aux militants Cyril Dion, Greta Thunberg ou Aurélien Barrau, auxquels il a consacré un livre.

Il siège également à l’Académie des sciences, qui a rendu un avis assez sévère — mais “équilibré”, selon Marc Fontecave — sur la feuille de route du gouvernement, notamment sur le soutien au développement des énergies renouvelables.

World.title: Spain sweats over its isolated territories in Africa
World.content:
But, more alarmingly for Madrid, that argument is no longer coming exclusively from Rabat. Questions over Spain’s centuries-old control of the fortress cities have also been raised in a U.S. Congress report, and by Israel’s ambassador to the U.N.

It is a sign of the level of concern in Madrid that the government is now having to make public declarations on a point of international law that — only a week ago — it would have thought was self evident.

“Ceuta and Melilla are not to be touched,” Defense Minister Margarita Robles said during a press conference on Monday. “Everyone must be very clear that Spanish territorial integrity and sovereignty are not up for debate.”

The government’s rejection of Morocco’s claims has done little to reduce worries in Spain over what would happen if Rabat dials up the pressure. This week, national newspapers have been filled with columns expressing fears of a “Green March 2.0” — pointing out the parallels with Morocco’s use of a mass popular mobilization to take over the province of Spanish Sahara in 1975.

José Manuel García-Margallo, who served as Spain’s foreign minister between 2011 and 2014 and is a member of the center-right People’s Party, said it was vital for Spain to show its control over the cities is not negotiable.

“Do you think the British would have allowed 60,000 Spaniards to enter Gibraltar?” he asked. “I’d encourage this government to be a little bit more British.”

World.title: Palantir funnels earnings to US to avoid European taxes, report finds
World.content:
Palantir pays no U.S. federal income tax because previous losses, tax credits, and R&D deductions offset its taxable income; and virtually no state income tax, with the exception of Maryland, which levies a digital services tax.

The profit gap between the U.S. and Europe is stark. In 2025, Palantir’s American business pocketed 47.7 cents in profit from every dollar of revenue — more than double the previous year’s 22.5 cents. Outside the U.S., the profit margin was just 6.3 percent. In some European subsidiaries, it fell to around 3 percent, according to the new report.

CICTAR argues that Palantir "intentionally and artificially" shrinks European profits — and therefore its European tax bills — to concentrate profits in the U.S. There is no claim in the report that such arrangements, often referred to as "profit shifting," are illegal. Multinational companies often reduce reported profits by paying subsidiaries or other related entities for intellectual property, loans or expertise.

In Sweden, for example, Palantir reported €13.7 million in revenue in 2024, but only €1.1 million in profit. At Sweden’s 20 percent corporate tax rate, that left the company with a tax bill of just €424,000.

In its Q2 earnings report on Monday, Palantir made no explicit reference to earnings from its European subsidiaries. Instead, it highlighted its U.S. business, where revenue rose 115 percent year-on-year to $1.57 billion (€1.36 billion), and boasted of its 62 percent profit margin.

A U.K.-based Palantir spokesperson said that the majority of the company's 2025 revenue and profitability was driven by its U.S. business. "Our tax position in each jurisdiction reflects the level of economic activity there, and we meet our tax obligations in every market in which we operate," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Was there ever life on Mars? The answer might be closer than we think
World.content:
Mars has long been seen as hostile and unfit for life — despite being the planet in the solar system most similar to Earth.

 

New research, backed by the latest findings from NASA's Perseverance rover, suggests the planet may once have had conditions suitable for life.

It's one of the biggest open questions in astronomy today and was a key topic at COSPAR, the world's leading space research conference organised by Italy's National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF) and currently underway in Florence.

"The combination of several lines of evidence, such as the discovery by NASA's Perseverance rover of minerals that on Earth are produced by micro-organisms, and of complex organic matter, is increasing the likelihood that Mars may have been inhabited, at least in the past," Teresa Fornaro, a researcher at the INAF Arcetri Observatory and professor of astrobiology in Florence who collaborates on the Perseverance mission, told ANSA.

Fornaro said any life on Mars would most likely have taken the form of micro-organisms living underground, shielded from radiation bombarding the planet's surface and drawing energy from the rocks themselves.

"So far, we've only gathered indirect evidence. The organic matter we've found, for instance, has a structure that's heavily altered, so it's difficult to trace back to its origin. We'll only have a definitive answer once we can analyse the samples here on Earth," she continued.

On the Red Planet: the ExoMars and Mars 2020 missions

That's why the results from upcoming missions to the Red Planet could prove especially significant.

Chief among them, according to Fornaro, is ExoMars, run by the European Space Agency (ESA), with its Rosalind Franklin rover taking centre stage. Launch is scheduled for 2028, with touchdown on the Martian surface expected in 2030.

The mission is already under way: an initial probe, the Trace Gas Orbiter, was sent in 2016 to study the Martian atmosphere.

The rover itself will follow in 2028, aiming to gather direct evidence to answer one central question — has life ever existed on Mars?

"Until now, rovers have only been able to explore the surface. Rosalind Franklin will be able to drill up to two metres into the ground, carrying the most advanced instruments ever sent to Mars," Fornaro said, highlighting the mission's innovative scope.

Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover, which began exploring the Martian surface in 2021 in search of traces of ancient organic life, is still active on the planet.

The Mars 2020 mission was originally designed to last one Martian year — around 687 Earth days — but has been extended indefinitely. The rover remains fully operational and its ongoing collection of rock and regolith samples continues to drive major advances in space research.

A sample collected in the summer of 2024 — the same one referenced by Fornaro — contained potential biological traces.

Though these still require further analysis to confirm, NASA administrator Sean Duffy described the find as "the moment when we have come closer than ever to life on Mars".

World.title: Wynn Al Marjan Island: UAE’s first casino resort set to open in September 2027
World.content:
After delays related to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, the first licensed casino in the United Arab Emirates is now set to open at Wynn Al Marjan Island in Ras Al Khaimah in September 2027.

 

In a quarterly call with investors on 4 August, Wynn Resorts CEO Craig Billings said that construction is “progressing rapidly” on the new resort, and the company expects the project to open its doors to the public in autumn next year.

Billings had announced in May that there would be a "modest delay" in the project, citing "logistical and shipping challenges in the region" after the war broke out following strikes by the United States and Israel on Iran in late February.

In October 2024, US group Wynn, which operates casinos in Las Vegas and Boston as well as in Macau, received the first commercial gaming operator's licence to be issued by the UAE, where gambling is currently banned.

It is now developing a 1,542-room luxury resort at Wynn Al Marjan Island in Ras Al Khaimah, one of the seven emirates that constitute the UAE.

"We are now actively progressing through the interior fit-out of the hotel rooms, with mechanical, electrical, and finishing work, all moving along in sequence," Billings said.

He added that the Middle East conflict was still affecting the casino's construction due to global supply chain disruptions and personnel movement.

"These disruptions have impacted both the timing and cost of the project," Billings said, estimating the additional cost at "approximately $600 million”, about half of which was attributed to the conflict, as well as higher material costs and shipping price increases.

Shares of Wynn Resorts rose 5% in after-hours trading.

Located 80 kilometres north of Dubai International Airport (DXB), Wynn Al Marjan Island is being developed on a 60-hectare island overlooking the Arabian Gulf.

As well as the casino, the resort will feature a 70‑story tower, 22 restaurants, bars and lounges, and a beach club with a private beach.

There will also be a luxury spa with salon and fitness centre, designer boutiques, events facilities, entertainment and nightlife, a kids’ club, multiple pools and a full-service marina.

World.title: Peter Gill, acclaimed playwright and director behind 'The York Realist', dies aged 86
World.content:
Welsh playwright Peter Gill, whose intimate dramas and groundbreaking productions made him one of the defining figures of British theatre, passed away on Monday at the age of 86.

 

Born in Cardiff in 1939, Gill became one of the country’s most acclaimed theatre directors, as well as the author of several celebrated works, including “The York Realist” and “Small Change”.

Gill began his career as an actor at London’s Royal Court in 1958 at the age of 18. He later appeared with the Royal Shakespeare Company, playing Silvius in Michael Elliott’s celebrated production of “As You Like It”.

Doubting his future as an actor and encouraged by the Royal Court’s artistic director George Devine, he turned to directing.

In 1965, he directed DH Lawrence’s “A Collier’s Friday Night”. The production launched Gill’s directing career and began a lifelong association with Lawrence’s work.

By reviving plays like “The Daughter-in-Law” and “The Widowing of Mrs Holroyd”, Gill helped introduce generations of audiences to some of the novelist’s overlooked plays.

Across his career, Gill would go on to direct around 100 plays.

His influence extended far beyond the rehearsal room, too. In 1976, Gill became the first artistic director of Riverside Studios in west London, where he staged his own productions, presented work by international theatre companies and established workshops to develop actors.

After joining the National Theatre as associate director in 1980, Gill founded the National Theatre Studio in 1984, a space that gave artists the freedom to experiment and develop productions away from the pressure of public performance.

Gill was equally respected as a playwright. Drawing on his working-class Catholic upbringing in Cardiff, his work explored family, class and sexuality and often found the drama in ordinary lives.

Among his best-known plays were “The Sleepers Den”, “Small Change” and “Kick for Touch”, but “The York Realist” – his acclaimed 2002 play about the relationship between a Yorkshire farmer and a London theatre director – remains his most celebrated.

He was appointed an OBE in 1980 for services to theatre and later reflected on his career in “Apprenticeship”, the memoir he published in 2008.

Paying tribute, Gill’s agent Mel Kenyon said his work possessed a "rare emotional delicacy" and was "beautifully observed and finely tuned".

Kenyon described him as “a gentle man with a fierce intelligence”, adding: “Whenever we talked, I walked away a wiser person. He taught me so much just by being him. He was a singular man, a kind, generous and curious man. I will miss him greatly.”

Theatre director Michael Grandage called his contribution to British theatre “quietly seismic”.

“Future generations discovering Peter’s work will happen upon some of the finest plays written in the last 70 years with unquestionably some of the most beautiful prose in the English language,” he said.

Gill is survived by his nieces and nephews.

World.title: North Korea's Kim Yo Jong warns of military options over Japan’s move into 'war state'
World.content:
The powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un accused Japan of a "transformation into a war state" on Wednesday as Tokyo beefs up its military stance in the Pacific.

 

Japan has been gradually moving away from its post-World War II pacifist status, increasing military spending, ramping up defence pacts and deploying missile launchers to its outer islands.

In a statement carried by North Korean state media, Kim Yo Jong said Pyongyang's "leadership will set up additional military options which are obviously due to Japan's transformation."

"Japan, a war criminal state, is accelerating its transformation into a war state," said her statement published by the Korean Central News Agency.

Kim cited Tokyo's recent test-firing of Tomahawk long-range cruise missiles and its May participation in US-led drills in the Philippines as evidence of Washington's support for "dangerous military moves" in the Pacific.

Tokyo is moving "to formulate the possession of the capability for pre-emptive attack", she said. "We will never remain a passive onlooker to the military evolution of Japan which may pose a grave threat."

Kim Yo Jong delivers a speech in Pyongyang, 10 August, 2022 AP Photo

On Wednesday, Japan's defence ministry confirmed to the AFP news agency that the Tomahawk experiment last week was Japan's first.

Tokyo's defence minister said on Tuesday the military needs to be boosted with a "sense of urgency and crisis," as a new government assessment warned of growing threats from China, Russia and North Korea.

Japan occupied all of Korea before its 1945 surrender in the Second World War, after which the peninsula was divided into separate states along the 38th parallel.

The legacy of the violent colonial period continues to weigh on the foreign policies of both North and South Korea.

"If the descendants of militarism, who have inherited the genes of cunning and aggression, have seized deadly weapons in their hands, something unpleasant will happen," Kim's statement said.

Japan has hosted US military bases ever since its surrender in World War II.

The nation raised its military expenditure by 9.7% to $62.2 billion (€53.9 billion) in 2025, equivalent to 1.4% of GDP, its highest share since 1958.

China, a key ally of North Korea, has also recently expressed alarm at what it sees as "new militarism" by Japan.

Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaks during a news conference at the prime minister's office in Tokyo, 27 July, 2026 AP Photo

Relations have worsened since Tokyo's hawkish new Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made comments in November suggesting Chinese action to seize Taiwan could merit a reaction from Japan's military.

Beijing has long claimed Taiwan is part of its territory and has not ruled out taking it by force.

Pyongyang has repeatedly declared itself an "irreversible" nuclear state since leader Kim Jong Un's 2019 summit with US President Donald Trump collapsed over the scope of denuclearisation and sanctions relief.

World.title: Greenpeace warns: sea advances, Portuguese coast at risk
World.content:
In a recent report published by Greenpeace, "Destruction All Along the Coast - A portrait of a Portuguese coastline at risk" (source in Portuguese), the organisation warns Portugal about the imminent risks posed by climate change and by decades of development and urban pressure.

 

More aware of the issue, or confronted with a more glaring scenario, Portuguese people are already witnessing this summer the shrinking stretches of sand on many of their favourite beaches.

The advance of the sea and the retreat of the beaches are nothing new. However, the storms at the start of the year have worsened the situation. On average, beach retreat "ranges between 10 and 20 metres, reaching 40 metres in some areas", the Greenpeace report warns.

In an assessment of Portugal's 2,500 kilometres of coastline, from north to south of the country, the report estimates that 40% of Portuguese beaches could disappear by 2100.

Greenpeace says Portugal "has become the epicentre" of climate change impacts and major risks because of its long coastline and a rise in sea level that is faster than the global average.

The report also shows that more than 100,000 people live in coastal areas at risk of flooding.

"We cannot keep waiting for a beach to disappear, for a cliff to collapse or for an infrastructure to be at risk before we act", argues Toni Melajoki Roseiro, director of Greenpeace Portugal.

Roseiro believes that, given all the knowledge already available, political decisions now need to be taken to "protect people, nature and a territory that belongs to everyone".

25% of mainland Portugal's coastline is retreating

According to the Portuguese Environment Agency (APA), in more than 25% of the mainland coast the sea has advanced inland by up to two metres per year in some regions. The situation in Cascais is among the most alarming, with mean sea level rising by 9.7 centimetres over the past 25 years.

Although climate change is frequently cited as the main threat, the report highlights urban and tourism expansion, excessive construction in sensitive areas and the artificialisation of the shoreline as factors that have increased risk and destroyed or reduced the capacity of natural systems such as dunes and salt marshes.

These natural barriers are the first line of defence against erosion, flooding and saltwater intrusion, and their destruction increases the likelihood of catastrophic events.

This year's storms exposed some of the problems highlighted in the report, with flooding caused by the heavy rainfall, rising water levels, lack of soil permeability, as well as a shortage of sediment on beaches. Costa de Lavos beach, in Figueira da Foz, where a retreat of 50 metres has been recorded over the past decade, and Faro beach, which has lost 25 metres in width since 1950, are examples of this.

Beaches will disappear and flood risk is rising

From north to south of the country, the outlook is bleak. In Espinho, the coastline is retreating by 5.2 metres per year. Viana do Castelo has lost 30% of its beach area since 1990 and Póvoa de Varzim faces a high risk of erosion and flooding.

In the central-western region, Aveiro is one of the most critical areas, with projections of up to 40 metres of retreat at Costa Nova over the next twenty years.

The report also forecasts that 18% of the Mondego estuary could be inundated by 2100.

In Lisbon and on the Setúbal Peninsula, Costa da Caparica is the area that has suffered most from retreat, having lost around 200 metres of sand since 1960.

Almada is also under pressure, with 12% of its urban area at risk of flooding and, as has already been demonstrated in recent winters, parts of Lisbon such as Algés, Alcântara and the Baixa district of the city are likewise hotspots for flooding.

The Alentejo coast, also under growing pressure from tourism and urbanisation, is among the most affected. It is estimated that up to 50% of Alentejo's beaches could disappear by 2100 and that, in the Algarve, around 40% of beaches may be lost.

The most critical areas, with severe coastal erosion and unstable cliffs at risk of collapse, are Vilamoura, Quarteira, Vale do Garrão and Praia da Rocha.

On the other side of the Algarve, Tavira Island, the Ria Formosa, Barrinha de Alvor and Praia do Ancão also stand out as coastal ecosystems that are particularly vulnerable.

Carvoeiro Pedro Armestre / Greenpeace

Luxury developments heighten risks

Portugal is not short of legislation. However, the rules are not always strictly applied and enforced, nor is there sufficient coordination between the various authorities when decisions are taken.

The Legal Framework for Territorial Management Instruments (RJIGT), which sets out the rules for organising and managing land use in Portugal, includes Coastal Zone Plans (POC) that establish, among other provisions, the requirement to apply a terrestrial protection strip 500 metres wide, measured from the shoreline inland. This strip can be extended to 1,000 metres when necessary to safeguard important coastal ecosystems.

For Greenpeace, development along the coast is a "multiplier of critical risks" at a time of profound climate change, particularly because of rising sea levels.

The report warns of a particularly worrying situation in the municipalities of Sesimbra and Grândola, in the district of Setúbal, where there have been many "examples of protective rules being overridden".

The report highlights projects in the municipality of Sesimbra, such as Pinhal da Prata, Pinhal do Atlântico and Etosoto, which occupy more than 260 hectares in protected areas and have gone ahead without adequate environmental assessments.

In Tróia, the "Na Praia" project, covering 96 hectares and envisaging a luxury resort with villas, a spa and a heliport on protected coastal dunes, is one such example. However, work on this resort was suspended following action by an environmental association and, in March 2026, a fire at the construction site postponed the opening, which had been scheduled for June.

Tróia Pedro Armestre / Greenpeace

In Comporta, the Torre project, with two hotels, 234 residences and a golf course, includes developments planned over more than 1,000 hectares, while Costa Terra and Comporta Dunes, with golf courses less than 500 metres from the waterline, are other examples cited in the NGO's report as poor examples in terms of coastal protection and the safeguarding of protected environmental areas.

In its final remarks, the NGO also calls for guarantees of public access to the coast and beaches, another issue it raises in the wake of several controversies over beaches in Comporta being fenced off by private owners.

The advance of the sea and mounting development pressure are challenges that demand an urgent response. Greenpeace's report advocates compliance with existing legislation, stronger enforcement and more robust political decisions to protect communities and coastal ecosystems over the coming decades.

World.title: 'Stolen intellectual property': German court rules AI music generator Suno broke copyright rules
World.content:
AI music generator Suno, which allows users to generate songs via prompts, has lost a copyright infringement lawsuit to German licensing agency GEMA.

 

In the January 2025 filing, GEMA argued that Suno was using songs to train its AI models without obtaining any licenses or paying the artists.

The decision, handed down on Friday 31 July by the Munich Regional Court, ruled that Suno’s use of the songs was in breach of both the German and US copyright law, and that the AI platform unlawfully obtained, processed and reproduced music that was represented by GEMA.

“Today, the Chamber made one thing crystal clear: AI models built on stolen intellectual property have no protection under the law,” said GEMA’s CEO Dr Tobias Holzmüller after the legal victory (via Reuters). “AI service providers must pay for licenses rather than helping themselves to our members’ works free of charge. Today, the court’s verdict has significantly strengthened Europe’s position as a cultural centre.”

GEMA Board chairman Dr Ralf Weigand shared: “This ruling sends a powerful international message: creativity has value, and creators’ rights must be respected in the age of artificial intelligence.”

He added: “Through this decision, GEMA has set an important precedent not only for its more than 100,000 members, but for creators worldwide. The fact that we can now enforce our rights in countries including the United States gives creators hope and confidence at a time of profound technological transformation.”

Suno will need to pay damages to GEMA. The sum has not yet been confirmed.

Previously, Warner, Sony Music Entertainment and Universal Music Group filed lawsuits against Suno and Udio for copyright violations. Surprisingly, the 2024 filing led to Warner settling the lawsuit by signing a licensing deal with Suno.

World.title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ becomes second fastest film in history to cross $1 billion box office milestone
World.content:
It’s finally happened, after just six days.

 

The new Spider-Man adventure, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has crossed the $1 billion mark at the global box office, becoming the second fastest movie to reach that milestone after 2019’s Avengers: Endgame.

Endgame captured a record breaking $1.2 billion worldwide in its opening weekend.

Sony and Marvel’s latest Spidey film, starring Tom Holland as the web-slinging hero, has defied all box office expectations, which bodes well for the MCU's upcoming Avengers: Doomsday - a culmination of multiple superhero story arcs which is seen as a make-or-break moment for the studio considering Marvel's under-performing and critically shrugged movies in the last five years.

The success of Brand New Day is down to several factors: euphoric word-of-mouth; positive reviews; a more grounded and character-based adventure which doesn't require any prior multiverse homework; and the draw of married couple Tom Holland and Zendaya, who are fast becoming the most profitable box office stars currently working.

Tom Holland and Zendaya at the Spider-Man: Brand New Day premiere in London - Wednesday 29 July 2026 AP Photo

Both actors are having one hell of a summer, starring in both The Odyssey and Brand New Day. Between them, they currently have a reported box office total of $1.8bn with both films – a figure which should continue to grow when The Odyssey is released in South Korea today, as well as China (14 August) and Japan (11 September).

In December, Zendaya will star in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three – which, based on the first two instalments, could make around $800m at the global box office.

And there’s still the outside chance that the couple could appear in December’s Doomsday...

For the time being, Brand New Day is the fourth movie of 2026 to earn $1 billion, following The Super Mario Galaxy Movie ($1.012 billion), Michael ($1.016 billion) and Toy Story 5 ($1.068 billion). The Odyssey has grossed $912 million to date and is about to be the fifth release of 2026 to join the billion-dollar club.

It's very likely that Brand New Day will surpass them all to climb to $2 billion, a metric that only seven other movies have ever achieved.

In Euronews Culture's review for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, we wrote: " Director Destin Daniel Cretton, who has taken the reins from regular director Jon Watts, does a great job in committing to the character's comic roots reset, making the stakes believable, and ensuring the emotion matches the spectacle."

We added: "Despite its shortcomings and not being the slam-dunk the MCU so badly needs, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is bolstered by consistently strong action sequences and a terrific performance from Holland, who can now safely be crowned the greatest on-screen Spider-Man. All four of his solo outings prove how badly Marvel needs him on its roster of heroes."

Read the full review here.

World.title: Fire tornadoes have reached Europe: What makes them so dangerous?
World.content:
Europe's record-breaking hot and dry summer is fuelling major wildfires, with France and Greece among the countries battling large blazes. Scientists say some of these fires are producing an unusual and dangerous phenomenon known as a fire whirl, or fire tornado, in which intense heat and wind combine to create spinning columns of flames and smoke.

 

According to wildfire researcher James Urban, assistant professor at Worcester Polytechnic Institute in Massachusetts, this extreme fire behaviour has been observed across Europe in recent days.

To better understand the phenomenon, researchers at Worcester Polytechnic Institute in the US recreated fire whirls under controlled laboratory conditions. Urban says the spinning motion develops when wind interacts with the terrain and the shape of the fire.

How do fire tornadoes form?

"So, fire tornadoes, or as we call them, fire whirls, are a scenario in which a fire has a strong rotational flow around it, and sort of a strong rotation flow around it. And that can be caused by the wind and interactions with the local topography, as well as the shape of the fire line itself. These fires are associated with extreme fire behaviour because they can allow the fire to burn more intensely and then also change direction rather quickly, which can be a major hazard to the fire service responding to the fire."

Urban explains that fire whirls form when air is drawn into a fire from different directions. Obstacles such as vegetation, nearby fires or geographical features can force that airflow into a spinning pattern, increasing the fire's intensity.

"In a fire whirl, or commonly called a fire tornado, the fire entrains in air from the sides. And what can happen is through obstructions with, you know, other fires or obstacles such as vegetation or local geographical features, the flow can become constrained and create a recirculation pattern, causing it to circulate and sort of spin and that can allow the fire to burn more rapidly and get the fire ... the flames closer to the ground – allowing them to burn the vegetation more quickly – resulting in more intense heat release and a more intense fire."

What makes fire tornadoes so dangerous?

One of the greatest dangers is the ability of fire whirls to throw burning debris far ahead of the flames, allowing fires to spread unexpectedly and potentially trapping firefighters.

"Fire whirls can lead to a phenomena called firebrand spotting, where burning debris is launched ahead of the fire front and this can lead a very rapid fire spread, which is hazardous to the fire service, as well as nearby communities. But also, it can cause the fire to jump, essentially, over the fire service, increasing the chances for them to be trapped. And so when firefighters are operating in conditions where there are fire whirls occurring, they have to be very careful."

Urban believes these events reflect a broader shift in wildfire behaviour as climate conditions become more favourable for extreme fires.

Authorities across southern Europe continue to battle major wildfires as prolonged heat and dry conditions increase the risk of further outbreaks. Extreme heat, driven by human-caused climate change, increases the likelihood and intensity of wildfires.

World.title: Low water levels in the Danube revealing Nazi shipwrecks
World.content:
There are believed to be about 200 Nazi ships on the floor of the Danube near Prahovo, Serbia. Ferries, tourist boats, and shipping have also become severely restricted due to the drought.

Europe's second-longest river, the Danube, has reached levels so low that sunken German battleships from World War II have emerged from the dried-out riverbed.

Near Prahovo, a Serbian port where the Danube separates the country from Romania, a rusty hull and broken mast has become visible where the Nazis once purposely sunk their own ship to avoid capture by the Russians.

Both the Rhine and the Danube have seen World War II-era ships appear due to low water levels Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

The Serbian government has long sought help from the European Union to remove what are believed to be hundreds of ships, some still laden with weapons, from the river floor. But pinpointing their exact locations without accidentally disturbing the explosives still onboard has been an issue.

Low water levels in the Danube have pushed some power plants in parts of Central and Eastern Europe to the brink of shutting down.

The Danube flows through ten countries, including Germany and Austria Image: Djordje Kojadinovic/REUTERS

Ferries, tourism boats, and shipping on both the Danube and the Rhine river have been drastically reduced in recent weeks due to the drought.

In recent years, climate change has made lower water levels in Europe's key waterways a recurring issue.

Tne Nazis sunk hundreds of ships in the Danube to ward off a Soviet advance in 1944 Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

World.title: Germany news: Lightning strike cuts Bavarian town in two
World.content:
08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 Low Rhine levels could push up German inflation

Low water means that barges cannot carry as much cargo as they usually would Image: Rüdiger Wölk/IMAGO

Persistently low water levels on the Rhine could temporarily push Germany's inflation rate up by as much as half a percentage point, economists have warned.

Low water levels are forcing ships to carry much lighter loads, driving up the cost of transporting chemicals, energy supplies and other industrial goods.

Traders said tanker and barge transport costs from Rotterdam to Karlsruhe have climbed to around €150-160 per ton, compared with about €45 at the end of June.

"The German inflation rate could temporarily rise by up to half a percentage point as a result," Berenberg economist Felix Schmidt told the Reuters news agency.

ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski also said shortages and disrupted deliveries could make a wide range of goods more expensive.

"If ships can only be loaded to one-third of capacity or less, correspondingly more ships have to be used, or more expensive alternatives such as trucks or rail," Hamburg Commercial Bank chief economist Cyrus de la Rubia said.

Economists also warned that the disruption could last for months. In previous years, Rhine water levels have often not recovered significantly until November.

World.title: South Korea: Police raid Starbucks HQ over 'Tank Day' fiasco
World.content:
Starbucks Korea faced major backlash after being accused of trivializing a 1980 massacre. Police say their internal investigation was not thorough enough.

Police raided Starbucks' nation headquarters in South Korea on Wednesday, the company confirmed, after a controversial promotional event led to large protests and boycotts of the coffee chain across the country.

"The Seoul police raided the headquarters of Starbucks Korea this morning as part of the ongoing investigation," said a spokesman for the Shinsegae Group, which operates Starbucks Korea.

What was the controversial promotion?

This past May, Starbucks advertised large to-go cups they called "tank tumblers" and seemed to refer to the Gwangju Uprising as "tank day."

On May 18, 1980, the ruling military junta violently put down a pro-democracy protest in the city of Gwangju. At least 165 civilians were killed when the army rolled tanks out into the streets to quell the demonstation.

The Starbucks promotional event also appeared to allude to statements made by the government at the time to deny that they had tortured a student protest leader to death.

The backlash was swift, and led to protest and boycotts against the coffee giant in what is the company's third-largest market after the United States and China.

President Lee Jae Myung also expressed his outrage, and Shinsegae Group chairman Chung Yong-jin and Starbucks Korea CEO Son Jung-hyun resigned following a public apology.

What are police investigating?

Starbucks Korea said it conducted its own internal investigation into the matter and found no evidence of wrongdoing. However, the firm admitted that the inquiry had been hampered by, amongst other things, not being able to compel the people involved in planning the promotion to hand over their phones.

Police told the Yonhap news agency they were looking for evidence that executives knowingly trivialized the 1980 massacre.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: India: Heavy monsoon season claims more than 100 lives
World.content:
08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 Indian lawmakers demand Zuckerberg apology over removal of Modi's video

A parliamentary standing committee in India demanded an apology from Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg on Wednesday, the Press Trust of India reported, after Prime Minister Narendra Modi's speech was briefly removed from Facebook.

The controversy began when a selfie-video posted by Modi on July 23, addressing students about a leaked medical entrance exam question paper, was briefly taken down.

A notice initially told viewers that the video had been taken down due to a "legal request," which Meta later told news agency ANI that the removal was the result of a technical error.

While the video was restored within hours, the incident sparked a significant backlash from lawmakers of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party ,who have been demanding a personal apology from Zuckerberg.

A letter to the secretary of the IT ministry said that Zuckerberg's legal protection and immunity should be withdrawn is an apology was not issued within three days.

"The removal of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi's video addressing students and Gen Z regarding examination controversies and strict actions against paper leaks from Facebook for 5-6 hours viewed very seriously by the Committee," said the letter.

In July, police in the southern Indian city of Hyderabad registered a case against Meta India head Arun Srinivas over multiple videos posted on Facebook that allegedly depicted Modi in an "abusive manner." Indian social media at the time was flooded with anti-Modi content amid student-led protests in New Delhi and dozens of other cities.

Meta has repeatedly drawn the ire of the Indian government over content posted by its users and has faced criticism from opponents who say it does too little to curb hate speech and misinformation on ⁠Facebook and Instagram.

Meanwhile, the government has also steadily expanded its oversight of content on social media platforms, regularly directing companies to remove accounts and posts under India's IT laws.

On Tuesday, the Times of India reported that the central government was set to raise a range of concerns with Meta's global team during a meeting in India on August 5-6.

World.title: Turkish court orders X to block Imamoglu candidacy account
World.content:
Ekrem Imamoglu, a member of the main opposition Republican People's Party, is widely seen as the main challenger to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's 23-year rule.

The social media platform X announced that it was complying with a Turkish court order to block access to the presidential candidacy account of imprisoned Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, which has around 225,700 followers.

According to a copy of the order posted by X on Wednesday, an Istanbul court ordered the platform to restrict access domestically to Imamoglu's account to protect national security and public order.

However, X said that it is challenging the order in court. "Although Türkiye's laws force us to comply with the order, we are challenging the order in court and, in the spirit of full transparency, are sharing the court order," it said.

Imamoglu's main X account already blocked

Elon Musk has sought to portray X as a defender of free speech since taking control of the company in 2022 but he has drawn criticism for having done away with dedicated measures for content moderation.

In May 2025, Imamoglu's main X account, which had nearly 10 million followers, was blocked in Turkey under a similar order. At the time, X also filed a legal challenge against the order, arguing against the restriction.

"Our challenge against this order remains pending before the Constitutional Court, awaiting a decision following our recent legal filings," X said.

X said that that failing to comply with these orders could result in severe sanctions, including the throttling of its services in Turkey.

Istanbul's suspended mayor Imamoglu on trial To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who is Ekrem Imamoglu?

Ekrem İmamoglu, the popular former mayor of Istanbul, is the main political rival of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Imamoglu had his university degree revoked on March 18, 2025, before being arrested on terrorism and corruption charges a day later. His arrest sparked Turkey's largest protests in over a decade.

In March 2026, Imamoglu's trial finally began, with prosecutors seeking 2,430 years in prison for him.

World.title: Ukraine: Russian strikes on Kyiv, surrounding region kill at least 17
World.content:
At least 17 were killed as explosions rocked Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight. Russian missiles tore through residential buildings and warehouses, part of an intensifying campaign against Ukraine's capital.

Russia launched a wave of missile attacks on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv and its surrounding region early Wednesday, killing at least 17 and wounding 44, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The attacks began after midnight with air raid sirens sounding across the capital for more than an hour. Ukraine's air force had earlier warned that ballistic missiles were incoming.

According to an air force report, Ukraine was unable to shoot down a single Russian missile during an overnight attack involving 115 drones and 28 high-speed missiles, including ballistic ones.

In his post on X, Zelenskyy said that "ballistic missile interceptors could have saved the lives of those killed today."

"It is very important that our partners understand that delays in supplying them, or an unwillingness to provide anti-ballistic systems, lead directly to such horrific casualties and destruction," he added.

What do we know about the Russian strikes?

Kyiv's military administration said seven sites in the city were hit. The strikes damaged residential buildings and warehouses:

"The enemy is once again deliberately striking civilians and civilian infrastructure," it said on Telegram.

Mayor Vitali Klitschko said one warehouse near the city center was destroyed and rescue teams pulled two people from the debris.

"There may still be people under the rubble," he wrote. "Search and rescue operations are proceeding."

The attacks began with air raid sirens sounding across Kyiv for more than an hour Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

Klitschko said early reports of a burning 20-story apartment building were inaccurate. But a large fire did break out on the edge of the city. Debris from a downed missile landed near a residential building.

The attack also caused an ammonia leak, which emergency crews worked to contain.

Ukrainian air defense units worked to shoot down the incoming missiles.

Attack comes amid intensified Russian strikes on Kyiv

Russia has struck Kyiv several times in the past month.

On Saturday, Russian strikes on the capital and its suburbs killed 10 people and wounded more than 30. That same day, Ukrainian drones sank a Russian ship in the Black Sea.

Both sides have stepped up long-range strikes in recent weeks. Russia used more than twice as many missiles in July as before, according to an analysis by the French AFP news agency. Ukraine has also increased drone attacks on Russian oil, gas, and supply sites.

On Tuesday, strikes in the Moscow region killed five people and wounded 10 others. The attacks hit warehouses used by the Russian retailer Wildberries. Moscow's mayor said the city's air defenses shot down at least 10 drones on Wednesday.

UN rights monitors have raised concerns over civilian casualties Image: Dan Bashakov/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Why does Ukraine want more Patriot interceptors?

Earlier, Zelenskyy has asked allies for more Patriot missile interceptors, saying the lack of these defenses "only encourages Russia to launch such attacks that take human lives."

Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump last Tuesday to lobby Washington for licenses to build Patriot systems inside Ukraine.

United Nations human rights monitors have raised concerns over increased civilian deaths in the war, which are now at their highest level since Russia's invasion began in February 2022.

Russia and Ukraine both deny targeting civilians in the war.

EU: Russia must pay for destruction it has caused

Meanwhile, European Commission President Ursula von ​der Leyen said, "Once again we wake up to the news of horrible atrocities by Russia through its aerial attacks on Ukraine."

In a post on X, she emphasized that Russia must pay for the destruction it has caused.

"And we are using the proceeds from the immobilised Russian assets to make sure it does," von der Leyen wrote, announcing hat the European Union will use €1.4 billion ($1.6 billion) in interest generated from frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine.

The money came from interest on cash balances, which are part of the Russian central bank's assets that were frozen by the EU in the wake of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Edited by: Rana Taha, Roshni Majumdar

World.title: AI ecosystem's 'circular' investment: risk or advantage?
World.content:
Amid talk of an AI sector bubble, one aspect is under scrutiny. Many big AI players are invested in smaller ones, who then buy the bigger firm's products. This brings risks and advantages.

Reports that Nvidia is in talks to give financial guarantees of almost $250 billion (€217 billion) to OpenAI for a massive data center project show two sides of the artificial intelligence boom.

On one level, it shows the monumental scale of AI's financial muscle and potential. On another, it shows the risks of a so-called "circular" financing system at the core of the AI ecosystem. If one domino falls, would others fall with it?

"The interconnected nature of the AI ecosystem is real," Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments, told DW. "But near term risks are mitigated by the strong balance sheets, cash flows and credit quality of the major providers funding the buildout."

Jan Frederik Slijkerman, a tech sector strategist at ING, agrees that the exceptionally strong financial positions of big tech companies such as Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet (Google parent company) mitigates against the risks.

He says the degree of collaboration regarding AI is "fascinating" but does not see a "a systemic industry-wide risk arising from the observed interdependencies".

The circular model

Circular financing typically works as follows: a company pays money to another for a product or deal, or invests in that company or provides a loan or lease. Then that company buys the products or services of the first company.

It can be seen across the spectrum of AI deals.

The emergence of OpenAI's ChatGPT kickstarted the AI boom Image: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto/picture alliance

For many, the moment the AI revolution began was when ChatGPT, developed by OpenAI, was launched in November 2022. The chatbot's capabilities brought AI into the mainstream. Its success quickly attracted a massive $10 billion investment from software giant Microsoft, enabling it to develop more powerful models.

In return, OpenAI became a key customer for Microsoft's cloud services, which it is investing ever more heavily into as the AI boom gathers momentum.

It set the template for future deals. Amazon and Alphabet began investing billions into OpenAI's rival Anthropic, which has built the hugely successful Claude chatbot. In return, Anthropic uses Amazon's web services and Google's cloud services as well as buying its chips.

Nvidia: King of the Jungle

Yet that is all relatively small potatoes compared with what AI computing giant Nvidia has brought to the table.

"Nvidia sits at the center of the AI ecosystem, acting not only as a technology supplier but also as a strategic investor helping accelerate adoption of its platform," says Tan.

Slijkerman says Nvidia plays a vital role, as it contributes to the development of a variety of new businesses, from healthcare to autonomous driving. "Its investments help support the growth of the broader AI ecosystem while also facilitating the deployment of AI infrastructure," he says.

The story that Nvidia is in talks to provide $250 billion to OpenAI, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, would be just the latest megadeal the $4.6 trillion company has bankrolled.

Nvidia's chips are at the center of the AI ecosystem Image: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty Images

Jensen Huang's company is at the center of the artificial intelligence boom thanks to its industry-leading chips. Since 2024, it has invested heavily in multiple AI start-ups, including Open AI, Mistral and Elon Musk's SpaceX. In turn, these companies all are committed users of Nvidia's chips.

It has also begun to invest heavily in so-called 'neocloud' providers, such as CoreWeave and Nebius. These start-ups rent out cloud space for AI computing. As well as investing, Nvidia itself is also purchasing cloud space from the firms.

Nvidia is stepping up its spending and dealmaking in 2026 too. It struck a partnership with South Korean conglomerate SK Group recently, worth potentially $500 billion in business.

Throughout 2026, such circular dealmaking has become even more pronounced across the sector. OpenAI has struck close to $1 trillion worth of deals with the likes of Microsoft and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), agreeing to become one of AMD's biggest shareholders.

Microsoft and Nvidia have also invested heavily in Anthropic, with Anthropic in turn agreeing to step up its purchases of cloud capacity and chips from both.

Advantages and risks

The scale of the cross-pollination can bring advantages. "Interconnected ecosystems can accelerate innovation by aligning incentives across infrastructure providers, model developers, application companies and end users, helping new technologies scale faster," says Gary Tan,.

Slijkerman says he does not see the circular trend as a form of "financial engineering". "These relationships make strategic sense because they help participants expand their market reach and accelerate adoption," he says. "They can also create mutual financial benefits."

Yet there are risks. Fears of an AI 'bubble' continue to stalk global markets. Tech and semiconductor stocks fell sharply last week amid doubts over profitability in the sector, relative to the vast sums being invested in data centers and other AI-related spending.

AI bubble incoming? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If AI revenues do not grow sufficiently, companies that have received funding from bigger players might face financial challenges. In turn, they may stop buying the bigger company's products and their valuations will fall.

Some analysts have drawn comparisons to the dot-com bubble and subsequent crash, which happened after valuations surged in the early days of the internet. Circular financing was a factor in that crisis, too, but many observers reckon the AI boom is ultimately built on more solid foundations.

"While some individual companies or business models may ultimately disappoint, the broader investment cycle appears to be supported by genuine demand and real economic value creation," says Slijkerman.

Tan agrees and says a bigger risk in future problems is interest rates. He thinks if interest rates rise, it could have a significant impact on many AI companies as they will be penalized by the time they become profitable.

"AI cash flows are long dated, so the direction of the yield curve may ultimately matter more than the availability of capital," he says.

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

World.title: White House revokes visa of Brazil's ambassador to US
World.content:
The move was in response to Brazil delaying formal diplomatic approval of the US ambassador to Brasilia and denying visas to several US diplomats. Brazil has rejected the decision.

The administration of Donald Trump has moved to revoke the visa of Brazil's ambassador to the US, sources in the State Department told media outlets on Tuesday.

Ambassador Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti's visa revocation was reportedly in response to the denial of visas to two American diplomats who sought to visit Brazil ahead of upcoming elections.

The US has also accused the Brazilian government of stalling Trump's ambassadorial choice to the South American country.

Brazil rejected Washington's decision, describing it as an escalation and saying it crystalized the US's interest in interfering in the country's upcoming presidential election.

"Today's decision is not an isolated incident. It is part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons," the office of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said in a statement.

What do we know so far about the visa revocation?

State Department officials reportedly said the decision could be quickly reversed if Brazil takes appropriate action and accepts Trump's ambassadorial choice.

The Associated Press cited one State Department official as saying on condition of anonymity that despite the revocation of her visa, Viotti is not being expelled from the US.

"The action was that the ​visa of a senior diplomat here was revoked or canceled. That is not the same thing as kicking the person out of ​the country. It means that they are here but without a visa, and would have their ​visa restored if ‌the balance is restored by giving agreement to our chosen ambassadorial nominee," a State Department official was quoted by the Reuters news agency as saying.

Despite the move, the State Department official reportedly stressed Washington's valuing of the relationship with Brazil and its respect for the Brazilian people in whatever government they choose through free and fair elections in Brazil.

"We want to be back in a situation where we have a normal, productive, transparent relationship with our colleagues," the official said.

Why is the US revoking the Brazilian ambassador's visa?

Last month, Brazil announced denying visas to officials from the US State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor. It said their planned visit aimed to undermine Brazil's electoral system ahead of the October elections.

The State Department denied the allegations, saying the pair had planned to visit Brasilia in late July to meet government officials, religious leaders and others about "election integrity, religious freedom and freedom of expression."

Brazil slapped with 50% tariffs — who's next? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Before that incident, Brazil for weeks withheld the formal approval for the ambassadorship of Daniel Perez, a Florida state representative and close ally of Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Perez was nominated by Trump on June 1.

"Basically we've had a situation in which our diplomats were being denied the ability to do routine common work between the two countries, and so you know under these ​circumstances, with the long delay and no ⁠promise of ending the impasse of the agreement, we've taken reciprocal action with respect to a Brazilian diplomat here to make the point ⁠that it can't always be one-sided," Reuters quoted the unnamed State Department official as saying.

Tensions between the Trump and Lula administrations

The incident is the latest in diplomatic tensions between the Trump administration and that of Brazil's leftist President Lula.

Trump is a staunch supporter of Lula's right-wing predecessor Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.

Like Trump with his election loss to Joe Biden in 2020, Bolsonaro had also falsely claimed widespread election fraud.

His son Flavio Bolsonaro is the right-wing presidential candidate in the October vote. Brazil denied the US officials' visa as Flavio Bolsonaro renewed unfounded claims that the country's electronic voting system is insecure.

World.title: La Audiencia Nacional pregunta a la Guardia Civil si tuvo alguna información que pudiese “alertar” de la entrada masiva en Ceuta
World.content:
La entrada irregular de más de 70.000 personas en Ceuta desde Marruecos, producida fundamentalmente el pasado jueves, comienza a judicializarse. La Audiencia Nacional ha solicitado a la Guardia Civil que informe de si tuvo algún indicio o información, los días previos a la avalancha, que alertase de que esta se iba a producir. La investigación se inició a raíz de una denuncia del partido Iustitia Europa en la que pedía al tribunal que investigase los delitos “contra la seguridad del Estado, delitos contra la Nación, favorecimiento de la inmigración ilegal y tráfico de personas, organización criminal y omisión del deber de perseguir delitos”.

La cuestión de si hubo indicios o alertas previas que pudiesen haber preparado a los efectivos situados en la frontera, que fueron completamente superados por la avalancha humana, es una de las claves de esta crisis. El ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, insistía este miércoles en que el Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI) no alertó de una llegada masiva de migrantes a Ceuta. Pero sí admitía que hubo avisos en los días previos de que, como es habitual en verano, podía haber “una ampliación, una elevación” del número de entradas irregulares por mar en la ciudad autónoma y de que en esta ocasión se podían “ver fomentadas” por la sentencia del Tribunal Supremo de comienzos de julio que prohibía las devoluciones en caliente de aquellas personas que entrasen a nado.

En una providencia a la que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS, la magistrada titular del Tribunal Central de Instancia número 3, María Tardón, solicita además a la Jefatura de Información del instituto armado que dé detalles sobre los días más críticos de la crisis migratoria —el 30 y el 31 de julio—, “particularmente en lo relativo a las operaciones de rescate de las personas que se hayan localizado en las aguas territoriales españolas, sus circunstancias personales conocidas, así como, en el caso de personas fallecidas, si constara la causa y la data de la muerte y, en el caso de las personas supervivientes, su identidad y datos de localización”.

Más información Playa de Trampolín: el refugio a sol abierto para centenares de subsaharianos que resisten en busca de asilo

El balance provisional de fallecidos es de 77. En las primeras horas, tras la entrada irregular de más de 70.000 personas del jueves, se recuperaron del mar 20 cuerpos. Al día siguiente fueron unos 40. Sus cuerpos se custodian ahora en un hangar refrigerado en el viejo hospital militar de la ciudad autónoma. Las autopsias casi están terminadas y se buscan formas de colaboración con Marruecos para identificar a los fallecidos.

No es la primera decisión de la instructora dentro de esta, de momento, incipiente causa: este martes, la magistrada solicitó a la Policía Nacional un informe sobre la entrada “irregular masiva” de migrantes en Ceuta en los últimos días para dilucidar si se trató de “una acción concertada o dirigida” por algún “grupo criminal”. La solicitud busca establecer si la Audiencia Nacional es competente para investigar y más tarde juzgar los delitos denunciados por Iustitia Europa, partido que forma parte de las acusaciones populares de, entre otros, el juicio al hermano de Pedro Sánchez o de la causa contra la esposa del presidente del Gobierno, Begoña Gómez.

World.title: Pistas para un viaje de verano a Portugal: de las playas del Algarve a los azulejos de Lisboa
World.content:
Ciudades y pueblos llenos de encanto, pistas para comer bien y barato y algunos trucos para descubrir el país

Año tras año, Portugal es un destino de vacaciones recurrente. Pero decir Portugal puede tener muchos significados: están las playas del Algarve que acogen a los amantes del surf, los pueblos del centro del país llenos de encanto y calles empedradas o los paisajes que dejan el Duero y el Tajo a su paso por el país vecino. Además del magnetismo de Lisboa y Oporto, dos ciudades llenas de vida y de historia.

Esta es una guía de destinos para quienes este verano viajen a Portugal.

Además, dos pistas gastronómicas para saber dónde comer y qué pedir en Lisboa y Oporto. Así como una visita cultural imprescindible en la capital lusa.

Y la experiencia viajera en primera persona de Paco Nadal, dispuesto a regresar una y otra vez al país.

World.title: Glasshouses feel cost of drought as sprinkler ban imposed
World.content:
Glasshouse operators in the Westland region could lose tens of millions of euros after a ban on sprinklers comes into force on Wednesday.

The glasshouse industry has not been exempted from the ban, which has been imposed by the Delfland water authority as an anti-drought measure.

All sluice gates in the region have been closed to protect drinking water from being contaminated by saltwater from the sea. Inspectors will check if companies are complying with the ban on using water for sprinkling.

“These measures are urgently needed to prevent irreversible damage happening,” a spokesman for the water board told Omroep West. “The glasshouse owners have been given until midnight [on Tuesday] to fill their reservoirs.”

Glastuinbouw Nederland, which represents the industry, said a two to three-week ban would cost companies around €150 million.

It has asked the water board if companies can spray their crops with purified waste water or seawater. “Almost any water is better than no water,” a spokesman said.

A ban on drawing water is also in force in parts of the Brabantse Delta region, around Breda. The ban, which initially covered the hours from 9am to 9pm, was extended last week to 24 hours and include fruit growers, who were previously exempt.

On the island of Terschelling, off the coast of Friesland, sheep have been banned from grazing and inspections of dykes have been stepped up amid concerns that the drought is causing cracks to appear.

World.title: Two women die trying to help a child in the sea at Callantsoog
World.content:
Two women died after going into the sea to help a child in trouble off Callantsoog in Noord-Holland on Tuesday afternoon.

A 39-year-old British woman, who had been missing overnight, was found dead on the beach at Groote Keeten, north of where the group ran into difficulty. A 26-year-old woman from Gelderland died on Tuesday after being pulled from the water and given CPR.

The two women went to the aid of a child who was at risk of drowning at about 4.30pm and then got into trouble themselves, broadcaster NOS reported. The child and another swimmer were brought ashore by the lifeguard service and taken to hospital for checks.

The alarm was raised at the Voordijk beach entrance, between Callantsoog and Groote Keeten. Four KNRM lifeboat stations took part in the search alongside the lifeguard service, the coastguard and police, using boats and helicopters from surrounding areas.

The search was called off shortly after 9pm on Tuesday because of the tide and resumed on Wednesday morning.

Police are not investigating the circumstances further, regional broadcaster NH reported. Neither woman has been named.

World.title: Belgium and Netherlands open new high-voltage power line
World.content:
The Netherlands and Belgium have opened a new high-voltage power line that will allow 30% more electricity to flow between the two countries.

The so-called Brabo III project connects Antwerp’s harbour to the Rilland high-voltage station across the border in Zeeland. The scheme is designed to reduce strain on the electricity grid and reduce electricity prices in both countries.

Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten and his Belgian counterpart Bart de Wever both attended the official opening in Antwerp. Jetten said the link was an important step towards ensuring European countries can produce their own energy.

“In recent years that has rapidly become a security issue,” he said. “It might not be how the Brabo III project started, but in today’s world it is an important element.”

De Wever said the line, which will supply power to companies such as BASF and Ineos, was “a new artery for our industry”.

Belgian grid operator Elia has spent 10 years building the power line, including two 192 metre-high masts at the Kallosluis, which links the Schelde to the Waaslandkanaal.

The Netherlands will be able to export up to 30% more solar and wind energy on high production days, while at other times it can import more power to meet rapidly increasing demand.

Utrecht has currently frozen all new applications for high-voltage electricity connections because the network has reached saturation point, while operator Tennet warned earlier in the year that some areas were approaching maximum capacity.

World.title: Bomb disposal experts called in at Limburg wildfire
World.content:
The wildfire near Venray in northern Limburg is under control, but efforts to fight the blaze are being hampered by the presence of unexploded munitions in the ground in an area that experienced heavy fighting at the end of the Second World War, the Limburg-Noord safety authority told broadcaster NOS.

Something that may be an unexploded shell was spotted in the Boschhuizerbergen nature reserve on Tuesday and experts from the defence ministry’s bomb disposal unit were called in. Heavy fighting took place around Venray during the war.

Explosions have been heard in the area over the past two days, but a fire service spokesman told NOS it is not certain these came from munitions. Intense heat can turn resin and moisture inside trees to steam, bursting the wood with a bang.

Keeping crews back from the buried ordnance is not slowing the operation down, the safety authority said, because the heat in those parts of the reserve would be unbearable either way.

Days of work ahead

“The fire stayed stable overnight,” Erik Thijssen of the safety authority told NOS on Wednesday morning. “There was no further spread.” He said the all-clear had not been given but the situation was “stable and manageable”.

Thijssen said putting the fire out completely would take several more days.

An emergency ordinance issued by the mayor of Venray on Tuesday afternoon remains in force. It bars people from entering the area and from flying drones over it.

Helicopters and crews

Defence ministry Chinook helicopters are due back in the air between 10am and 11am, the local safety authority told regional broadcaster L1 Nieuws.

The helicopters had dropped almost 900,000 litres of water on the fire by Tuesday evening, drawn from the Maas in buckets holding 7,600 litres.

Around 100 hectares have burned. The fire is being held inside “stop lines” – a railway line, an asphalt road and wide forest tracks – and firefighters are being rotated in from North Brabant, Utrecht, Drenthe and Friesland.

World.title: Fourth teenager arrested in anti-terrorism investigation
World.content:

A fourth teenager has been arrested by police investigating a suspected terror plot, the Dutch prosecution service has said.

The 18-year-old was arrested at his home in Kesteren, Gelderland, on Friday evening by a police special intervention team (DSI) acting on information from the intelligence agency AIVD.

A magistrate in Rotterdam ordered him to be detained in custody for the next 14 days. His contact is restricted with his lawyer.

No weapons were found at his home and prosecutors said there were no signs an attack was imminent.

“At this point in the investigation we have not identified a clear target or moment for an attack,” the prosecution service (Openbare Ministerie) said in a statement.

Last week three youths aged 16, 17 and 19 were arrested in overnight raids at homes in Rotterdam, Alkmaar and Eindhoven.

The eldest suspect, named as Mohammed K., was convicted two years ago of planning attacks on nightclubs and police stations in Belgium, none of which took place.

The other two were among a group of 14 people aged between 14 and 30 who were arrested last April on suspicion of inciting terrorism via the social media platform TikTok.

World.title: Dutch man arrested for racing on German motorway at 235km/h
World.content:
A Dutch man has been arrested for driving his Porsche 911 at speeds of up to 235 km/h on a German motorway while allegedly under the influence of cannabis.

The section of the A3 near Koblenz where he was stopped has no speed limit, but the 23-year-old man was pulled over for “extremely dangerous” driving after he weaved in and out of traffic and tailgated a police car.

A drug test revealed traces of THC, the active ingredient in cannabis, in his system. The man told police he ran a coffeeshop in Eindhoven with his father and regularly took the drug “for professional reasons”.

Police said traffic was relatively heavy for the time of day when the man was stopped just after midday on Monday. “It was only through good fortune that there were no traffic accidents,” they said.

The man has been charged with racing on the highway and dangerous driving. Police confiscated his driving licence and ordered him to pay €10,000 in bail before being released.

He was collected from the police station in Montabaur, 25km west of Koblenz, by his father.

In a separate incident across the border, a man from Rotterdam was arrested after reaching speeds of 246 km/h on the A15 while under the influence of drink and drugs.

The 40-year-old was stopped after passing a speed check near Papendrecht on Tuesday night on a section of motorway where the limit is 100 km/h.

His car was impounded and his licence seized by police after he was charged with dangerous driving and driving under the influence.

World.title: Fast food outlets almost double in under 20 years
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Netherlands had 19,435 fast food outlets at the start of 2026, an increase of 88% since 2007, according to figures published on Wednesday by national statistics agency CBS.

The count covers cafeterias, sandwich shops, food stalls and ice cream parlours, which now make up slightly more than half of all the country’s 38,600 food outlets.

Restaurants grew more slowly over the same period, rising 73% from 11,055 to 19,165. Because fast food outlets expanded faster, they overtook restaurants in 2020 and have outnumbered them since.

Cities and the coast

Nearly 20% of all fast food outlets are in the four largest cities. Amsterdam has 1,605, Rotterdam 975, The Hague 790 and Utrecht 445.

Measured against population, however, the densest concentrations are not urban. The national average is close to 1.1 outlets per 1,000 residents, and it is tourist areas that push well beyond it.

Vlieland has 8.3 outlets per 1,000 residents, the highest in the country, followed by Schiermonnikoog on 4.1 and Terschelling on 3.1. Coastal municipalities in Zeeland, Zandvoort in Noord-Holland and Valkenburg aan de Geul in Zuid-Limburg also rank highly.

The east and northeast have fewer outlets per head than the national average. Staphorst in Overijssel has the fewest, at 0.3 per 1,000 residents, almost four times below the average.

World.title: NEC draw 0-0 at Olympiacos to boost Champions League hopes
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

NEC Nijmegen kept their hopes of a place in the Champions League alive with a 0-0 draw against Olympiacos in Greece.

The match was an even contest, with both teams notching up 10 chances over the 90 minutes.

The home side dominated the early exchanges, but Dick Schreuder’s side were stronger in the second half as Cape Verdean midfielder Jamiro Monteiro and Noé Lebreton went close for NEC.

Monteiro, newly signed from PEC Zwolle, replaced Japanese midfielder Kodai Sano, who was left out of the team at his own request pending his expected move to PSV Eindhoven for €14.5 million.

Former Ajax forward Dusan Tadic came on in the second half to make his debut for NEC at the age of 37, replacing the 35-year-old Bryan Linssen in the front line alongside the 38-year-old captain Tjaronn Chery.

It was NEC’s first taste of European football since a team coached by Mario Been lost 1-0 to HSV Hamburg in the UEFA Cup in 2009.

The two teams will play the return leg in Nijmegen’s Goffertstadion next Tuesday, August 11, with the winners going through to a play-off against either Union Saint-Gilloise of Belgium or Norwegian side Bødo/Glimt for a place in the lucrative group stages.

World.title: Unexploded WWII ordnance discovered under busy Warsaw street
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Part of central Warsaw was shut down today after unexploded ordnance from World War Two was found buried under a major road during construction work. The discovery, which came just days after the city commemorated the anniversary of its wartime uprising against Nazi-German occupation, led to traffic being diverted and residents being warned to stay away from their windows and avoid going outside while bomb disposal experts worked to safely remove the item. W Al. Solidarności znaleziono niewybuch, najprawdopodobniej z czasów II wojny światowej. ℹ️ Czytaj więcej: https://t.co/Fv6oe84XiM pic.twitter.com/BfjQPZveYZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 4, 2026 The object, reportedly around 70 centimetres long, was found early on Tuesday morning on Solidarity Avenue, a major thoroughfare, during modernisation work on tram lines. “We were digging a trench and I literally just touched it with the tip [of my digger],” the operator of the excavator who found it told broadcaster TVN. Staff working at the site were immediately evacuated to a safe distance. Police later confirmed that the item is unexploded ordnance, and that initial findings indicate it dates from World War Two. Bomb disposal experts arrived at the scene in the afternoon. However, they have not confirmed precisely what type of ordnance was discovered or its origin, reports Polsat News. Warsaw was the site of major fighting during World War Two, beginning in 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded and occupied Poland. In 1943, the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the largest single act of Jewish resistance during the war, took place. On 1 August 1944, the Polish underground Home Army launched the Warsaw Uprising, which was the largest single act of armed resistance anywhere in German-occupied Europe during the war. In response, the Germans destroyed much of the city, around 85% of which lay in ruins by 1945. Warsaw’s historic Old Town was meticulously rebuilt after the war. But many other parts of the city were redeveloped by the newly installed communist authorities, including Solidarity Avenue (which during the communist era was named after Polish-Soviet Red Army General Karol Świerczewski). Thousands of vehicles drove over the unexploded ordnance every day for decades. “Warsaw is marked by history, and there are many such surprises,” Witold Urbanowicz, spokesman for the city’s tram operator, told news website Interia. After the fall of the Warsaw Uprising – which began 80 years ago today – the German occupiers expelled the city's entire population. However, some survivors decided to remain among the ruins. They became known as "Robinson Crusoes" and this is their story https://t.co/UuVbfbcpQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 1, 2024 Unexploded ordnance is regularly found in Poland. In May this year, around 200 anti-personnel mines dating from World War Two were discovered at the construction site of a student dormitory at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. In October last year, two men were hospitalised after an artillery shell that one of them had brought home from a forest exploded in his apartment while the pair were under the influence of alcohol. Earlier that year, wild boars unearthed 21 mortar shells buried in a forest since the war. In 2023, 72 unexploded artillery shells were discovered during renovation work at a primary school and four pieces of World War Two ordnance were found in the walls of a church undergoing renovation. Wild boars dug up 21 mortar shells from World War Two that had been buried in a Polish forest. The unexploded ordnance has now been safely removed without harm to either the animals or humans https://t.co/W9kaPr1BNw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
