The opposition’s main grievance was the absence of the Catholicos from the opening session. The authorities did not invite him, and he did not bless the work of parliament. Opposition lawmakers described this as an unprecedented event in the history of independent Armenia.

Under the constitutional law governing the National Assembly’s rules of procedure, both the president and the Catholicos of All Armenians have the right to deliver opening remarks at parliament’s first session. This time, however, only President Vahagn Khachaturyan addressed lawmakers. Earlier, the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin said it had received no invitation for the Catholicos. When journalists asked Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan about Garegin II’s participation, he replied: “I do not know such a Catholicos.” The incident reflects the long-running dispute between the Armenian authorities and Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II. More than two years ago, Prime Minister Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He initially argued that Garegin II could not lead the Armenian Apostolic Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and fathered a daughter. Pashinyan later accused him of links with foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party also included the removal of “the de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Lawmakers also fiercely debated the nomination of Ruben Rubinyan, the ruling party’s sole candidate for speaker of parliament.

Opposition MPs repeatedly referred to his research work at Istanbul Policy Center in Turkey in 2017–18. They asked whether he had interacted with local residents and even questioned what they looked like.

“Ask me directly whether I met representatives of the Turkish intelligence services in Turkey and whether they recruited me. Ask me: ‘Is that true?’ And I will answer: ‘No,'” Rubinyan said.

Parliament resumed its first session today. Lawmakers have already settled one of the main items on the agenda. In a secret ballot, they elected Ruben Rubinyan as speaker with 63 votes in favour and 28 against.

The opposition Armenia bloc boycotted the secret ballot. MPs from the second opposition force, the Strong Armenia faction, voted against Rubinyan’s nomination.

In the previous parliament, Rubinyan served as deputy speaker. Between 2022 and 2026, he also acted as Armenia’s special envoy for the normalisation of relations with Turkey. A few days ago, Rubinyan said he would be unable to continue in that role if parliament elected him speaker. The ruling party has not yet announced who will succeed him.

“Where is the Patriarch?” Opposition MPs visit him to receive his blessing

On the opening day of the session, opposition MPs began chanting, “Where is the Patriarch?” after the president’s address. During the oath-taking ceremony, they pointedly refused to stand or recite the oath. They said they were protesting the Catholicos’s absence. However, they signed the written text of the oath, allowing them to take office formally.

At the end of the first working day, MPs from both opposition factions visited the Catholicos’s residence.

The Mother See’s information service said Garegin II blessed the opposition lawmakers. He spoke of an “alarming situation and serious problems” facing the country. He also criticised what he described as the authorities’ “illegal and unconstitutional actions” against the Church.

Catholicos receives opposition MPs at the Mother See

The Catholicos praised what he described as the opposition MPs’ “devotion and filial love for the Church”. He said their stance was especially important at a time when “the authorities continue their campaign of repression, while national benefactor Samvel Karapetyan remains under arrest for speaking out in defence of Holy Etchmiadzin”.

In June last year, Armenian authorities opened a criminal case against Russian businessman and billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. Prosecutors accused him of publicly calling for the seizure and usurpation of power. In an interview with local media, Karapetyan discussed the escalating conflict between the government and the Church. He said he supported the Church and added: “If Armenia’s political forces fail to resolve this situation, we will have to intervene in the campaign against the Church in our own way.” His supporters founded the Strong Armenia party after his arrest, and he has remained under house arrest since December last year.

105 MPs in the new parliament

The three political forces that entered the National Assembly secured the following number of seats:

The ruling Civil Contract party – 64 seats

The Strong Armenia faction – 29 seats

The Armenia bloc – 12 seats

Strong Armenia leader and businessman Samvel Karapetyan did not enter parliament. During the election campaign, his allies confidently predicted victory and even said Karapetyan would become prime minister. However, he is ineligible to serve either as an MP or as prime minister. Under Armenia’s constitution, anyone holding citizenship of another country cannot hold either office. Karapetyan holds Armenian, Russian and Cypriot citizenship.

Former President Robert Kocharyan headed the electoral list of the Armenia bloc, making him its candidate for prime minister. However, Kocharyan declined to take up his parliamentary seat. His son, Levon Kocharyan, who also ran on the bloc’s list, accepted a mandate and has already joined parliament. He also served as an MP for the Armenia bloc in the previous legislature.

“I will do everything to ensure our children never experience war”

Rubinyan thanked the more than 700,000 voters who backed Civil Contract. He said they had given the ruling party “a mandate to continue Armenia’s democratic reforms and peace agenda”. According to Rubinyan, those voters had defended the country’s sovereignty and independence.

He said the time had come for Armenians to enjoy peaceful lives, have children and raise them without fear.

“My son, who is almost two years old, and children of his age have never experienced war. I will do everything to ensure that my children, your children and all our children never have to learn what war is,” he said.

Rubinyan also thanked those who voted for opposition parties out of conviction rather than in exchange for election bribes.

“It is time to change the political discourse,” Rubinyan says

Addressing opposition MPs, Rubinyan raised the issue of the tone of parliamentary debate. He said society, political circles and journalists had formed a common view of parliament in recent months. According to him, many now see the National Assembly as a place for pointless arguments, slander and insults.

“They say this parliament will be even worse than the previous one in that respect. It seems everyone expects exactly that from us. I want to propose that we break this curse together,” the speaker said.

He argued that the opposition factions had largely stayed away from the work of the previous, eighth convocation of parliament.

“All we saw here was political confrontation, shouting and radical speeches. It is time to change the narratives that have dominated Armenian politics over the past six years. I propose that we make this parliament a place for vigorous but respectful debate that never crosses the boundaries of decency.”

At the same time, he warned that if the opposition rejected his proposal and continued “down the well-trodden path”, the ruling party was ready to respond “in the toughest possible way”.

“Why did we take our seats?” Opposition MPs explain

Ishkhan Saghatelyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, argued that neither the opposition nor the ruling party had truly won the election.

He again claimed that the authorities had used administrative resources during the campaign and imprisoned opposition figures.

“This parliament has a serious legitimacy problem. We are here to organise political struggle and advance national goals. We are here to raise the concerns of Armenia’s citizens, speak about the prisoners held in Baku and Armenia’s occupied territories, and, yes, defend the people of Artsakh’s right to a collective return.”

Hayk Farmanyan, an MP from the Strong Armenia faction, echoed that message.

“We accepted our mandates to remain true to our Armenian identity, to fight for our national values, and to defend our dignity, our identity and our Church.”

Comment

Political analyst Lilit Dallakyan shared her impressions of the new parliament’s opening session on social media:

“Well, I ‘congratulate’ the Armenian people on the start of work by a new, high-quality, substantive parliament that is supposedly ready to tackle Armenia’s complex challenges.

The daily exchange of ‘Your father is a murderer’ [directed at MP Levon Kocharyan, son of former President Robert Kocharyan] will now gain a new, equally substantive argument: ‘Your uncle is a Russian oligarch’ [directed at MP Narek Karapetyan, nephew of Strong Armenia leader Samvel Karapetyan]. That will, in turn, prompt the reply: ‘You are Turkish dictators’ [directed at the authorities].

The only positive aspect is that this season of the series is unlikely to interest anyone or distract people from the real problems that are rapidly emerging.

At a time of profound change across the world, Armenian society and every individual will have to look for solutions to their own problems. Ultimately, that will bring about the changes the country needs.”

First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

World.title: Opinion: ‘Abkhaz diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive’
World.content:
Against the backdrop of the Pacific island nation of Nauru withdrawing its recognition of Abkhazia’s independence, prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania reflects on what Abkhazia’s foreign policy doctrine should look like.

Nauru, a small island nation in the Pacific region of Micronesia, recognised Abkhazia’s independence in 2009 but withdrew that recognition in late July 2026. The move reduced the number of countries recognising Abkhazia’s independence to four. Abkhazia’s foreign ministry said Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure”.

Akhra Bzhania said: “Around 230,000 irregular migrants crossed the EU’s borders in 2025–26 alone. All of them fled countries that enjoy broad international recognition.

Why didn’t they stay in Morocco, Mali or Afghanistan? Presumably because having a flag outside the UN headquarters does not automatically mean you live in a genuine state – one where you can influence public life, where your voice matters and where your dignity will never be trampled.

Being a recognised country and being a country where people want to live and are willing to die for it are two different things.

You may achieve the first and never attain the second. But if you have the second, then you have accomplished the most important task: building a country that belongs to its citizens. That is what defines a modern state. And that is precisely what should become the main instrument for Abkhazia’s integration into the international community.

Bzhania continued: “We must send a clear message to the international community that, despite sanctions, isolation and the threat of war, the people of Abkhazia have built a society based on the rule of law and freedom. Without being members of international institutions, we have incorporated the core principles of international conventions on civil and political rights into our system of governance.

We see ourselves as part of the international community and believe we deserve our rightful place within it. To achieve that, our diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive. It should focus not on waiting for or preserving acts of recognition, but on consistently demonstrating our statehood and expanding our international contacts.

No one else is obliged to do this for us. By recognising our sovereignty, Russia effectively made Abkhazia a subject of international law. But it cannot solve our problems on our behalf.”

Bzhania continued: “We must use every tool at our disposal to achieve our goals: the resources of the diaspora, cultural, trade and sporting ties, personal connections, migration policy and regional logistics. In this game, we need to keep raising the stakes.

Today, there is a window of opportunity for such an active policy. It is no secret that relations between Georgia and the West are at their lowest point since the 1990s. Those on whom Tbilisi relied to promote its anti-Abkhaz agenda have become disillusioned with Georgia, and we should take advantage of that. That includes reviving the active dialogue with European countries that existed in the late 1990s. After all, the hopes the West once placed in Georgia as a bastion of the free world in the Caucasus have, to a greater extent, been realised in Abkhazia.

Another key asset, which has remained almost entirely outside our foreign policy efforts, is the Circassian diaspora. Four million people spread across 50 countries represent a powerful resource we can genuinely rely on. More importantly, we should offer them the prospect of political cooperation.

Abkhazia can and should become the centre of the Circassian world as the only independent state of this sub-ethnic group. Our country can become the same kind of homeland for Circassians worldwide that Israel has become for Jews. If every Circassian, wherever they live, knows they will find protection and support for their interests in Abkhazia, it will create a strong foundation for advancing our shared interests.”

Bzhania concluded: “It will probably not happen tomorrow, no matter how much effort we put in. But it can happen within a foreseeable future if those efforts remain consistent and systematic.

In 2017, I had the honour of welcoming a delegation from Nauru’s parliament to Abkhazia on behalf of the Abkhaz parliament. They were wonderful, warm people. Unfortunately, ships at sea do not only meet – they also part ways. Today, Nauru has set a course away from Abkhazia, apparently believing it to be the safer option. I wish them well. As for us, we will continue on our own course.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nauru’s withdrawal of recognition of Abkhazia

World.title: “For safe and strong Georgia”: Saturday march in Tbilisi. Georgia protests video blog
World.content:
612th day of protests in Tbilisi

“For a Safe and Strong Georgia” was the main slogan of the traditional pro-European Saturday march held in Tbilisi on 1 August 2026.

Before the march began, participants observed a minute’s silence in memory of a teenager who was recently killed in central Tbilisi and who would have turned 18 today.

Hundreds of people gathered once again in Avlabari Square for the 612th consecutive day of protests. With construction work continuing on Rustaveli Avenue, the march followed an alternative route for the second Saturday in a row, starting at Avlabari metro station and ending outside the parliament building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: WA's NAPLAN results trigger 'concern' for year 3s
World.content:
Western Australia's NAPLAN results show 40 per cent of year 3 students are struggling with numeracy, but year 9 students are out-performing the national average in every category this year.

Figures also show year 3 and 5 students ranked below the average NAPLAN score for every category. Year 7 students ranked below average for every category apart from spelling, in which students achieved a mark of 543.1, compared to the national average of 541.6.

WA's year 9 students were the state's best performers.

Despite the younger years largely experiencing below-average scores, there were some improvements on last year's figures.

Year 5 grammar and punctuation saw a score increase of 0.8 per cent compared to last year, and year 7 numeracy was up 0.7 per cent.

The largest drop, however, was recorded in year 3 writing, which was down 1.7 per cent compared to last year.

Roughly 1.2 million students across Australia participated in NAPLAN testing this year and were assessed in five categories — writing, spelling, reading, numeracy, and grammar and punctuation.

When looking at how students ranked across the four score categories — "needs additional support", "developing", "strong" and "exceeding" — from lowest to highest, the stand-out figure from WA was year 3 numeracy scores, which saw 39.9 per cent of those students place in the bottom two tiers.

System 'working well'

WA Education Minister Sabine Winton said the NAPLAN figures were "encouraging" for the year 9 cohort.

"For me, the real value in whether we are actually having great outcomes in our educational system is the growth that you bring to each and every child, whether it's from term to term, from year to year," she said.

"It is clear our education system is working well to add to that growth, and it's working particularly well when you consider our year 9 results.

" No matter where the starting point is, our schools must be doing something fantastic over a number of years to get our year 9s into that strong position. "

Sabine Winton was buoyed by the state's year 9 results. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

But Ms Winton acknowledged that the year 3 numeracy scores were of "most concern" in WA and across the nation.

"It really does, I think, reflect what I hear anecdotally from my mates in terms of more children with development delays, the more complex needs coming into our school system," she said.

Opposition education spokesperson Liam Staltari shared Ms Winton's concern over the year 3 scores and said the "warning signs" should not be be ignored.

Liam Staltari says the government needs to do more to help students who are struggling. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"If I were the parent of an eight- or a nine-year-old, I would be concerned, because if we don't support our kids in those critical early years, we know that they fall behind later in schooling," he said.

Mr Staltari said the government needed to do more to set up children for success in year 3, pointing to low student-to-teacher ratios in WA classrooms and teacher burnout.

World.title: Murder accused to remain in custody as lawyers struggle to find suitable bail location
World.content:
Fierce opposition, community riots and an unmanned police station are among the issues that have left a 20-year-old man charged with murder in custody for months while he waits for lawyers to find a suitable location for bail.

Justin Bukulatjpi was charged with murdering a man and unlawfully causing serious harm to another person during a brawl in Milingimbi in April.

In May, the Northern Territory Supreme Court granted Mr Bukulatjpi bail to live with family on the Tiwi Islands — a decision that was strongly opposed by Crown prosecutor Deborah Mandie, who said the prosecution had a "very strong" case against him.

Ms Mandie told the court prosecutors would rely on more than 10 minutes of mobile phone footage of the incident, in which she said the accused could be seen wielding a knife above his head before the other man fell to the ground.

Despite that, Justice Judith Kelly said she had a "high degree of confidence" Mr Bukulatjpi would follow his bail conditions.

However, days before he was due to be released, traditional owners wrote to the NT police commissioner expressing concerns his presence would bring further unrest to the area, preventing his release.

A week later, there were riots in the community and the Tiwi Islands' executive director of township leasing blocked him from entering public spaces — actions that Justice Kelly described as "unacceptable".

Justin Bukulatjpi's planned bail to the Tiwi Islands was blocked by community riots involving at least 100 residents. (Supplied: Rebecca Parker)

Mr Bukulatjpi has faced court several times since his first appearance more than two months ago.

However, each of his proposed bail addresses have so far been found to be unsuitable, leaving him on remand as lawyers continue searching for an alternative.

Judge requests undertaking to the court

On Wednesday, defence barrister Louise Dart proposed her client live with family on Warruwi, a tiny Indigenous community on the isolated South Goulburn Island, 290 kilometres north-east of Darwin.

But the case was delayed again after Ms Mandie told the court the Warruwi police station was unmanned for five weeks at a time, effectively ruling out electronic monitoring, and argued that Mr Bukulatjpi remained a flight risk.

Ms Dart argued her client had strong family ties in the community and would have little opportunity to flee.

"It's a question of where would he go? He's a person of limited means, limited English … I don't think he's going to flee the jurisdiction," she said.

Judith Kelly says breaching an undertaking could be ruled contempt of court. (Supplied: Supreme Court of the Northern Territory)

Justice Kelly requested Ms Dart make enquiries as to whether any "men in authority, who may be able to exert more influence, on Mr Bukulatjpi" would be willing to provide an undertaking to the court to "use their best endeavours" to make sure he remained at the bail address.

She said a breach of such an undertaking could result in a charge of contempt of court.

"[If a] respected male [or] elder from the community is willing to put their reputation on the line … then it seems to me that that would probably overcome the sorts of concerns raised by Ms Mandie," she said.

The case has been adjourned until September and Mr Bukulatjpi was remanded in custody.

World.title: Kids' outdoor program halted as council raises safety concerns
World.content:
A popular outdoor education program has been temporarily shut by Mount Barker District Council, which organisers say came as a "shock".

Last week Forest School SA was ordered to cease operating at Anembo Park in Mount Barker due to property and safety concerns that the council said were identified during a site inspection.

Program founder Bell Gower said she received an email from the council ordering "all Forest School activities at the site cease immediately while the matter is being considered".

Forest School SA founder Isabella Gower next to the outdoor play equipment used by her students. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

"Council has significant concerns regarding the safety risks associated with the current activities being undertaken at the site," the email said.

The council observed "a number of matters of concern", the email said, including damage to existing trees, fire pits, evidence of fires and activities extending into land under the care and control of the Department for Infrastructure and Transport.

"During the inspection Council officers observed swings installed within the reserve and noted that the area being used for the Forest School is immediately adjacent to the South Eastern Freeway," the email, seen by the ABC, said.

"There [is] no physical barrier or fencing separating participants from the roadway at this location."

The council said a formal application would need to be submitted and approved before any further activities on the site could be undertaken.

Mount Barker District Council raised concerns about the proximity to the freeway. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

Ms Gower said the program had been operating at Mount Barker for about a year after relocating from Kuitpo, and had received council approval.

She said the closure has come as a "huge shock" to employees and families.

"We were in denial for a few days there, thinking that we would be able to work this out without ceasing operations," Ms Gower said.

"There has been a lot of emotions there from families, a lot of children saying, 'No, I don't want to go to a different place.'"

Ms Gower said she had submitted a formal application to resume the program and was waiting for a response, but doubted the program would resume at the site.

"We as educators use our professional risk assessment to be able to determine what we think is appropriate for the children to be doing," she said.

"I would not say that anything we have here is wildly dangerous."

Isabella Gower with her students at Anembo Park, Mount Barker. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

Ms Gower said the Scouts group had agreed to host the program as a short-term solution and anticipated that classes would resume next week.

"At the same time as this potentially being a lovely opportunity, it has been really disruptive to our families and the children who have been caretakers of this space for a year," she said.

Ms Gower said about 40 families were enrolled in the program, which attracted hundreds of participants during the school holidays.

School 'expanded significantly', council says

A council spokesperson said the district supported "nature-based learning" and had "been working with Forest School SA since early 2025 to regularise its operations".

"During this time, Council understood the program was operating from a small area near the tennis courts," the spokesperson said.

"However, a recent site inspection identified the operation had expanded significantly, with structures, cleared vegetation, fire pits and activity areas extending into adjoining land."

Council had "not shut down Forest School SA as an organisation", but had "directed that the current operation at Anembo Park cease until it can be lawfully and safely assessed", the spokesperson said.

"Council appreciates this may be disappointing for families whose children participate in the program," they said.

"For that reason, Council is committed to working with Forest School SA as quickly as possible to determine whether a compliant pathway forward can be achieved."

Parents feeling 'heartbroken'

Parent Teala Duke said the program was a "perfect fit" the learning needs off her five-year-old daughter, who attended twice a week.

"I was struggling to find somewhere for her to fit in or for her to really nourish her abilities … she likes to be out in the mud, exploring, cooking, cleaning," Ms Duke said.

Teala Duke says her five-year-old daughter is upset by the closure. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

She said her daughter was "absolutely devastated" by the temporary relocation and hoped the program could continue to operate at Mount Barker.

"It's heartbreaking. If the kids didn't have this area anymore it wouldn't be the same," Ms Duke said.

"There is other places we can do but they have adapted so well to his environment … they call it home.

"They've created a bond with this area. It's their space — we don't want it taken away from them."

World.title: 'Gone down like a lead balloon': Ex-FA boss on FIFA's World Cup backflip
World.content:
"It's gone down like a lead balloon."

This is David Gallop's view of FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-infamous World Cup privatisation proposal.

"It's so far off passing the pub test that I think it's like he let off a stink bomb in the middle of the pub and people ran screaming, leaving half a schooner behind," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"That's how poorly it's been received."

Mr Gallop has been one of Australia's foremost sport's administrators. He was CEO of the NRL from 2002-2012 before jumping ship to become the boss of Football Federation Australia for seven years until his tenure ended in 2019.

He has watched on this past week as Mr Infantino's failed sell-off plan has evolved into a full-blown crisis over his leadership.

"He's definitely under pressure now … to throw out an idea like this that's gone down so badly," he said.

Mr Infantino's proposal, dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise, would have seen the commercial rights of FIFA's most popular tournaments, including the World Cup, transferred to a private company, and a 20 per cent stake sold to investors, valued at $20 billion.

It's been reported Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law, was one of the private equity figures behind the plan.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump was under scrutiny at the World Cup. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

"Anytime you sell anything, you need to have good, compelling reasons, but particularly so when it comes to something like the World Cup and ... sport in general," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"You've got to know that you really need to do it. You really need the money. What are you getting for the slice of the asset and what are you giving up?

"Clearly people have not liked the idea that private investment, and therefore, a profit motive that comes away from the game to those private investors would be something that FIFA would contemplate."

'One-off sugar hit'

Mr Gallop said privatisation was not inherently wrong but required an overwhelming strategic and financial case to be valid.

"It will be a mistake to burn the furniture to heat the house," he said.

"You need to be setting up your sport and the business of your sport for sustainability, not for a one-off sugar hit of capital.

"These are the questions that have to be answered when one is looking at private sale of these effectively community assets that people feel strongly about."

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's plan to privatise has been met with derision by many football bodies. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

The proposal offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each, but Mr Gallop said FIFA's financial position only heightened questions about why such a proposal had been pursued.

"FIFA has $5 billion in cash now after the World Cup," he said.

" I think that's one of the reasons why a proposal to sell an equity stake has fallen so flat. They're not desperate for money. "

Within three days of the proposal, Mr Infantino and FIFA scrapped the plans.

Europe's UEFA, North America's CONCACAF and Asia's AFC, which Australia is member of, all opposed the plan.

UEFA, CONCACAF, as well as a growing number of national federations have taken it further by withdrawing their support of Mr Infantino's leadership.

Football Australia's chair Anter Isaac and CEO Martin Kugeler both declined an interview with 7.30.

The organisation has welcomed the decision by FIFA to scrap the privatisation proposal but is yet to weigh-in on Mr Infantino's, now under siege, leadership.

Mr Gallop said Australia's influence on the world game came less through political power than integrity.

Infantino's 'blotted copybook'

The integrity of Mr Infantino, like that of his predecessor Sepp Blatter has now been called into question.

Former FIFA President Sepp Blatter's tenure ended due to corruption. (Reuters: Stefan Wermuth)

Mr Infantino was elected in 2016 promising to restore confidence in FIFA, following a number of corruption scandals that occurred under Mr Blatter's 17-year reign as president.

Mr Gallop's time at FA straddled the terms of both men. He was also CEO in 2010, when Australia's bid to host the 2022 World Cup was beaten by Qatar, a decision that was mired in controversy and allegations of corruption.

"There was a bit of a stench around FIFA and Gianni came in with a pitch of transparency, accountability, consultation and putting football first," Mr Gallop said.

" I think it's fair to say this proposal, albeit backflipped on, has blotted his copybook in respect to what people expected from him and from his presidency. "

"[Especially} coming hot off the heels of a number of other contentious decisions, including the lifting of the red card on the USA player during the tournament."

United States' Folarin Balogun's red card was rescinded during the World Cup after a call from Trump to Infantino. (AP: Jeff Chiu)

Despite calls for Mr Infantino's resignation growing louder, Mr Gallop said his tenure at the top of world football might not be over just yet.

"I don't think it's necessarily so that he won't get re-elected. He has some big confederations against him at the moment, but he has others where FIFA has carefully funded development in a lot of smaller nations," he said.

Mr Gallop remembers representing Australia at FIFA congresses, sitting next to the small Caribbean nation of Aruba — "a population of a hundred thousand people."

"Behind us would be Brazil … millions of people, an absolute icon of world football … but everyone gets one vote; that's where your confederation structure comes into play," he said.

Mr Gallop believes the president's political future will depend on whether member associations believe the successes achieved under his leadership outweigh the damage caused by the failed privatisation proposal.

" Whether there's enough credit in the bank for all the good things that FIFA have produced … or whether this has blown them up will remain to be seen. "

Fan outrage

Patrick Clancy, head of the Football Supporters Association in Australia, told 7.30 many fans felt betrayed by the proposal.

Football's governing body has long been at the centre of controversy and corruption allegations. (REUTERS: Arnd Wiegmann )

"He's tried to privatise football at the expense of the game of football," he said.

"It's something that came out of nowhere and is not in line with what anyone has thought of before. And so I think that's the concern; where's it all going?"

His organisation is now very keen to understand where Football Australia stands on Mr Infantino and his leadership.

"These are very troubling times in world football and Football Australia needs to make its position very clear," he said.

Mr Clancy says football supporters want to see the game run properly.

"They want to feel that there is a degree of integrity and they don't want a money-hungry organisation that seems to be interfering with that organic nature of the game," he said.

"Within 24 hours, Infantino and FIFA completely changed the shape of world football.

" They blindsided almost everyone in the game, so goodness knows what's going to happen in the next seven days. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Australia's coach says no tour match ahead of India Test series
World.content:
Australia will again opt for a training camp ahead of the five-Test tour of India rather than play ​a traditional warm-up match before attempting to end a 22-year wait for a Test series victory on the subcontinent.

Australia also chose not to play a tour match before ​the 2023 series, ‌instead training on specially prepared, spin-friendly pitches in Bengaluru before the opening Test.

The decision drew scrutiny after India won the Nagpur opener by an innings ‌and 132 runs, setting the tone for a 2-1 series ⁠victory that allowed the hosts to retain the Border-Gavaskar ‌Trophy.

Ifs, buts and maybes for Australia in India The record books will show that Australia left India without the Border-Gavaskar Trophy, but the series defeat offers plenty of opportunity for introspection ahead of the Ashes.

Head coach Andrew McDonald ​said Australia would scout ‌a location to immerse themselves in conditions similar to India before the series opener in Nagpur starting on January 21.

"We've got a couple of options there," he told Cricket Australia website Cricket.com.au ​on ‌Wednesday.

"We have gone to the UAE previously and we have also gone into India last time into Bengaluru, so we're ⁠just working through what that ‌would look like in terms ‌of how we then manage the individuals."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

World.title: Police confirm 'no surviving occupants' after ute, car engulfed in flames
World.content:
At least four people have died in a fiery head-on crash between two vehicles on the Stuart Highway, south-east of Darwin, this afternoon.

In a statement, a Northern Territory Police Force spokesperson said the crash had occurred about 2 kilometres south of the turn-off to Marrakai Road, with police receiving multiple reports about 12:50pm.

"Police, Fire and Rescue Service crews and St John Ambulance attended the scene, where both vehicles were fully engulfed in flames," the spokesperson said.

" Sadly, there were no surviving occupants. "

Police are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the crash.

Both lanes of the Stuart Highway have been closed as authorities investigate the crash. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

NT Police Detective Senior Sergeant Michael Schumacher said "due to the extent of the damage, [investigators] are still working to formally identify the deceased and determine whether there were any additional occupants in either vehicle".

"Due to the severity of the crash, which appears to have been a high-speed head-on collision, both vehicles caught fire, making this an extremely complex investigation," he said.

"At this stage, we have confirmed at least four people have died.

"One vehicle, believed to be a goods van, contains one deceased person.

"The second vehicle, a dual-cab utility, contains three confirmed deceased."

Police have urged motorists to avoid the area. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

A section of the Stuart Highway has been closed in both directions.

Earlier this afternoon, traffic diversions were causing heavy delays to traffic and heavy duty vehicles were banked up on the side of the road.

"Detours for light vehicles will be implemented by the Department of Logistics and Infrastructure as soon as possible," the police statement said.

"Heavy vehicles are unable to pass through the area at this time, and motorists are urged to avoid the area and expect significant delays."

World.title: Hip hop artist-turned-novelist wins Miles Franklin award
World.content:
Omar Musa has won one of the nation's top literary prizes, the $60,000 Miles Franklin Literary Award, for his novel Fierceland, a family saga interrogating ideas of inheritance, complicity and colonialism.

The Malaysian Australian author described his win as "mind-blowing".

"You can never predict or expect something like this, but I'm really stoked to have my work recognised and acknowledged alongside such amazing peers," he tells ABC Arts.

"It also acknowledges the work of a lot of people behind the scenes. There's always this mythology about the solitary author up in their tower, scribbling away by themselves.

" But for me, fiction is often a collaborative [effort] with mentors and advisors and readers and editors. "

Fierceland — the second novel by Musa, who is also a hip hop artist, visual artist and former Australian slam poetry champion — also won the 2026 Victorian Premier's Prize for Fiction.

Key facts: The Miles Franklin Award was first awarded in 1957

It was established in the will of author Stella Maria Sarah Miles Franklin (author of My Brilliant Career)

It distinguishes a novel "of the highest literary merit" that presents "Australian life in any of its phases"

Past winners include Thea Astley, Peter Carey, Tim Winton and Melissa Lucashenko

The 2025 Miles Franklin was won by Siang Lu for Ghost Stories

The book tells the story of two siblings who grow up in Kota Kinabalu on the island of Borneo. The children of a palm oil baron, they must contend with his complicated legacy when, as adults, they travel back to Malaysia for his funeral.

The Miles Franklin judges described Fierceland as "a tour de force set against the backdrop of the destruction of Borneo's rainforests".

"Cleared to make way for palm oil plantations, this pulsing forest world is the moral centre of Fierceland and Musa's rhythmic prose hums its defiance," they said.

"As it charts a journey of personal and planetary redemption, Fierceland refashions the venerable, vernacular hikayat traditions of Malay storytelling into new Australian idioms."

Taking on a maligned industry

Musa grew up in Queanbeyan, a regional city located a stone's throw from Canberra.

His mother, a theatre-maker and arts journalist who grew up in western NSW, met his father when she travelled to Malaysia to direct the first Malay production of Hamlet.

His father was cast in the lead role.

Musa travelled to Borneo a handful of times as a child, but it wasn't until he was an adult that he reconnected with his Malay family.

"From my early 20s on, I would go at least once a year," he told ABC Radio National's The Book Show.

"And then a couple of years ago, I moved back to Kota Kinabalu in the state of Sabah, which is the easternmost state of Malaysian Borneo, where my dad comes from.

"I've described it as being a very enriching, confronting, confusing, soul-stirring experience, but one that was necessary for me as a human, but also for this book."

Musa's latest book is the 2026 short story collection The Vape Lord of Queanbeyan. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

Musa's debut novel, Here Come the Dogs — longlisted for the Miles Franklin in 2015 — was inspired by his childhood growing up in the suburbs.

"It was about race relations in Australia, what I see as quite a combustible society in certain ways," he says.

"I realised once I'd written that out of my system, I wanted to turn my attention towards the Malaysian Indonesian archipelago, towards my heritage and my history."

While he initially set out to write "seafaring epic that was all about the islands and borderlessness", the story that emerged was very different.

He was drawn instead to the forests and rivers of Borneo, today a hub of oil-palm cultivation, an industry imported to Southeast Asia from West Africa in the 70s and much maligned for its exploitative and destructive practices.

While Musa agrees this view is fair, he argues it's not the complete picture.

"Oil palm has a really bad name in the West and in some ways, rightly so, because if you're mowing down primary rainforest and replacing it with a mono-crop, that's an extremely destructive thing, especially in a world that's on the edge of ecological collapse," he says.

"But for families like mine, the rural poor in a lot of parts of Malaysia were brought out of poverty by some of those palm oil schemes."

Miles Franklin shortlist unpacked ABC experts review the shortlist of Australia's biggest book prize: who made it, who missed out and who they think will win.

Musa's father was one of nine siblings, and Musa was the only one of his cousins to grow up in Australia. Many of his family members worked on oil-palm plantations.

"When I'd go back to Sabah as a kid, I would spend time on the plantations and see what their lives were like," he says.

Musa felt his connection to the controversial industry gave him a unique perspective on the issue.

"Logging and oil palm are very dark, fascinating, complex worlds, but I'd only ever read about them in non-fiction," he says.

"I'd never read a novel that explored those worlds, at least in Malaysia and Borneo."

A tale of exploitation

Fierceland centres on a family of four: parents Yusuf and Jenab, and their children Roz and Harun.

Born into poverty and orphaned when he was seven, Yusuf worked hard for his family, amassing a fortune that granted his children a life of immense privilege.

At the same time, through his business interests, Yusuf was responsible for the large-scale destruction of rainforest and the dispossession of the people who lived there.

As they grow up, Roz and Harun struggle to reconcile the two sides of their father, who was both a loving parent and a hard-nosed capitalist.

"I was trying to tell the story of colonialism and exploitation in Borneo through this family dynamic," Musa says.

"I was also thinking about privilege and complicity and how we participate as individuals in systems that are much larger than ourselves, systems of oppression and exploitation, and whether we engage with those systems through choice or coercion."

The character of Roz — "a rebellious and self-destructive artist" — first appeared in a short story Musa wrote 10 years ago. (Supplied: Penguin)

The narrative opens in 1998, when Yusuf takes the children on an ill-fated trip into the forest, where they witness a traumatic incident that becomes a turning point in their lives.

At first, the journey up the river is magical, Musa says. Yusuf and the children are enchanted by the jungle.

"[But] once they're up the river, they suddenly realise that he's not there to protect the forest. He's there to cut it down, to make a whole lot of money out of it," Musa says.

"This is where a lot of the drama comes from in the book, the interaction between Yusuf Mansur and these people who are standing in his way."

Fierceland features multiple voices: not only Rozana and Harun, both as children and adults, but also side characters including their uncle, Pakcik Abdul Hamid, their father's right-hand man, Jibrail, and his best friend, known affectionately as Crazy Auntie, and, notably, the forest itself.

July's best books This month's best new books include an erotic novel set in a Tasmanian lighthouse, a 'wonderfully weird debut' about a woman's obsession with a cat and a Harlem heist novel.

The novel takes several other surprising turns, landing in Nigeria in the 70s, 19th-century Venice and the jungle court of the Rajah of Pandasan, where Joseph Conrad (who set several of his novels in Borneo) makes a cameo.

"In some ways, my book is a subversion and a critique of and a response to [Conrad's 1899 novella] Heart of Darkness, where the forest … becomes a kind of a metaphor for the hearts of man, and also is just a bit of an impressionistic backdrop for the lives of the European characters," Musa says.

"What I wanted to say with this book … was that the forest and nature is to be respected and it has an agency and a spirit of its own. It's not just something inert to be acted upon or to be exploited.

"I wanted the forest to speak for itself. I wanted, obviously, the local characters to speak for themselves, and have names and flesh and blood and flaws, unlike in a book like Heart of Darkness, where they … are just a blur in the background."

Australia's place in Asia

With narrative strands unfolding in both Malaysia and Australia, Fierceland situates Australia firmly in the Asia-Pacific region.

Roz and Harun's parents meet at university in Adelaide, where Yusuf is on a Colombo Plan scholarship.

A generation later, Roz and Harun are sent to elite private schools in Sydney, where Yusuf has extensive business interests.

Once they finish high school, Harun escapes to LA while Roz remains in Sydney, struggling to establish herself there as an artist.

On a flight from Sydney to Kuala Lumpur, Roz sits next to a man who surprises her with his knowledge of her home country.

She tells him: "Aussies don't usually give two shits about Malaysia, outside of food."

Musa says The Boat by Nam Le is among his favourite Australian books. "It casts a long shadow, in a good way, over Australian lit." (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

Musa sought to address this gap in his novel.

"It's sad that Indonesia, Malaysia, PNG are our closest neighbours, but Australians seem to know so little about them," he says.

"I'm trying to show those threads of connection and flows between different parts of this region, because we are part of this region.

"Unfortunately, over the last, let's say, 20, 25 years, there's a segment of the Australian population that has reverted to what I would say is more of an archaic view of Australia — that it's … an isolated outpost that's fearful of its region, which I think is pretty tragic, to be honest.

"I don't want to look back on the 90s as if it was just some golden age, but I do remember there was much more of an effort to present a vision of Australia as more integrated into [the Asia-Pacific]."

It's an aspect of the novel that takes on renewed significance amid recent debates around multiculturalism.

"It shows … that [debate] in a different light," Musa says.

World.title: Rescue helicopter contract in jeopardy after parliamentary inquiry
World.content:
New South Wales Ambulance is being urged not extend contracts with Northern NSW Helicopter Rescue Services (NNSWHRS) unless it is satisfied with workplace safety.

The recommendation came from a state parliamentary inquiry that was called to investigate Calvary Mater Hospital at Newcastle after a string of alleged maintenance failures.

The inquiry also examined wider issues arising from public and private partnerships in healthcare.

Committee chair Amanda Cohn said multiple witnesses detailed allegations of a toxic workplace culture at NNSWHRS, including instances of bullying and psychological abuse.

"We are really urging the [NSW] government to put these agreements under scrutiny now rather than wait for there to be a tragedy," the Greens MP said.

"Nobody wants to be left without a service — that's why it is so critical that this level of scrutiny happens now.

"If the government decides not to extend the current contract, then obviously going out to tender or considering another provider is something that takes time."

Amanda Cohn says the government should be thinking about its next move now. (Parliament of New South Wales)

The inquiry found the use of staff non-disclosure agreements had "prevented transparency, silenced potential whistleblowers and delayed the rectification of issues".

Whistleblowers targeted

According to the parliamentary report, former employees who raised compliance concerns were targeted by a "clique" led by senior management and human resources, with some facing "verbal insults and mental abuse".

It said the impact of the culture on staff had been "extreme" and that multiple staff had been rendered "unable to return to the workforce".

The Lismore-based rescue helicopter in action at Minyon Falls. (Supplied: Robbie Armfield)

The committee also heard accusations of noncompliant record-keeping by NNSWHRS and of failing to investigate reports of "multiple serious safety breaches".

One whistleblower alleged the rescue service had a "tick and flick" culture with regard to safety management and that "staff were encouraged to bypass genuine training assessments".

Ryan Park says contract negotiations will hinge on the report. (ABC News)

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said he was expecting a full and unredacted report into the allegations levelled against NNSWHRS.

"I think, more importantly, the [NSW] Ambulance expects it. The community expects it and deserve it" he said.

Under its contract with NSW Ambulance, which began in 2017, NNSWHRS has been providing aeromedical services including the provision of aircraft and crew to the northern part of the state.

The contract is due to end in May next year.

Mr Park said any contract negotiations would be dependent on the report.

"From there we will enter into negotiations or a process around what the next iteration of that contract looks like," he said.

"But very clearly, from my perspective as a minister, that is what I expect."

In a statement, a spokesperson for NSW Ambulance said it had "not progressed contract extension discussions with the NNSWRHS while it awaits the full and unredacted report".

NNSWRHS declined to comment.

World.title: Woman dies, child injured in three-car crash north of Cairns
World.content:
NationalQueenslandTraffic incident Woman dies, child injured in three-car crash north of Cairns Catherine Strohfeldt August 5, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 25-year-old woman has died and four people, including a child, were taken to hospital following a three-car collision north of Cairns. Shortly after 1pm on Wednesday, a 36-year-old man allegedly stole a Toyota LandCruiser utility in Palm Cove, a suburb 25 kilometres north of Cairns. Chief Superintendent Kevin Fitzgibbon said about 15 minutes later, the vehicle collided head-on with two cars – a RAV4 and a Subaru Impreza – travelling south along Smithfield Bypass, also north of Cairns. Three cars collided on Smithfield Bypass shortly before 1.30pm on Wednesday. Nine “My understanding is that the Toyota LandCruiser rolled,” Fitzgibbon said.



He said five people were injured in the crash, including the 25-year-old Kewarra Beach woman driving the RAV4, who died at the scene. Four people in the Impreza were injured, including a child, and taken to Cairns Hospital. One of the Impreza’s occupants, an adult man, was transported in a serious but non-life-threatening condition, Fitzgibbon said. He said the LandCruiser had been taken while the owner was working close to the vehicle, but it was unclear whether the keys had been in the car or if it had been a keyless ignition. “It was just a … vehicle open with the keys nearby,” he said.



While the 36-year-old was known to police, Fitzgibbon said officers did not pursue him at the time of the crash. He said the man then forced the driver of a fourth vehicle to take him away from the crash site, before police intercepted the car further south, on Reservoir Road. Paramedics took four people from the crash site to hospital. Nine “It is quite a dynamic investigation, essentially involving three separate incidents,” Fitzgibbon said. He said the driver of the fourth vehicle, who was not injured, dropped off the 36-year-old near where he was arrested about 2.15pm.



The 36-year-old was taken to hospital, where he remained under police guard on Wednesday night. “Our detectives anticipate he’ll be there overnight,” Fitzgibbon said, adding it was unlikely police would lay any charges before Thursday. The crash was “the kind of job that no police [officer] wants to go to”, he said, expressing his sympathies to the dead woman’s family. “I think the Far North community has every right to be upset and expect more from their fellow community members,” he said. Police urged anyone who might have seen the crash or alleged theft and carjacking – or who might have footage of the incidents – to come forward. World.title: The best public schools for HSC English, ranked
World.content:
Inside her office in the 1960s Castle Hill High School building in Sydney’s north-west, principal Georgina Cuthbertson can hear the school landlines ringing in the front office. And who might be calling? Parents, she says, all trying to apply to enrol their children at the school. “I’d probably knock back 15 a week,” she says. Year 12 students Xavier Bali, Netra Sangameswar and Hannah Tollens at Castle Hill High School. Sam Mooy The school can’t take any more students beyond its catchment – it has 1845 pupils and 51 demountables scattered over its campus.



Cuthbertson attributes the unrelenting enrolment demand to the school’s strong HSC results. Castle Hill High School was among the top dozen academically performing comprehensive schools in the state, according to a Herald analysis of HSC average scores, which provides the most granular data on HSC performance among public schools. A particularly strong subject at Castle Hill is English advanced, in which students recorded an average mark of 85, outperforming several fully selective schools. Unlike some public schools where only a small cohort of the students take the subject, 128 enrolled in the course at Castle Hill last year.



Head of English Lindy Jones says low staff turnover, having teachers who did HSC marking, and studying the same texts each year provided consistency, while a common set of resources developed over years helped staff work as a team to drive results. “They’re not going to have to scrounge around to find material that’s already there; it’s written up for them,” she said. Castle Hill High School’s head of English, Lindy Jones, has been marking HSC exams for 37 years. Wolter Peeters On HSC results day she leaves home at 5am to get to school by 6am so she can pore over the released marks the minute they are released. She spends part of the Christmas break looking at precise topics where students performed the best last year. “I saw the delight from my younger teachers last year when the HSC results came out, and they were just so happy,” she said.



Jones has been at the school since 1984, when it was surrounded by paddocks and when the local Country Women’s Association was involved in running debutante balls. But academic results have not always been guaranteed at the school. More than a decade ago the school noticed it was slipping behind other neighbouring schools. It adopted what is known as the ALARM (A Learning and Responding Matrix), which helped students deconstruct exam questions and write structured responses. “It actually taught staff how to look at responses and how to encourage students to write more conceptually complex responses,” she said. “I am a competitive person … There’s a personal pride that comes from seeing the success and seeing the joy that students get when they put in the effort or the hard work.”



Related Article HSC We re-ranked schools by HSC averages. This is what the most precise data reveals Year 12 student Netra Sangameswar said she was intimidated by English advanced before she enrolled in it. “When you’re in year 10, it’s like, ‘oh my god, English advanced … Am I ready for it?’” Her teachers helped her improve noticeably. “I think the teachers at Castle Hill High School have helped me take a more structured approach to my essay writing and make sure that I tick those boxes in terms of the analysis and help me argue my perspective on the text more clearly,” she said.



Killarney Heights High, Ashfield Boys High and Willoughby Girls High were other high-performing comprehensive schools in HSC English advanced last year. The state average mark was 81.8 for advanced and 71.6 for standard. Related Article HSC The best public schools in HSC maths, ranked – and how one non-selective surprised everyone Willoughby Girls principal Adrienne Scalese said the school’s strong results across all subjects was driven by its focus on literacy and mapping what skills they focused on from year 7 to ensure year 12 success. “To get that success in stage 6 we’ve spent a lot of time backward mapping to look at how we can embed those practices from year 7,” she said.



At the school, teachers work in different teams to develop ways for the school to achieve its goals identified in the school’s strategic improvement plan every four years – including in literacy. “So all of those teams worked on an action research project, and what they’ve been doing in those teams. Those individual staff have really mastered that. And then, from that team, we’ve taken that across the whole school. “So we’ll look at explicit literacy strategies related to writing, and so how we can get the best out of our students when they’re responding to extended responses.” Fully selective schools North Sydney Boys and North Sydney Girls were the top-performing schools for English advanced, while Killarney Heights High was the top-scoring school for English standard.



Most independent and Catholic schools do not report subject averages. The English advanced average at selective Sydney Grammar School was 88. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Young people are struggling like never before. These films ask why
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A few years ago, we had a small surge of films on a subject that was once thought too much of a downer to put on the screen: dementia. Julie Christie and Julianne Moore gently slipped into memory loss in Away from Her and Still Alice; Helen Mirren went on the road with a crumbling Donald Sutherland in The Leisure Seeker, followed by Colin Firth and Stanley Tucci in Supernova. And in one of the great films of this century, Anthony Hopkins lived through a whirl of confusion in Florian Zeller’s The Father. A cynic might say that once ageing became a subject for the Boomer generation, it became a subject. That can’t be said, however, for the new spread of films that get behind the worsening statistics on mental health among the young. Adolescence is turbulent for every generation, but it’s worse now. Bald figures tell their own gruesome story. Suicide is the leading cause of death among Australian youth; clinical depression among this age group doubled between 2011 and 2021. Experts point to factors ranging from the pandemic lockdowns to climate change anxiety. In 2021, The US surgeon general, described the situation in his country as “a youth mental health crisis”. Of course, we don’t experience our lives as statistics. A spread of films at the Melbourne International Film Festival about young people grappling with a world that seems overwhelming – and at the same time, very often, far too small – get close to the individuals behind the soaring lines on the graph. The more we are invited into their lives, the less sense we have of their distress as a social phenomenon: each one is so palpably living out a unique drama. La Gravida won the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival’s Critics’ Week. MIFF Marine Atlan’s La Gradiva, which won the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival’s Critics’ Week, is framed by a class trip to Pompeii, where the young French students grudgingly stand by while their teacher enthuses about mosaics and volcanoes. Their sex lives are their primary preoccupation, played out with the raw brutality of beginners. In some ways, they live in a kinder world than their parents did – nobody cares that class bad boy Tony is gay – but nobody notices how ravaged by abandonment and jealousy he is, either. We might look at their agonised intrigues and think they will be forgotten in a year or two but, when you’re 15, a couple of years is an aeon. Atlan and her co-writer, Anne Brouillet, researched their story by going on a real school trip, listening carefully to conversations around them.



“I have the impression that they are already confused by post-COVID,” says Atlan. “I think that it has led to a sort of relationship where their bodies are far away; they seem a bit dirty.” Her impression is supported by numerous studies that suggest that many of the students who spent their last school years under lockdown still find social situations difficult. Jane Beever as Lena in Goodbye Cruel World. MIFF Also from France is Goodbye Cruel World, Felix de Givry’s romantic story of a bullied schoolboy who writes to everyone in his class before he jumps into the local river. Otto’s death should be counted as murder, he tells them; they are his killers. His melodramatic hyperbole is funny, of course, but de Givry’s achievement is to convey the very real torment underlying it. Related Article Cinema Gillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder sizzle in this lurid slasher film Otto doesn’t drown, happily, but he can’t very well show up alive after such a grand farewell. Help comes from a girl from his school whose mother runs a cheap hotel. Lena finds him an empty room; locked inside, Otto gradually frees himself. Playful and sweet, the film also confronts the terrible desire to abandon life; Otto’s melancholy is so palpable that we understand intuitively, if not logically, how he got here. In the excellent Canadian film Blue Heron, first shown last year at the Locarno Film Festival, Sophy Romvari’s focus is on the rippling effect of one boy’s volcanic “oppositional defiant disorder” – meaning disobedience, taken to the max – on the other children in a recently arrived immigrant family. The story, a fictionalising of the director’s own experience, is seen through the eyes of Jeremy’s half-sister Sasha, who watches and later will try to explain his rages, his threats to burn down the house, his reckless criminal sprees. Edik Beddoes plays an inexplicably reckless young man in Blue Heron. MIFF



This is an apple-pie family, full of goodness. Why is this happening? You could blame it all on Jeremy’s being torn away from Hungary at a difficult age; you could blame the fact he’s the odd one out as the step-child. There are any number of pat answers, but his hostilities remain inexplicable. What remains for Sasha/Sophy is the dull thud of a blighted childhood; what kind of trauma Jeremy carries into adulthood can only be imagined. Surely one of the best films at MIFF, Big Girls Don’t Cry by New Zealand filmmaker Paloma Schneideman – billed as a queer coming-of-age story, but much more layered and ambiguous than that sounds – centres on 14-year-old Sid, growing up in a beach town that comes alive for just a few weeks each summer. Sid just wants to hang with the cool kids; the humiliating choices and risky behaviours she pursues to that end will have any parent – and anyone who is or once was a teenage girl – watching through their fingers. Big Girls Don’t Cry is one of the best films at this year’s MIFF. MIFF Sid isn’t suffering any kind of mental health disorder, except the oceanic one that is just being young, but she is walking a wire that traverses that territory. “I’m kind of obsessed with the tiny tragedies of day-to-day life,” Schneideman told PinkNews. Not to be asked to a party, for example, is a devastation. “What is happening to Sid is the most defining, tumultuous shit of her life to date – and yet life goes on.” It’s not only fiction that can burrow inside these feelings. Ross McElwee, director of the landmark 1986 documentary Sherman’s March, spent 14 years making Remake, a film about his son Adrian, who died of a fentanyl overdose at the age of 27. McElwee filmed Adrian, along with everything else, all his life; he had a mountain of material showing an ebullient child with a big grin, transforming in front of us. Documentary maker Ross McElwee tries to understand what happened to his son in Remake. MIFF “It will forever be a deep mystery, how this happened,” says McElwee, 79. “Because he’s clearly a happy, very clever, good-natured boy for all of those years. And so how he became the person he ended up is a mystery to me. And I know that’s part of mental health issues and also the availability of these drugs in the US.” But how much can be blamed on opiates? “I mean, he got kicked out of schools, places where he thought he’d be quite happy. After he got into his teenage years he just didn’t like anything. And it was very troubling.”

World.title: Case ‘closed’: A-G rejects criticism of DPP after advice from top silk
World.content:
NationalNSWDPP Case ‘closed’: A-G rejects criticism of DPP after advice from top silk Michaela Whitbourn August 5, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NSW attorney-general has rejected findings that the state’s top prosecutor authorised her office to pitch a negative story about a sitting judge to the media, declaring the matter “closed” after receiving legal advice that a controversial report was flawed. Michael Daley released advice on Wednesday from a trio of barristers, led by former Bar Association president Noel Hutley, SC, who concluded that evidence before a parliamentary committee did not justify the majority’s findings against Director of Public Prosecutions Sally Dowling, SC. Attorney-General Michael Daley rejected findings of a parliamentary inquiry against DPP Sally Dowling, SC. Marija Ercegovac, Sam Mooy, Nick Moir “I express my gratitude to counsel and the Crown Solicitor’s Office for the prompt provision of the advice. This matter should now be regarded as closed,” Daley said. “The Director of Public Prosecutions should be permitted to devote her undivided attention to the important work of prosecuting those who commit serious crime and keeping our community safe.”





During her evidence before the upper house justice and communities committee last year, Dowling admitted her office effectively gave a story about Wass to 2GB in October 2024. District Court Judge Penelope Wass. Dowling vehemently denied she authorised the ODPP’s media manager providing the information to 2GB, and said she only became aware that her office was the source of the story more than a year later, in December 2025. The majority did not accept her denial. Dowling said that she “was, as is my usual practice, also reading emails and texts concerning various prosecutions and other ODPP business” during a crucial meeting. The legal advice said that “[in] the absence of any clear findings of fact about what did occur at the meeting … it seems to us wrong for the committee to have concluded that the [DPP] ‘authorised’ the proactive pitch of the story”.



“Any such conclusion – and an ‘authorisation’ is undoubtedly a conclusion, not a finding of fact – first requires a factual foundation,” it said. Dowling giving evidence at the NSW upper house inquiry last year. “The [DPP’s] denial of that proposition, and account of the meeting, was given by way of sworn evidence, was inherently plausible, and was corroborated by other evidence – including that of the person who pitched the story. “Further, there was no positive basis upon which to reject the [DPP’s] account and proceed to find that she, in fact, gave false evidence. For such a serious finding to be substantiated, something more than mere disbelief of the [DPP’s] evidence was required.” Daley said that in light of this advice the government “cannot and will not” support the majority’s recommendations that it consider establishing “a formal inquiry with compulsory powers” into the incident and a new parliamentary oversight committee for the office of the DPP.



Related Article Exclusive

Courts ‘Outrageous’: Legal heavyweights back Dowling after controversial report The legal advice concluded it was also open to Daley to “reject the finding that the story was not in the public interest”, after the majority of the committee found there was no “genuine public interest” in the ODPP pitching it to 2GB. The 2GB story concerned Wass’ invitation to an Indigenous youth she was sentencing for an aggravated break and enter involving the sexual touching of an elderly woman. Wass invited him to give what she called a “Welcome to Country”. Rather than a welcome, which was not culturally appropriate, he delivered a short acknowledgement of the “traditional owners and custodians of this land” via video link. The advice to Daley said there was “no evidence to suggest that inviting an offender to perform a Welcome to or Acknowledgement of Country has ever occurred before or since”.



“In our view, if it is accepted that a unique event in a process of sentencing a member of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community had occurred, the fact that the event might prompt any manner of criticism of different participants in the legal system cannot be a reason for concluding that reporting on that event is not in the public interest.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: How a covert tree camera caught an ex-bikie’s massive illegal asbestos dump
World.content:
NationalNSWPollution How a covert tree camera caught an ex-bikie’s massive illegal asbestos dump Ben Cubby Updated August 5, 2026 — 7:26pm ,first published 6:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A former associate of the Rebels bikie gang has been found guilty of secretly dumping 73,000 tonnes of asbestos waste in Sydney’s north-west after one of the biggest pollution stings in the history of the NSW Environment Protection Authority. Andrew Hughes and his company Ant Civil Pty Ltd are facing penalties of up to $4.2 million for creating a massive unlicensed waste dump at Wheeny Creek in the Hawkesbury region. An aerial view of the Wheeny Creek site in northern Sydney, now partially grassed over. Nick Moir The Herald had previously revealed that thousands of truckloads of construction waste were taken to the property between September 2020 and June 2022 and spread out across much of the 26-hectare lot, raising the height of the land by several metres. What Hughes did not know was that the bush track that led to his property was being watched by cameras, drones and EPA officers.



A covert surveillance camera in a tree captured 661 truck movements in one five-week period between March and April 2021. Andrew Hughes was found guilty of dumping contaminated waste. The surveillance footage, coupled with thousands of text and WhatsApp messages seized in a raid on Hughes’ home in June 2022, helped secure convictions on six charges related to pollution in the NSW Land and Environment Court this week. “We are pleased the court agreed with our assertion that the defendants were using the Wheeny Creek property as an unlawful tip or waste facility,” an EPA spokesperson said. “By knowingly transporting and spreading asbestos contaminated fill, the defendants caused significant land pollution and also failed to comply with our legal directions to clean up and remediate the site.”



The site has not been cleaned up. Hughes sold the property – which he had bought for $510,000 in 2019 – for $50,000 in November 2024. The current owner, demolition contractor Samuel Mitchell, did some remedial works including collecting over a tonne of asbestos-contaminated fragments from the surface, and built a supporting wall that aims to stop contaminated sediment flowing downhill from the dumpsite into an ecologically significant wetland. Building waste and rubble seen at the edge of the Wheeny Creek wetlands. Wolter Peeters The material dumped at the site is legally classified as asbestos waste because it contains asbestos mixed with other substances. A technical report used as evidence by the EPA said that, as well as asbestos, samples from the site had “varying quantities of foreign materials that were generally consistent with construction and demolition waste including terracotta and ceramic tile fragments, crushed concrete and bricks, plastic, timber, particle board and masonite, glass, polystyrene, PVC and metallic debris”.



Hughes, who now lives in South-East Asia, had earlier argued he could not afford to return to Australia to give evidence in court because he feared for his life and his presence in Sydney would require a 12-man security team at a cost of $500,000. Related Article Exclusive

Pollution ‘Major pollution incident’: Toxic sludge poisons pristine Sydney river, expert says Affidavits filed by Hughes’ lawyer Zali Burrows during the case included a report from a psychiatrist who is the uncle of Hughes’ wife. The psychiatrists’ report said Hughes was anxious and suffered from a depressive illness because of the inadvertent disclosure of his name in an interview transcript which had formed part of a separate investigation into a 2016 murder that was unrelated to the Wheeny Creek case. While Hughes did not give evidence at that murder trial, his name was unredacted in a transcript given to the lawyer of one of the five men who were ultimately found guilty, the court heard.



Burrows said Hughes had said there was a “$400,000 contract out to murder him” and that, during a return visit to Sydney in January 2025, he had been violently bashed up in a carpark in Greystanes. It was also claimed that after the EPA began its investigation into illegal dumping and issued clean-up notices to Hughes that he “received numerous calls from silent numbers and unknown persons seeking to meet up with him in secluded locations”. The wetland in a valley below the Wheeny Creek site. Sydney Morning Herald As well as the $500,000 cost of a security detail, Hughes said returning to Sydney would require $15,000 in return flights, $33,000 in accommodation and $3700 for a nanny. Justice Beasley was unpersuaded by Hughes’ reasoning and did not allow him to give evidence by audio-visual link.



The company ANT Civil Pty Ltd was found guilty of causing building and asbestos waste to be transported to the property. Beasley said Hughes was found to have control of Ant Civil Pty Ltd and was responsible for its actions despite the business being registered under his wife’s name. He was also found guilty two charges of causing the property and access road to be polluted with asbestos waste, one charge of using the property as a waste facility without lawful authority, and of failing to comply with a clean-up notice. A date for sentencing is due to be set at a hearing on August 14. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.
