A big finish from Watson could be enough to snare him the Coleman, and although Mitchell says the Hawks won't go out of their way to target him in the next three weeks, they would celebrate his achievement if he gets there.

"It'd be great if it happened," Mitchell said.

"But he's young and he's got plenty of opportunities in front of him.

"I certainly hope that's not the focus of the lads going into a game like this. But I won't be shying away from it if he gets that opportunity, of course."

Watson, fondly dubbed "The Wizard", is already a superstar of the competition despite being just 21 years old and 61 games into his AFL career.

"The level of consistency is probably the best thing that we've got from Wizard this year," Mitchell said.

"And it's probably one season earlier than most. He's certainly maturing. Like, he's 21 years old and he's quite popular, and how he handles that is really impressive."

Third-placed Hawthorn (14-5-1) haven't won at the Gabba since 2016, but they have only played three games at the venue since then.

Mitchell wants his team to use Friday's blockbuster against two-time defending premiers Brisbane (13-7) as an interstate finals rehearsal.

"I think if you look at the ladder most Victorian teams are going to have to win interstate at some point, and this is a start for us," said Mitchell, who earlier this week re-signed with Hawthorn until the end of 2030.

The Hawks have a number of selection queries heading into the crunch clash with Ned Reeves (knee), Karl Amon (knee), Mitch Lewis (concussion) and Henry Hustwaite (face) all under injury clouds.

Meanwhile, an American court has formally dismissed charges against Hawthorn player Connor Macdonald for his off-season misadventure.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Macdonald and teammate Dylan Moore spent a night in a US jail after being charged with trespassing for climbing onto a cherry picker.

Moore's case was wrapped up last month, while Macdonald's case has also now been concluded with the pair having previously agreed to complete a substance abuse counselling program.

"It's probably nice for them to have it off their back," Mitchell said.

"They're both having really good seasons and really pleased with their performances. Sometimes dealing with adversity can make you grow, and I think they've both done that this year."

AAP

World.title: Pay war on ice as Australia's netball stars sign truce
World.content:
A pay war has been averted — for now — after Australia's Super Netball players agreed to an updated collective player agreement for 2027.

Under the new collective player agreement (CPA), Super Netball players will receive improved pay and conditions, more time off and greater ability to sign individual sponsorship deals.

The 12-month bridging agreement to the CPA has been agreed between Netball Australia, the Super Netball clubs and the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA).

It means Super Netball clubs can start contracting players and preparing for the 2027 campaign.

Before this week's agreement went through, players had been in contract limbo.

Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026 Messy and drawn-out pay negotiations are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the Aussie Diamonds.

The protracted pay dispute also meant plans to expand Super Netball had been placed on hold until at least 2028, despite a new five-year broadcast deal with the Nine Network starting in 2027.

With the CPA now locked in for 2027, attention will turn to a longer-term deal for 2028 and beyond in coming months, with Netball Australia hoping to avoid a repeat of a drawn-out pay dispute.

The ANPA want a revenue-share model, as well as better pregnancy and parental leave policies as part of a longer-term deal.

Netball Australia interim chief executive Mark Falvo said the 12-month bridging agreement struck the right balance between delivering immediate benefits for players, while also positioning the sport for future growth.

"We are at a pivotal moment for our sport," Falvo said in a statement.

"This agreement gives our players, clubs and the league certainty while we enter a period of significant commercial opportunity for netball.

"There is more work to do on meeting some of the asks for the athletes and the clubs, but this agreement delivers meaningful outcomes for players today while demonstrating our responsibility to balance the long-term sustainability of the league."

The news of the fresh CPA comes on the back of Sports Entertainment Group (SEG), headed by Craig Hutchison, putting the final touches on their takeover of the licence of the Giants Super Netball club.

SEG already owns the Melbourne Mavericks as well as multiple basketball clubs, with the Giants set to become the latest franchise to go under their SEN Teams banner.

The flurry of netball news comes just days after the Australian Diamonds suffered a shock 46-45 semi-final loss to Jamaica at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The Diamonds were hot favourites to snare gold, but had to settle for bronze with a 80-65 win over England in the third-versus-fourth play-off match.

Although New Zealand walked away with the gold medal, their domestic competition faces an uncertain future after losing around $3.7 million in 2026.

With no broadcast deal in place, rumours are bubbling the Premiership in New Zealand could be placed on hold for 2027, or downgraded to amateur status.

It means a flurry of Kiwi players could seek out Super Netball deals for next year as they seek financial security.

New CPA deal:

Increase to the total player payment pool (minimum and maximum amounts) by greater than the Consumer Price Index (CPI)

Players to receive a one-off payment upon the signing of a commercial partner for the Super Netball league

Additional time off through condensing hours for club commitments that will free up an additional two weeks of time off per year

Option for athletes to enter into multi-year contracts

Greater ability for athletes to secure their own individual sponsorship deals

Increased health insurance and meal allowances

AAP

World.title: De Minaur wins all-Australian clash as Popyrin gets through in Montreal
World.content:
Fallen star Alexei Popyrin has dug deep for a morale-boosting victory to join Alex de Minaur in the second round of the Canadian Open in Montreal.

Two years after upstaging the great Novak Djokovic in a seismic US Open triumph, Popyrin has slumped to number 139 in the world as he battles a crisis of confidence.

But after toiling through qualifying just to make the main draw, Popyrin toiled for another two hours and 12 minutes to see off Argentine Roman Andres Burruchaga 4-6, 7-5, 6-3 to notch his first ATP-level win since May in the Masters event.

The breakthrough was only Popyrin's ninth win of a lean 2026 campaign and vaulted the one-time world number 19 into a second-round contest with US seventh seed Taylor Fritz or another Argentine, Thiago Agustin Tirante.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

De Minaur, meanwhile, looked to be cruising before fellow Sydneysider James Duckworth put the world number seven through the wringer late on.

Runner-up in 2023, de Minaur was a set and 3-1 up before Duckworth fought back hard seeking a first win over his countryman in three meetings.

But de Minaur held firm to fend off six set points and progress 6-2, 7-6 (6) and book a third-round date with either Britain's Cameron Norrie or Peru's Ignacio Buse.

"In the first set everything was flowing," de Minaur said after the one-hour, 46-minute dogfight.

"I was up a break, had a couple more chances to go up by a double break and all of a sudden it slips away.

"Then all of a sudden momentum shifts and we got into a battle. So I am glad I was able to sneak through. There are a couple of things I need to tighten up on, but we live to fight another day."

While de Minaur and Popyrin move on, fellow Australian Adam Walton crashed out with a 6-3, 6-4 loss to American Jenson Brooksby.

In the women's WTA event in Toronto, Tahlia Gibson continued her stellar 2026 season with an upset 7-5, 6-1 second-round win over Polish 18th seed Maja Chwalinska.

Gibson's 28th win of a breakout year earned her a crack at Russian 16th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova.

AAP

World.title: NRL club claims player Keith Titmuss contributed to training death
World.content:
A rugby league player who died of heat exhaustion at pre-season training contributed to his own death by not managing his weight and diet in the off-season, his former club says.

The family of Keith Titmuss, who died in November 2020 after collapsing during pre-season training, is suing the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles for damages owing from negligence in his death, including failing to implement the NRL heat policy.

In a defence filed in the NSW Supreme Court the club has claimed it was not responsible for the death of the young man because he did not inform coaching and medical staff of his worsened physical state through the off-season.

"NRL training is inherently dangerous," the club wrote in its defence.

"Any injury, loss and damage suffered by [Titmuss's family] … was caused or contributed to by the deceased's own negligence."

Former NRL player's mother speaks on lawsuit The mother of Manly player Keith Titmuss, who died of exertional heat stroke following a 2020 Sea Eagles training session, breaks her silence on her family's multi-million-dollar lawsuit against the NRL club.

Manly Warringah alleged Titmuss failed to properly train or diet during the off-season and put himself in danger by not stopping training when he felt sick.

"Players were instructed … if they were feeling ill or feeling like they were not coping with the physical demands [that] they were to inform coaching staff," the club said.

The club also filed in its defence that it conducted a fitness test on the 20-year-old four days before he died and found "no red flags".

The session at the Sydney Academy of Sport at Narrabeen involved outdoor sprint tests before moving inside for an intense cardio session.

A 100-passes drill and a cardio circuit involving up-downs/burpees, bear crawls and "fireman carries" was conducted inside the facility's dojo, the parties agree.

The temperature was about 21 degrees Celsius during the session but the humidity was 92 per cent, court documents state.

Manly Warringah admitted the dojo was not fitted with air-conditioning but said there were multiple floor-standing fans, the back doors were open and hydration breaks were enforced.

The player's family alleged the fans were not switched on during the session.

There were 10 staff to monitor the 15 players inside, the club said.

NRL player Keith Titmuss died after 'inappropriate' training session, magistrate finds A magistrate who oversaw the inquest into the death of a young Manly Sea Eagles player recommends the NRL consider mandating a two-week period of controlled training acclimatisation after off-season breaks as part of an existing review.

A 2024 coronial inquest into his death concluded the budding NRL player died of exertion heat stroke, with a pre-existing heart condition unlikely to have played a part.

The work-out at the club's Narrabeen gym, which followed an outdoor session, was "more likely than not inappropriate", the coroner found.

Evidence at the inquest was that paramedics at the scene noted Titmuss's temperature at 41.9C, while his heart rate was more than 140 beats per minute.

Titmuss's family claimed the precautions instituted by Manly Warringah were not sufficient to meet its own heat policy guidelines, alleging the club is liable for the young man's death.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"[Manly Warringah] owed a duty of care to the deceased as an employee and … breached the duty of care owed," the statement of claim said.

Titmuss's family alleged the player started to struggle physically after an outdoor sprint test three days prior, which the club denied.

The club instituted a heat policy after former prop Lloyd Perrett said he was planning to sue the club over a training session in late 2017 which left him hospitalised with heat stroke after suffering a seizure.

Manly Warringah and the NRL were contacted for comment.

AAP

World.title: How Australia can harness home support in lead up to Brisbane 2032
World.content:
Water Polo Australia has hailed the enormous success of the World Cup finals in Sydney, saying that it proves Australia is in an ideal position to host more World Aquatics events in the lead up to the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games.

Sydney hosted the eight-team World Cup finals over five days at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre, the first time a major global Water Polo event had been hosted in the city since the 2000 Olympics.

Australia's Stingers won a hugely impressive bronze medal, following on from their memorable silver medal at the Paris Olympics to firmly establish themselves as one of Australia's most likeable and backable teams.

Meanwhile, the Sharks finished an enormously credible fourth, beating world champions Spain in a heroic penalty shoot out in the quarterfinals to underline their status as a team that is building to be a genuine medal contender for the 2032 Games.

But more importantly, more than 10,000 spectators came through the doors across the five days, creating a memorable atmosphere at the former Olympic venue.

The Stingers won a brilliant bronze medal in Sydney. (Supplied: World Aquatics/Julius Dimataga)

And the Australian players certainly appreciated it.

"To have a whole pool full of our friends and family, and the water polo community, it's really special … this is such a huge part of our careers and something that we'll never forget," Sienna Hearn said after the semifinal loss to the USA.

"The atmosphere [in Sydney] is so special for all of us and makes us want to try even harder for our friends and family."

The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, were the most successful Australian team at the Paris Olympics, winning a stunning silver medal. This is the secret to their success.

Bronte Halligan noted that it was the home support that made the difference for the Stingers as they fought back from defeat against the USA to win bronze.

"Any game on home soil is unreal. But then to win a medal, at a world event, on home soil is just phenomenal," she said.

"The crowd was epic, they got us through the game, we stayed in it, we got the result and I couldn't be prouder of the girls."

Head coach Bec Rippon agreed, calling the crowd "amazing".

"We don't get many opportunities to play in these big moments — and for this team the semifinal the other day was only the second ever semifinal that we've played in," she said.

"So to have opportunities like this, under pressure, with a crowd, you can't buy that kind of experience.

"We have such a privilege of going overseas and playing in front of other nations' home crowds, so it was really amazing to be able to do that for our fans, friends and family here tonight who follow us all over the world."

Water Polo Australia hungry for more

Teenager Bless Daly is among the new guard of Australian water polo players on the rise. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

It's not a surprise that Water Polo Australia wants to see more of that support over the next six years and beyond.

"We were really keen to make sure we leveraged the home crowd advantage," Water Polo Australia chief executive Tim Welsford told ABC Sport the day after the tournament, his voice still hoarse from cheering on during a thrilling week of water polo.

"In the early stages of planning there was a very clear line of sight on what we wanted, to have the opportunity for kids to come into the centre, to buy a Sharks or Stingers top, to put the war paint on their face, the zinc, and sit in the crowd and support their team.

"That was a very clear vision for us about what we wanted to deliver in terms of the user experience inside the venue, and I think we went very close to nailing that.

"I think anyone who was in the venue, and it probably came across on the broadcast, will tell you how electric the atmosphere was.

"And that wasn't just the Australian games, even the men's gold medal game between Hungary and Greece, we had this beautiful picture of all the Greece fans in the blue seats, all the Hungary fans in the green seats, and we had all the Aussie water polo purists sitting in the middle.

"And at 7 o'clock on Sunday night, we still had the most incredible atmosphere."

Supporters cheer on Team Australia at the bronze medal match between Australia and Russia during the 2026 World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup at Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Remarkably, Water Polo Australia was able to garner such incredible community buy-in with just eight months lead-in time.

Welsford said that if they were given longer, they could layer even more onto the event and what they could achieve.

"We've got an appetite to do more of this into the future," Welsford said.

"That's why we really sort of pushed to make every post a winner this time so that World Aquatics, considers us … a really safe pair of hands for them to be able to allocate events to, that they know they're going to get a great result here.

"I'm confident they walked away with that exact feeling.

"We talked often about what does success look like [for this event], and you've got all those [attendance and social media] metrics and I think that's a really important piece and we will measure those, of course.

"But the community-building success was just incredible — people that are reaching out saying, we need to host more of these.

"Australia is cherry ripe for this type of thing … There is a real appetite here for us to do this again. And so we want to support that community groundswell.

"We would love to have it back."

Bec Rippon led the Stingers to two major global medals in the last three years. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo )

Some of the metrics truly have been encouraging, with almost 14 million social media views in the lead up to and during the event, coupled with the huge attendances.

"Our numbers in the last three months have been bigger than our Olympic year in terms of the social media views," Welsford said.

"This is an unbelievable opportunity for us to be able to showcase the sport."

Water Polo, although a relatively niche sport in Australia, is huge in Europe.

And despite being a long way from the sport's heartland, one of the key features of the tournament was how much support other nations received — none of which was by accident.

Water Polo Australia reached out to the embassies of all nations participating in the event to help drum up support within their communities, which was realised in a vibrant, multicultural crowd celebrating the sport throughout the five days.

Even the thorny issue of Russia's involvement — the women's team qualified and became the first international Russian team to compete on Australian soil since the country was banned in the wake of the Ukraine War.

"I think everybody understandably was a little bit on edge a little bit around how that would play out, and we are continually empathetic to the Ukrainian community and what's going on over there at the moment," Welsford said, noting that Australia, as an organising committee, does not get the option to select which teams qualify for the event.

"So it's our job to then accept our lot and make the best of the situation and try and put on a great show for everyone," he added.

"We did have a Ukrainian protest, they were really well organised, extremely peaceful, they did everything they could to amplify their message and we thank them for doing it in the way that they did as well."

National Aquatic Centre essential for aquatics legacy

Australia will hope for even more events in the lead up to 2032 as the dream of a National Aquatic Centre is realised. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

A key factor in being able to host more events will be the development of the National Aquatic Centre in Brisbane, a venue that Water Polo Australia, along with their diving and artistic swimming counterparts, really lobbied for before getting Swimming Australia on board.

"The National Aquatic Centre concept was actually initiated firstly by water polo, but then in conjunction with diving and artistic swimming," Welsford said.

"Under Rob Woodhouse's leadership, [Swimming Australia] sort of joined the scheme a couple of years ago, but it was largely driven by the other three aquatic sports.

Proposed design for 2032 aquatic centre revealed The state has chosen three firms to design the aquatic centre: ARM Architecture, NH Architecture and Queensland-based Arkhefield.

"But since Rob's come on board, it's been fantastic that it's been all four of us and we've been really well united and supportive of each other, making sure that we can all get something that's really ticks the legacy box for us.

"People will talk about 2032 and what that means, but even last night talking to the Sydney 2000 crew, there were so many events in the lead into 2000 that we hosted here locally.

"People and countries wanted to come out and have that experience prior [to the Games].

"So in the context of us hosting this year, this is the start of it for us.

"We want more of these international style events here over the next six years and we believe countries will want to come, particularly given the experience they've had over the last five or six days.

"We want to do more of that as we move forward.

"The National Aquatic Centre delivers us that legacy venue that we need. I think if anybody experienced what Sydney Olympic Park was able to do for us — not that was built for the Olympics, but it was the Olympic venue — it stands up so well in terms of a legacy asset for us to be able to use.

"You know, 26 years after the Olympic Games and 30 years after it's been built, it's still being used as a world-class event for aquatics.

"It's a phenomenal opportunity that we need to make sure we get right in terms of the National Aquatic Centre."

World.title: Stokes claims cricket has drinking culture, not just England
World.content:
Former England captain Ben Stokes has hit back at claims his side had a drinking problem, instead claiming cricket as a sport has a drinking culture.

Stokes, who abruptly retired in June, appeared on a podcast with former England teammate Stuart Broad where he addressed a range of different topics.

Among those was a suggestion that England's team has a drinking problem after a number of off-field incidents during last summer's ill-fated Ashes tour to Australia.

"God, that's such an extreme thing to put on a team," Stokes told Broad on the For Love Of Cricket podcast when asked whether England had a drinking problem.

Ben Stokes's retirement a perfect example of his main character energy Ben Stokes has been the centre of England's cricketing universe for 15 years. In announcing his retirement mid-match, he highlighted how damaging that main character energy can be.

"I think cricket has just a drinking culture and it hasn't changed. We're in 2026 where the game has gone more professional over the years, and one thing that I think has just stayed within cricket is its relationship with alcohol, from club cricket and then works its way up. It's just stayed there and it's been embedded within the sport.

"The relationship with alcohol and cricket is just something that hasn't moved on as the game of cricket has become more professional.

"There's been more science and medicine, there's more nutritional information, there's more this, there's more that, but the one thing that has been a constant and stayed around and has been for a very long time is its relationship with alcohol.

"So for people who think that the English cricket team has a drinking culture, I'd say no.

" I would just say cricket has culture that is associated with alcohol. "

England's team under Stokes faced heavy criticism during its mid-Ashes break in Noosa last year, which came with the team already in an 0-2 hole.

Opener Ben Duckett was filmed by fans while heavily intoxicated and struggling to find his way back to England's hotel, while during the final Test in Sydney, it emerged that vice-captain Harry Brook had gotten into an altercation with a bouncer on the team's New Zealand tour.

"I think it can be a problem," Stokes said of cricket's drinking culture.

"If you look at everything over the years, you look at a lot of people that have been involved within cricket and have had bad relationships with alcohol. It's just, I don't know what you do to change it."

Ben Stokes's Ashes understudy Harry Brook (right) was involved in an altercation with a nightclub bouncer in New Zealand prior to the Ashes. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley/ECB)

Stokes also referenced his own personal experience with alcohol throughout his career.

He was arrested in 2017 after his involvement in a street brawl near a nightclub with then-teammate Alex Hales and served an eight-match suspension for the incident.

"I've had … I don't want to say problems, but I've had relationships with alcohol at times over my career that have been potentially dangerous, if that makes sense, but it's completely different to me now," he said.

"I just think that there's this relationship with alcohol within cricket that has been the same from the 80s.

Former Australian Test batter David Boon (centre) has become well known for his love of beer, namely the 52 he consumed on a flight to the UK. (Getty Images: PA Images)

"As the game has got better and better and better, that thing has just stayed around. That's my opinion on cricket and alcohol."

Stokes's theory regarding cricket and its athletes' relationship to alcohol is not without credence.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

In Australian cricket, the story of David Boon drinking 52 beers on a flight to the UK ahead of the 1989 Ashes series is spoken about as the stuff of legend.

Boon appeared on a podcast in 2023 saying he regretted the whole episode.

"I've got to be brutally honest here, I won't deny it happened. We all do stupid things in our lives and I'll finish by just being serious," he said on the BackChat Sports Show.

"You have fun, you do something and then you think: 'Shit, what about the ramifications to everything else', to your family, to your children.

""It caused some crap over the years, and it's something that I regret a lot. Can't deny it but I do regret it. And I was stupid to be able to do that when you're in the public eye."

World.title: Age is just a number as Roar announce youngest-ever A-League manager
World.content:
Brisbane Roar have made A-League history, announcing the youngest-ever manager to lead the women's side moving forward.

At just 27 years of age, Johnathan Clemente has been named the new Roar coach ahead of the ALW season.

He arrives at Brisbane on a two-year deal, coming from Melbourne Victory where he was an assistant under Jeff Hopkins with the ALW side.

"I am incredibly honoured at the opportunity to lead one of the most successful clubs in the country, with one of the best squads in the league and to do it in one of the most beautiful places in the world," Clemente said in a statement.

Wests Tigers owners throw financial lifeline to women's A-League team The Central Coast Mariners women's team ensured a place in A-League soccer competition thanks to the Holman Barnes Group.

"I see exciting parallels between Brisbane Roar and my own journey. We've been hungry, ambitious and have spent the past few years building strong foundations. Now it's our time to come together and establish ourselves at the pinnacle of women's football in this country."

Despite his young age, Clemente has plenty of coaching and managerial experience.

He was the youngest ever head coach of a National Premier League side when he took over Heidelberg United at the age of 20.

During his three seasons with the club, 10 players were developed and signed to A-League squads.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

During his time with Victory, Clemente also led the NPLW, Female Pathways and the Melbourne Victory Afghan Women's Team programs.

Brisbane Roar finished fourth on the ALW table last season, and lost their two-leg semifinal to Wellington Phoenix 3-2 on aggregate, going to extra time in the second leg.

"Alex Smith and the squad were tremendous last season, finishing fourth and were one game away from a grand final, with a host of exciting, young, local talent. "I'll be looking to build on the great work, create consistency and continue the upward trajectory of the program," Clemente said.

"Our team will be built around shared principles, not set structures, with the objective being not how we play, but how we feel.

"We want our fans to believe in the fluid football they'll see, we want our young girls in the crowd to believe they can represent Brisbane one day and we want our squad to believe that when you represent our team and our state, anything is possible."

Women in Sport Spotlight We put the spotlight on women making a big impact on and off the field in the sporting world — from the grassroots through to the elite level.

The previous youngest managers were both 29 years of age, when Jess Fishlock took charge of Melbourne City in the W-League during the 2016-17 season, and Alex Epakis when he became manager of Perth Glory ALW side in 2020.

The youngest manager of an ALM side was Des Buckingham, who was 31 when he became manager of Wellington in 2017.

The Roar are not worried about Clemente's age, with sporting director James Gow stating the 27-year-old impressed when the club was recruiting for a new manager.

"Johnathan is a coach with a very clear idea of how he wants to play, train and develop his team. We conducted a thorough recruitment process, and his desire for the role and clarity in how he works stood out," Gow said.

"Despite his young age, he has a lot of experience in the A-League Women's space. He really buys into the strategy we as a club wish to execute. We are looking forward to welcoming him and seeing him get to work."

The ALW and ALM seasons will both begin in mid-October.

Tech.title: Ted Lasso returns at an important time for Apple TV
Tech.content:
The end of season 3, which happened in 2023, promised a lot of change and what seemed like a happy ending for much of the main cast. Among many other things, Ted (Jason Sudeikis) was heading back to the US to spend time with his son, Roy (Brett Goldstein) had just been promoted to head coach of AFC Richmond, Coach Beard (Brendan Hunt) got married at Stonehenge, and Richmond’s leadership group of Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), Keeley (Juno Temple), and Higgins (Jeremy Swift) were flirting with the idea of launching a women’s team. It had the energy of a sitcom ending, and the episode was even called “So Long, Farewell.” But it’s that fledgling women’s team that spurs the show’s return.

The season 4 premiere almost feels like a different show at first, and that largely comes down to location. At the outset, Ted is working part-time at a grocery store in order to have more time to parent, and Rebecca, Keeley, and Higgins have come to Kansas City in an attempt to convince him to be the inaugural coach of the new team. It’s like a reunion episode of sorts, with old friends catching up for the first time in years, which helps viewers understand what has happened in that time. It also drags out Ted’s inevitable decision to say “yes” across a full episode.

Image: Apple

The premiere serves as a transitory moment for this new era of Ted Lasso, and from there the show shifts back to England and takes on a much more familiar feel — but with some significant changes. Part of what makes season 4 feel like a reboot is the players. Ted and most of the rest of the coaching staff and club leadership are back, but the actual team itself is all new. That means that favorites like Jamie Tartt (Phil Dunster), Sam Obisanya (Toheeb Jimoh), and Dani Rojas (Cristo Fernández) aren’t in the show at all aside from some brief mentions (or at least they weren’t featured in any of the five episodes Apple provided press ahead of time). In their place is a scrappy squad of up-and-coming players, and an assistant coach named Alice (Tanya Reynolds) who provides a more stern counterpoint to Ted’s relentless optimism.

It’s a risky bet eschewing beloved characters for a bunch of newcomers, but, at least early on, season 4 of Ted Lasso manages to recapture much of what made the show such a success, but in a new context. The players on Richmond’s women’s side aren’t coddled millionaires, but rather athletes trying to find their way in a still underfunded and undersupported field. One thing I appreciate is that it doesn’t gloss over the very real challenges of women’s football, from lackluster media support and facilities to the rash of devastating injuries that plague its players. This provides plenty of opportunities for Ted to learn and impart his folksy wisdom, and for the eclectic new cast to reflect this challenging landscape. There’s an intense goalkeeper who was ignored by bigger clubs because she refuses to wear gloves (Jude Mack), a mom who made the team after spontaneously deciding to attend an open tryout (Faye Marsay), and a star striker who is balancing her athletic career with getting a law degree (Abbie Hern).

Recapturing the exact magic that made Ted Lasso’s early seasons such a phenomenon is probably impossible, and the new season is premiering at a very different time for Apple TV. Much has happened since its 2020 debut — service-defining shows like Severance and Pluribus didn’t even exist then — but many of those changes also bode well for Ted Lasso. Not only is Apple TV seemingly on an upward trajectory, but a controversial yet very successful men’s World Cup has reignited interest in the sport (particularly in the US), while the next women’s World Cup looms on the horizon. Those seem like prime circumstances for an impactful return for Ted and friends. The show may have changed, but its importance for Apple hasn’t.

Ted Lasso season 4 starts streaming on Apple TV on August 5th.

Tech.title: Don’t screw this up, Marvel
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

Though Brand New Day’s current box office is undeniably impressive, it’s not exactly surprising when you take a beat to remember how consistently well Sony and Marvel’s recent live-action Spider-Man projects have performed in the past. Both Spider-Man: Homecoming and No Way Home cleared the $100 million mark during their opening weekends, and it only took Far From Home six days to pull in $185 million. What’s different here is how quickly Brand New Day has shattered records and cemented itself as one of Marvel and Sony’s most fruitful collaborations.

The film’s a testament to the fact that people do still have an appetite for big-screen comic book spectacle when the stars align just right. But the things that make this latest Spider-Man project work so well haven’t been present in the Sony-free parts of Marvel’s interconnected universe.

Editor’s note: This post contains Spider-Man: Brand New Day spoilers.

Even though Jon Watts’ Spider-Man trilogy eventually started mucking around in the multiverse, those films told relatively self-contained stories that were focused on building a grounded world around Tom Holland’s Peter Parker. Taking that approach highlighted the character’s evolution as a solo hero and made it interesting whenever he got roped into situations with the Avengers.

Brand New Day feels like director Destin Daniel Cretton and cowriters Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers striking a strong balance between Sony’s solo Spider-Man movies and Marvel’s larger crossover events. There are a handful of classic Spider-Man rogues in the mix, like John Bernthal’s Punisher and Michael Mando’s Scorpion, who get their fair share of bombastic action sequences. Mark Ruffalo’s Hulk is running around too, but Brand New Day’s story is really about Peter dealing with the emotional consequences of erasing himself from the world’s memory.

As ridiculous as that all might sound (especially to non-comics fans), they’re details that Sony and Marvel’s previous Spider-Man collaborations laid the groundwork for. You could watch Watts’ trilogy and go into Brand New Day mostly understanding what’s at stake and how characters got to where they are emotionally. The MCU has struggled to maintain that kind of narrative cohesion during its sprawling Multiverse Saga, which began with WandaVision and will end with Avengers: Secret Wars. Marvel has been trying to keep far more plates spinning with its shared universe of films and series compared to Sony, which just pumped the brakes on making Spider-Man spinoff movies. But the mixed reactions to trailers for the studio’s next big feature makes it seem like people might not exactly be excited about what’s coming next.

Avengers: Doomsday will bring most of Marvel’s heroes together once again to fight a version of Doctor Doom portrayed by Robert Downey Jr. The movie will probably use the multiverse to explain why Doctor Doom looks exactly like Iron Man, and it will definitely bring a handful of the live-action 20th Century Studios X-Men to the MCU. Marvel is clearly using Doomsday and next year’s Avengers: Secret Wars to put a period on the Multiverse Saga and start fresh after years of the franchise being too unwieldy.

Image: Sony / Marvel

The films and Downey Jr.’s rehiring are also Marvel’s way of moving on from the Kang-filled future Marvel gave up on after jettisoning Jonathan Majors. Kevin Feige has been open about new iterations of the X-Men being key to Marvel’s plans for the future. But if the studio wants audiences to really become invested in Charles Xavier and his students, it would do well to lean into some of Brand New Day’s strongest beats.

Rather than introducing Sadie Sink’s Jean Grey as a charming telepath, Brand New Day presents the character as a teenager willing to destroy anyone who gets in her way as she searches for her sister. Both of the Greys are mutants with natural abilities that make them dangerous, but what pushes Jean to deadly violence is the way the government is hunting them down in hopes of weaponizing them. By framing Jean as one of its villains, Brand New Day both keeps its story relatively grounded and gives you a way of understanding how the MCU is touching on classic elements of X-Men comics lore. Jean might not want to hurt innocent people, but she does in a very public way, and it’s easy to imagine her actions becoming the basis for human-mutant tensions going forward.

Brand New Day’s ability to tap into those ideas without feeling like a stealth X-Men movie is one of the more impressive things about it. And now that Spider-Man has given us a promising taste of the MCU’s new mutants, Marvel has a chance to keep audiences hooked if it doesn’t drop the ball like Fox.

Tech.title: Now you can securely link multiple phones to one Signal account
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

You can link more devices with one phone number on Signal now, including an Android phone or iPhone. Signal already supported linking PCs and iPads, but not additional phones. When you link a device on Signal, you can check and respond to new messages across all of your linked devices. You can also choose whether or not to transfer an end-to-end encrypted copy of your previous messages to each newly linked device to mitigate the risk of devices that might be shared, lost, or compromised.

The update is rolling out now with Signal version 8.20 on Android and version 8.22 for iPhone / iPad.

Signal also says it has made “significant interface improvements to better support large devices,” including several improvements for foldable phones, which helped enable support for Android tablets. However, Signal says the large-screen version of its Android app is “still a work in progress,” and that it’s working on optimizing the interface for its Chromebook app, as well.

Tech.title: AMD’s data center business is booming while gaming takes a backseat
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Driven by demand for AI capacity, AMD’s data center revenue more than doubled year-over-year in its latest earnings report, reaching $6.7 billion. That’s up from $5.8 billion in Q1, and jumping 107 percent from the $3.2 billion it reported for the same period a year ago. During Tuesday’s earnings call, AMD CEO Lisa Su said the company expects “data center segment revenue to more than double year-over-year in 2027,” as well.

At the same time, AMD’s gaming revenue fell 31 percent compared to last year, to $779 million, as price hikes and component shortages slowed sales for the Xbox Series X / S, PS5, and Valve’s Steam Deck. On a call after the earnings were released, Su told analysts that, “Gaming graphics revenue also declined year-over-year, as higher industry-wide component costs contributed to higher graphics card prices and weighed on overall demand.”

Image: AMD

“Revenue increased 50 percent year-over-year to a record $11.5 billion, driven by continued strength in our Data Center business, which represented 58% of company revenue in the quarter,” wrote AMD CFO Jean Hu. Its overall PC and gaming business revenue grew six percent compared to last year, with Client revenue up 23 percent thanks to Ryzen processor sales.

“AI is driving a significant expansion in demand for compute across all of our markets, and our leadership portfolio and growing customer visibility position us exceptionally well to capture this expanding opportunity and deliver substantial revenue and earnings growth in the years ahead,” said AMD CEO Lisa Su.

Update, August 4th: Added comments from AMD’s earnings call.

Tech.title: SpaceX made more revenue as an AI company than a space company
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

SpaceX’s AI revenue grew more than three times to $2.6 billion from the year before, mostly because of deals that the company made to provide compute to other AI companies, according to SpaceX’s quarterly earnings. The AI division, which the company said in its documents to go public was the source of most of its value, lost $1.5 billion this quarter, slightly less than in the same quarter last year.

SpaceX made deals with Anthropic in May and Google in June to provide compute to the other two AI companies, putting it in competition with other neoclouds such as CoreWeave. The increased presence in AI is also driving the company to spend more — capital expenditures reached $18.37 billion.

“We’re building AI compute capacity at scale faster than anyone else, we believe, and we’re significantly improving our AI models,” Elon Musk said on an investor call.

Despite its name, SpaceX said in the documents for its IPO that it expected most of its value to come from AI. SpaceX had the biggest-ever IPO in June. One of the things that the company said it could do better than anyone else was build data centers in space. The company has three segments: space, AI, and “connectivity,” which is the Starlink internet service. Space had $962 million in revenue this quarter, and SpaceX remained the biggest user of SpaceX rockets. The Starlink service had $4.2 billion in revenue.

Grok, SpaceX’s AI model that has been in hot water for undressing women and children without their consent, had fallen far behind other companies in the AI race. So before the IPO, SpaceX rented out the data center capacity it had initially built for itself. The company also agreed to acquire Cursor, providing it with an enterprise AI product. The acquisition has not yet closed, though Musk said on the call they’re “close to that,” but didn’t want to “jump the gun” on regulatory approval.

SpaceX is still losing money, but the loss this quarter narrowed to $143 million dollars. Musk’s grandiose plans — data centers in space, an addressable user market of more than the US GDP — don’t just come with a big price tag in AI. The costs of developing technology in its space division also rose by $389 million from the year before, with Starship as the primary driver of spending. Starship is key to Musk’s plan to expand its connectivity business, the only profitable part of the company.

Starship has to be able to launch heavier versions of the satellites that make its Starlink internet business profitable. Some of these satellites have already been manufactured, and in today’s documents, SpaceX said it had launched 20 of them. It’s not clear how far away the full deployment — of 60 satellites at once — is.

Though SpaceX beat analyst estimates, according to Bloomberg, its shares declined after market, following an initial pop of enthusiasm.

Update 5:40PM ET August 4th: Adds revenue from space and connectivity sectors of the business, as well as details on SpaceX’s history with AI, and details from the investor call.

Tech.title: EA is now a private company
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Electronic Arts has officially become a private company. Last September, EA announced that an investor group led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners would be taking the company private in a $55 billion deal, and on Tuesday, EA said the deal successfully closed. The PIF will reportedly own 93.4 percent of the new company.

The deal includes $20 billion of debt financing — making it the largest leveraged buyout ever — which could mean big changes at EA to justify the deal. As of late, EA has been focusing heavily on its big tentpole franchises, including things like Battlefield, its sports games like EA Sports FC and Madden NFL, and The Sims. Given the stakes of the deal, it seems likely that EA will depend more on bankable releases rather than experimenting on smaller games — a strategy that many of the industry’s biggest publishers, including Ubisoft and Xbox, are shifting toward as well.

”As we begin this next chapter, I’m more optimistic than ever about what we’ll create together,” CEO Andrew Wilson said in a message to staff. “The opportunities ahead are extraordinary, and they’ll be brought to life by our creativity, our ambition, and our belief in what’s possible.”

The deal for EA follows other major video game industry acquisitions in recent years, including Microsoft’s $68.7 billion deal for Activision Blizzard, its $7.5 billion deal for Bethesda Softworks parent company ZeniMax Media, and Take-Two’s $12.7 billion deal for Zynga.

Tech.title: Telegram CEO says an extortionist planted CSAM in a chat to get it pulled from the App Store
Tech.content:
Last night Apple briefly removed Telegram from the AppStore because a user had planted illegal porn in a public chat.

Telegram was restored within hours. But I want to explain what happened — to warn other app developers and help protect online communities from similar attacks.

Because Telegram quickly removes illegal content from public groups using all kinds of moderation tools, the attacker had to resort to a technical trick. He inserted AI-modified illegal content by editing an old message in an active group chat. As a result the content was effectively hidden from the group’s members, preventing them from seeing/reporting it.

The attacker was a takedown extortionist: someone who demands ransom from group owners in exchange for not targeting their communities. These extortionists use automated accounts to plant illegal content in public groups and then report it directly to Apple, attempting to trigger the removal of legitimate communities whose owners refused to pay them.

From a practical standpoint, illegal pornographic content in Telegram’s public groups is not a systemic problem. Our moderation is effective. The fact that attackers must resort to backdated, effectively invisible content and other technical tricks proves this.

⚠️ However, there are two important lessons here for app developers and online communities:

— Extortionists have found a way to manipulate Apple into overreacting. Apple removed Telegram from the App Store before contacting us. This creates a potential systemic risk for every mobile app that hosts user-generated content. If an app used by more than a billion people can be removed from the App Store without prior warning, any app can be.

— The tactics used by takedown extortionists are evolving, putting communities across social platforms at risk. Telegram has extensive experience identifying the tricks used by coordinated reporting gangs and protecting legitimate communities (even when doing so risks our own app being temporarily removed from the App Store). Other platforms may not be equally prepared.

Stay vigilant! ☝️

Tech.title: Wispr Flow launches a Granola-styled meeting notetaker
Tech.content:
Update August 5, 12.10 am PT: Wispr Flow has officially launched its notetaker for Mac. The notetaker, similar to the one of Granola’s, uses system audio to transcribe a meeting without joining one. It also cleans up transcripts, creates action items, and lets users query across meeting history with the help of AI. Users can see a live transcript and ask AI to catch them up as well.

Our original reporting based on Wispr Flow’s terms change is below

Dictation app Wispr Flow is preparing to launch a meeting notetaker, according to the tool’s updated Terms of Service.

The company also sent an email to its customers about the change in both its terms and its privacy policy to accommodate related features.

Upon investigation, the refreshed terms have added sections about the use of meeting data and the notetaker. The company said the notetaker will generate transcripts, summaries, actions, and insights, writing:

For Notetaker, Input may also include Meeting Data, including meeting audio, participant information, meeting metadata, speaker labels, meeting transcripts, and other information processed in connection with a meeting. Output may include AI-generated meeting transcripts, summaries, action items, meeting insights, speaker attribution, and other meeting-related content.

With the launch, the startup will take on other meeting notetakers such as Granola, Fireflies, Read AI, Otter, and Fathom. Wispr Flow’s co-founder Tanay Kothari had previously talked about building an AI assistant in interviews. With a meeting notetaker, Wispr Flow would gain additional context about its users and could automate more tasks beyond cleaning up spoken sentences.

It’s not clear if the startup wants to launch a Granola-style notetaker that relies on system audio and transcribes the meeting without keeping a recording, or build a full-fledged meeting recording tool.

To date, Wispr Flow has raised more than $81 million, with the company valued at $700 million at its last round. In May, Bloomberg reported that the company was in talks for a new round, valuing it at $2 billion.

Wispr Flow didn’t respond to our request for further comment.

Tech.title: Elon Musk repeatedly one-upped his execs on SpaceX’s first earnings call
Tech.content:
Elon Musk spent SpaceX’s first earnings call making some out-of-this-world claims about the company’s business and future prospects, while his fellow executives kept trying to bring his ideas closer to Earth — providing a hint of what’s to come now that his rocket-launching, compute-leasing, satellite-based telecom is public.

The conference call, held Tuesday, was the latest in a years-long succession of Musk making outrageous promises that his executives then have to make more digestible for the investing public — like at Tesla, where a recent analysis by TechCrunch showed that the world’s richest man is increasingly focused on futuristic topics while his colleagues spend their time talking about the actual business of selling cars.

Let’s start with one of the biggest ideas Musk floated on the call: that he expects SpaceX’s Starlink service to “deliver a majority of the world’s internet” in “less than 10 years.” Musk made the comment in the context of SpaceX preparing to launch the first “V3” versions of its Starlink satellites, which have much higher bandwidth than previous versions.

Here’s what he said:

It’s kind of hard for people to wrap their minds around this, but like, it’s not out of the question that at some point, Starlink will deliver a majority of the world’s internet, at least in countries where we’re allowed to operate, which is the vast majority of countries. So this is, you know, important to bear in mind, and it’s not in like the infinity future. It’s, you know, less than 10 years.

Contrast that with what chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell said just a few minutes later, emphasis mine:

The significant amount of capacity we’re able to add to the Starlink constellation from the V3 satellites will enable us to continue providing even better service — and it’s pretty great already — but to do so while serving more and more customers over the world. In fact, in the years ahead, we expect Starlink will represent a significant portion of global internet traffic, which Elon also talked about.

It’s a far more lawyered-up claim to make, even though it’s still obviously ambitious.

But that was not the only instance where Musk optimistically diverged. At one point, SpaceX chief financial officer Bret Johnsen offered investors one of the few new financial targets discussed on the call. Johnsen was highlighting SpaceX’s relatively new business of renting out compute power to other AI players, which has helped the company generate billions in fresh, fast cash.

I’ll once again emphasize the big promise Johnsen made during his prepared remarks, and note how carefully he phrased it. It’s a very hedged and quite specific claim that he’s making. It’s clearly meant to excite investors while also leaving room for the company to avoid legal exposure if it misses the projection:

Looking ahead, we continue to see robust demand in all three of our business segments, but in particular in our cloud services arrangements. We see increasingly favorable economics with each agreement we sign, and as Elon mentioned, we expect the supply-demand imbalance in the compute market to continue. The current economics have translated into a less than one-year payback on our new capital deployments for compute. For example, in the first few weeks of the third quarter, we’ve already contracted an additional $6.7 billion of cloud services revenue over a six-month period that begins ramping starting in October of this year. We believe this puts us on a trajectory, including contribution from Cursor, to reach $100 billion of ARR, or annualized revenue run rate by the end of this year, based on our expected revenue in the month of December of this year.

Musk, 20 minutes later, bulldozed that carefully constructed statement before immediately inflating it:

To be clear, the $100 billion ARR in December is not a question mark. That’s… that’s what we would achieve if we basically did nothing. So like, you know, I think it may be higher than that. It probably will be higher than that.

Musk also riffed on another major prediction about overall revenue on the call, pumping up a goal that SpaceX laid out just two months ago in its IPO documents:

It’s probably also worth mentioning that our internal projections for reaching a trillion dollars in revenue, not ARR, but revenue, have moved up from 2031 to 2030. So prior to the IPO, the financial projections we had were reaching a trillion dollars in revenue in 2031. We now expect that to be in 2030. And there’s a non-zero chance of that being in 2029.

The pattern kept repeating throughout the call. A shareholder question about progress on the “human landing system” that SpaceX is developing for NASA’s Artemis moon missions using Starship prompted Musk to all but claim that the prototype rocket will be ready to fly people by the end of next year. He later said SpaceX would be flying Starship rockets once a day, or “possibly more,” by this time next year.

Shotwell immediately followed Musk’s comments about human flight to clarify that SpaceX is still focused on NASA-mandated milestones, and offered a more vague (but still ambitious) goal (again, emphasis mine) that “we want to put boots on the ground, boots on the moon, in 2028.”

None of that will happen unless SpaceX can prove that Starship can fly without failing and, crucially, become fully reusable. A huge part of making it reusable is the heat shield that keeps the Starship upper stage from exploding when it re-enters Earth’s atmosphere. The company saw the best results from its improved heat shield on the most recent Starship test flight, which splashed down in the Indian Ocean last month and is still intact. But before the rocket stage had even been recovered, Musk was willing to claim on Tuesday that he’d “consider the heat shield problem solved at this point.”

Musk has made many wild promises about SpaceX that never came true, such as when he said in 2016 that he’d put humans on Mars in six years. The difference now is that SpaceX is a public company, and ostensibly subject to regulation and fines if the company and its executives make promises they know can’t be met.

Of course, the Securities and Exchange Commission has pulled way back on corporate enforcement, especially against public companies. The Department of Justice is doing the same. And if SpaceX can’t follow through on Musk’s wide-eyed claims, investors won’t even be able to do much in civil court — because the company has all but inoculated itself against those kinds of lawsuits by incorporating in Texas.

Tech.title: Lucid’s turnaround plan hinges on $1.4B in cash savings, robotaxis
Tech.content:
Lucid Motors said Tuesday that its “operational reset” will focus on $1.4 billion in cash reductions along with three other “must win” and potential money-making priorities that include robotaxis, its factory in Saudi Arabia, and launching a mid-sized electric vehicle.

But that mid-sized vehicle, which is supposed to start at under $50,000, is now delayed until next year. It was supposed to start shipping by the end of 2026.

“Our objective is clear: Mid-size will launch only when every process and quality requirement have been met,” Lucid’s new CEO Silvio Napoli said on a conference call Tuesday. “We will not repeat the mistakes of the past by bringing a product to market before it is ready.”

The turnaround plan, led by Napoli, aims to pull Lucid out of its spiral of growing EV inventory and unchecked spending. To reach that $1.4 billion in cash savings, Lucid said it will reduce capital expenditures by $500 million and projected savings of between $600 million and $800 million in inventory, according to its second-quarter earnings statement. The company said it will also reduce operating expenses by $200 million.

The effort, if successful, will provide sufficient liquidity runway well into 2027, Napoli said during Tuesday’s earnings call with investors.

Napoli didn’t mince words during his first quarterly earnings call as CEO.

“The way we operate has to change,” he said. “While there is no question that Lucid brought leading innovations and outstanding products to the market, we have disappointed on several fronts, and for far too long. We have not executed consistently, we miss commitments, launched products before they were ready, underinvested in service, responded too slowly to quality issues, and allowed complexity to slow decisions down.”

Napoli has already set some of this plan in motion. The company has shaken up its leadership ranks and hired several top execs, including a new chief financial officer, chief technology officer, chief customer officer, chief digital officer, and chief transformation officer. Napoli has also cut in half the number of people who directly report to him and in June directed the company to lay off 18% of its workforce, or around 1,500 employees, just four months after the EV maker made a cut of 12%.

Lucid also eliminated the second shift of EV production at its factory in Casa Grande, Arizona. The layoffs and elimination of that second shift generated $158 million in projected annualized savings, Napoli said during the company’s earnings call.

Despite these moves, Lucid’s second-quarter earnings show a company that continues to lose money. The EV maker reported revenue of $405 million, up from $259.4 million in the same quarter last year. It reported a net loss of $1.26 billion, or $3.30 a share, compared with a loss of $855.3 million, or $2.80 a share, a year earlier.

Lucid said it ended the second quarter with $3 billion in total liquidity.

While a reduction in spending is central to this reset, Napoli listed several must-win projects, including its upcoming mid-sized EV, finishing its AMP-2 factory in Saudi Arabia, and its robotaxi program with Uber and Nuro, that will eventually make it profitable.

The midsize EV, known as Cosmos, will be the first model from Lucid’s mid-sized platform, which “remains an essential element of Lucid’s strategic plan,” Napoli said. But “the work ahead is substantial,” he said on the call. Napoli said Lucid has so far “not executed consistently” and “responded too slowly” to quality problems, which is why he’s delaying the vehicle.

Napoli is also bullish on its robotaxi program with Uber and Nuro and sees it as an opportunity to boost earnings outside of selling directly to consumers. In a sign of this program’s value to Lucid, the company has created a new business unit called Lucid Technologies that will be led by chief digital officer Kai Stepper. The new unit will focus on AI, an advanced driver assistance system, and digital technology.

“We project the margins vastly exceeding those of the traditional retail model,” Napoli said, referring to the robotaxi program that integrates Nuro’s self-driving technology into Lucid’s Gravity SUVs. Uber will operate the premium robotaxi service, which will allow users to hail the self-driving vehicles on its app.

Nuro and Uber are testing a fleet of 100 vehicles in Houston and the San Francisco Bay Area. The company said that last month it began delivering production validation vehicles assembled at a facility in Coolidge, Arizona. Regular vehicle production for the robotaxi will begin in the fourth quarter with an expected launch in late 2026.

On the call, Napoli also took a moment to slap down speculation from last month that the company had hired consulting firm AlixPartners to consider bankruptcy.

“Their engagement has been focused solely on supporting our cost-savings plan and streamlining our operations; we will be wrapping up their assignment once that work is complete, which we expect at the end of this month,” he said.

This story has been updated with more information from Lucid’s earnings call.
